title: Arizona Cardinals will induct Larry Fitzgerald into Ring of Honor during Denver Broncos game
summary: The Arizona Cardinals announced on Monday that the team will induct Hall of Fame wide receiver Larry Fitzgerald into the Ring of Honor on October 25th against the Denver Broncos. From the team: Congratulations to Fitz on his accomplishments.
full_text: Aug 8, 2026; Canton, OH, USA; Larry Fitzgerald poses with bust during the Pro Football Hall of Fame enshrinement at Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Arizona Cardinals announced on Monday that the team will induct Hall of Fame wide receiver Larry Fitzgerald into the Ring of Honor on October 25th against the Denver Broncos. From the team: The Arizona Cardinals Football Club today announced that the team will honor Hall of Fame wide receiver LARRY FITZGERALD at halftime of its October 25 th game vs. the Denver Broncos presented by Gila River Resorts & Casinos. In a ceremony that day, Fitzgerald will be placed in the team’s Ring of Honor and also have his jersey number (11) retired. “No one who has ever worn a Cardinals uniform is more deserving of this honor,” said Cardinals owner MICHAEL BIDWILL . “His excellence on the field was only surpassed by the way he represented our team and our community off of it. We are all grateful for the opportunity to recognize Larry in this way and for our fans to celebrate all he has meant to our franchise and the state of Arizona.” Fitzgerald will be just the sixth player in franchise history to have his number retired – joining S Larry Wilson (8), S Pat Tillman (40), T Stan Maudlin (77), TE J.V. Cain (88) and HB/DB Marshall Goldberg (99) – and the 20 th member of the Cardinals Ring of Honor. Selected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame’s Class of 2026, Fitzgerald became just the eighth wide receiver ever selected to the Hall of Fame in his first year of eligibility. He joined Raymond Berry, Lance Alworth, Paul Warfield, Steve Largent, Jerry Rice, Randy Moss and Calvin Johnson Taken by Arizona with the third overall pick in the 2004 NFL Draft, Fitzgerald spent all 17 NFL seasons (2004-20) with the Cardinals and finished his career as the franchise all-time leader in games played (263), receptions (1,432), receiving yards (17,492) and touchdowns (121). His 263 games played are the most in NFL history by a wide receiver with a single team. Fitzgerald ranks second in NFL history behind only Hall of Famer Jerry Rice in career receptions and receiving yards and sixth in career TD receptions. Rice (13) is also the only wide receiver in league history selected to more Pro Bowls than Fitzgerald (11). Below are more highlights from Fitzgerald’s historic career: An 11-time Pro Bowl selection and 2016 Walter Payton NFL Man of the Year co-recipient. Fitzgerald joins Rice (13) as the only WRs in NFL history selected to the Pro Bowl at least 11 times. Named to the NFL 100 All-Time Team and the All-Decade Team for 2010’s. Owns NFL records for the most seasons with 90+ receptions (8), most seasons with 50+ receptions (17), consecutive seasons with 50+ receptions (17), consecutive seasons with 700+ receiving yards (16), receptions with a single team (1,432), career games with 150+ receiving yards in the postseason (3), receiving yards in a single postseason (546), receiving touchdowns in a single postseason (7), 100-yard receiving performances in a single postseason (4) and is the only player in NFL history to average 100+ receiving yards and 1+ TD in every postseason game played (min. 5 games). Twice led the NFL in receptions (2005, 2016) and twice led the league in TD receptions (2008, 2009). Only player in NFL history to lead the league in receptions 11+ years apart (second-longest streak is six years by Jerry Rice). Ended his career with at least one reception in 256 consecutive games, the second-longest streak in NFL history (Rice – 274). Led the Cardinals in receiving yards 13 times. In NFL history, only Rice (15) led his team in receiving yards more times. Finished his career with more tackles (41) than dropped passes (35). Had the fewest dropped passes by any player in NFL history with at least 1,500 career targets. Had more career receptions at State Farm Stadium (669) than any other player in NFL history at a single venue. During the Cardinals run to Super Bowl XLIII following the 2008 season, had the most prolific postseason of any WR in NFL history. His records for receiving yards (546) and TD receptions (7) in a single postseason still stand. Started all nine postseason games played, totaling 57 receptions for 942 yards and 10 touchdowns. One of just nine players in NFL history with 10+ touchdown receptions in the postseason. One of just nine players in NFL history to have least five games of 100+ receiving yards and three games with 2+ touchdown receptions in the postseason. Congratulations to Fitz on his accomplishments.
author: Seth Cox

title: Update on former Cardinals QB Kyler Murray’s status with the Vikings
summary: Love him or loathe him, former Arizona Cardinals quarterback Kyler Murray will always be a part of franchise history. He is a former first overall pick and played seven seasons with the Cardinals. After Mike LaFleur was hired as the new head coach of the Cardinals after a historical 14 loss season, there were discussions […]
full_text: (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images Love him or loathe him, former Arizona Cardinals quarterback Kyler Murray will always be a part of franchise history. He is a former first overall pick and played seven seasons with the Cardinals. After Mike LaFleur was hired as the new head coach of the Cardinals after a historical 14 loss season, there were discussions immediately about the quarterback room. RELATED: BRISSETT HAS NEW DEAL. CAN HE NOW FOCUS ON THE JOB? Who to keep? Did they want a QB competition between Murray and Jacoby Brissett? Cut bait? Trade one? Release or trade both? At the time, there were several free agent options such as Aaron Rodgers and Russell Wilson. The draft was approaching, and Arizona owned the #3 overall pick, which could be traded so that they could accrue more draft picks and get the young quarterback they wanted. The decision that was made was to release Murray on March 11 and then anoint Brissett as the starter in 2026. The very next day, Murray inked a one-year deal with the Minnesota Vikings for $1.3 million, the veteran’s minimum. His won-loss record with the Cardinals was 38-48-1. He passed for 20,460 yards and tossed 121 touchdowns. He ran for 3,193 rushing yards and scored another 32 times. And now, he has been competing with former first-round draft pick J.J. McCarthy for the starting role with the Vikes. Head coach Kevin O’Connell came out and stated the QB competition could be won by either athlete. Before Tuesday’s practice, O’Connell informed the team that Murray was now the starting quarterback for the 2026 season, according to Alec Lewis of The Athletic . That didn’t take long. Minnesota has yet to play a preseason game. O’Connell told Lewis: “It’s just the appropriate time now to give our team and everybody clarity on the direction we’re taking.” The Vikings had 10 training camp practices with the lion’s share of first-team reps taken by Murray. Their team media just assumed that O’Connell and his offensive coaches had already seen what McCarthy could do and wanted to get to know their shiny new toy. LINK: VIKINGS NAME MURRAY STARTING QB OVER MCCARTHY Murray has quite a few offensive weapons at his disposal in Minnesota, with WR Justin Jefferson front and center. Jauan Jennings was signed away from the San Francisco 49ers, and T.J. Hockenson is one of the league’s best tight ends. Aaron Jones is the stud running back, and the team drafted a fullback this year by taking the draft’s #1-ranked player at that position in Max Bredeson. ESPN ranked all teams’ offensive weapons as the Cardinals were ranked #6. So, if Murray had remained in the desert, he would have had plenty of offensive help. But the Vikings ranked #8, which means he is on a really good offensive unit. View Link The Vikings see Murray as the answer to their most important position. O’Connell added: “As he knows, he’s holding the pen on his story, and we’re going to support him and try to help him continue to improve as a young player at the most difficult position in sports.” Although on a one-year deal, if Murray plays well and remains vertical, a new contract will certainly be announced sometime in December to keep him in-house for the long run. Their offense is predicated on a running quarterback and shorter passing plays with heavy tight end usage. The coaching staff has already fused formations and concepts that suit what Murray does best. The other quarterbacks on the roster besides Murray and McCarthy are Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer. Most NFL clubs will retain three signalcallers on their main roster and at least one on the practice squad.
author: Barry Shuck

title: What was your biggest takeaway from the Arizona Cardinals preseason opener?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Cardinals fans and fans across the country. title: Cardinals Red/White practice: How is the team shaping out?
summary: The Arizona Cardinals are working diligently to get ready for the remainder of the preseason lineup. These three exhibition games will give the coaching staff definitive answers on which players to retain on the final 53-man roster. For now, it is just battle after battle for not only roster spots, but positions on the depth […]
full_text: Cardinals OG Isaiah Adams (74) with OT Christian Jones (75) | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Arizona Cardinals are working diligently to get ready for the remainder of the preseason lineup. These three exhibition games will give the coaching staff definitive answers on which players to retain on the final 53-man roster. For now, it is just battle after battle for not only roster spots, but positions on the depth chart. RELATED: PREDICTING FINAL ROSTER AFTER HOF GAME On Sunday, the Cardinals held their annual Red/White practice, open to the public, at State Farm Stadium in Glendale. Thousands of fans filled the lower bowl. Included was a Kids Interactive Zone on the Red Zone Bridge. Let’s start with the quarterback room. Jacoby Brissett, despite missing all of that time in the spring, is the obvious starting candidate. While we all saw how accurate rookie Carson Beck was on long throws in the Hall of Fame Game, Brissett is struggling with the deep ball. He had 7-8 deep balls that were either too far or too much to the side from his intended receiver. Most were to Marv Harrison. The pair did stay after practice and worked on this. What’s unusual about this is that Brissett has been nailing his deep passes with good accuracy. But not today. Carson Beck with a dot deep down the right sideline. Followed by a NO-LOOK pass for six. pic.twitter.com/xg8SsXBymE — Donnie Druin (@DonnieDruin) August 10, 2026 Beck continues to impress. He had some great ball placements but did have a pick. In the two-minute drill, he was definitely in charge and had a no-look pass for a touchdown, which made the crowd happy with loud applause. He hit fellow rookie WR Reggie Virgil for a touchdown in the back of the end zone that was laid in perfectly. Virgil looks really good, and then will make a dumb rookie mistake, so the learning curve is still there. Jaylen Brooks looks like a keeper. He picked up right where he left off from the HOF Game and has proven to be a tough kid. He is fearless going across the middle. Gardner Minshew continues to step in with the first team and has shown consistency with a good touch on the intermediate throws. He appears comfortable running this offense and right now is penciled in as QB2. It is obvious this coaching staff wants Brissett to run this offense, but Minshew shows an eagerness to step in or step up. With the running back room, it is looking more and more like Tyler Allgeier is standing in the starting role with rookie Jeremiyah Love as his backup. However, in Madden 27, Love is a beast, especially in the passing aspect. Allgeier looks great when he is looking for a gap and will hit the hole hard, but he does not have good hands while trying to catch balls. He will catch two, then drop a pair – once he was wide open. Somebody better stick him in the receiver room quickly for tutelage because both Love and James Conner can make a difference in the passing game. This offense requires backs who are involved in the short passing game. Each practice, it seems more likely that Trey Benson might become the odd man out. He did not suit up for this practice. Bam Knight spent the majority of practice as a kickoff returner. It is speculated that if he is assigned this duty, then he can make the final roster as a kickoff returner and a third-down back. Love looks great at everything he does. He has great cutting ability with extremely good hands in the short game. He is getting his fair share of first-team reps, which is good if Allgeier can’t learn to catch passes. Soon. Most likely, come time for the real games, Love will see plenty of live snaps. When the herd arrives, you don’t keep your prize bull locked up. In the 1-on-1 drills, TE Trey McBride beat S Budda Baker in the right corner of the end zone with a soft, accurate throw by Brissett. McBride earlier had a false start called on him. I LOVE THIS CATCH FROM MARVIN HARRISON JR #PMSLive https://t.co/wLx1zZX78C pic.twitter.com/7LmlMZ81R1 — Pat McAfee (@PatMcAfeeShow) August 10, 2026 Harrison has had a great camp, but today he was targeted but just couldn’t haul in any passes. A good number of passes sent his way weren’t catchable. Ihmir Smith-Marsette has shown quite a bit of talent and has flashes. He had two nice plays and could become yet another weapon on this offense. He continues to impress. However, he has got to find a way to stay on the field, and the receiver room is chock-full of talent this year. Another receiver who everyone is watching is Bryson Green. He grabbed several balls that had him extend his entire length. The rookie Virgil continues to impress. Kendrick Bourne is quietly showing why the team hustled after him in free agency. The most impossible decisions with this coaching staff will be which six receivers to keep. They could easily retain eight guys, and in probability, they will want at least eight. This team is going to cut some good talent in the receiver room. Virgil, Green, Smith-Marsette, Bourne, and Brooks are all looking like good players. Isaiah Adams is still the leading man for the right guard position. That became obvious in the Hall of Fame Game when Arizona trotted out its entire second-string offense, and rookie Chase Bisontis started with that unit. The two are still handling first-team reps, but Adams is getting the most. In the Cardinals’ first official depth chart, he is listed as the starter and Oli Udoh at RG3. Bisontis does look more and more comfortable with each practice and gets off on the snap count every time. Let’s go ahead and state this right now. The Cardinals have a new offense that will eventually become successful, just like the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers. This year’s roster has great talent at receiver, running back, and the league’s best tight end. However, all of this will be lost if the offensive line does not gel and become a cohesive group. In most practices, they look lost and are not working as a complete unit. The fact that there are three new players will justify why this is taking so long. And the amount of pre-snap penalties is staggering. An expensive and great-looking rim is nothing mounted to a tire that can’t hold air. As shown during the HOF Game, the second-team offensive line group seems to be playing well while the starters are having issues. Pre-snap penalties are an everyday affair with this group. Holding is another problem. LG Isaac Seumalo will look great on one play, then lost on another. He hasn’t started melding with C Hjalte Froholdt quite yet. That needs to be consistent, as the bond between a center and guard is critical. The official depth chart lists Elijah Wilkinson as the starting RT, but his backup, Josh Fryar, isn’t far behind. This will continue to be a position battle. Fryar looked really good in the HOF Game with only one penalty and zero sacks allowed. One player who is standing out is DE Darius Robinson. Most have written him off, and some of the media have stated they thought this might be the last Cardinals training camp for him. But he is balling and having a strong camp. Which spells “hooray!” to all Arizona fans. A pass rusher opposite Josh Sweat is sorely needed. He is showing both speed and power and has gotten into the offensive backfield frequently with an unofficial two sacks today. Not sure what this means, but LB Eku Leota, CB Elijah Jones, and S Kitan Crawford all were featured with the first-team defense. We know the defensive backfield is the strongest and deepest group on the roster, but seeing these three, who appeared to wrap up spots on the second team, was a different wrinkle. But then news came that S Joey Blount was placed on IR and Kei’Trel Clark did not suit up, so everyone was elevated. Leota is looking really good and is fighting to not only make this final roster, but he could be a special teams guru and get plenty of defensive snaps. Right now, he is considered a bubble player and needs to stand out in preseason games. LB Cody Simon is having a…

title: Falcons training camp 2026: News, updates, injuries and more from Day 11
summary: After practicing in the afternoon on Monday, Aug. 10th, the Falcons were back to early morning practice on Tuesday. Players were in pads and ready for full contact, and it was extremely hot. Atlanta executed a number of roster moves between yesterday’s practice and today’s. Let’s review: The newest Falcons were at practice today and […]
full_text: FLOWERY BRANCH, GEORGIA - JULY 29: Head coach Kevin Stefanski of the Atlanta Falcons speaks during training camp at IBM Performance Field on July 29, 2026 in Flowery Branch, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images After practicing in the afternoon on Monday, Aug. 10th, the Falcons were back to early morning practice on Tuesday. Players were in pads and ready for full contact, and it was extremely hot. Atlanta executed a number of roster moves between yesterday’s practice and today’s. Let’s review: Activated OL Jawaan Taylor off PUP Signed DE Cam Sample Waived LS Phillip Florenzo, waived-injured OL Jack Nelson Signed RB Trey Sermon Signed TE Trey Muse Waived/injured WR Le’Meke Brockington and LB Malik Verdon The newest Falcons were at practice today and got some reps, but there’s not much to report about them at this point. Still getting up to speed. Stefanski did not speak to the media at all today, so we did not get an update on how limited any of the injured players may be right now or what their timetables to return look like. Stefanski will speak before tomorrow’s practice. You can find my reporting from today here: Notes and quotes from Tuesday: Jessie Bates, D’Sean Hand, Divine Deablo and Avieon Terrell were held entirely out of practice, and Drake London did some individual drills but didn’t participate in 7-on-7s or 11-on-11s. Jawaan Taylor got some action but was very limited as they work to bring him up to speed. I don’t think that’s a complete list of which players didn’t practice, but they’re the ones I visually confirmed. Michael Penix Jr. was fully dressed and padded up for practice but was limited. He looked decent though and was moving around fine. Had some nice throws to Jahan Dotson and Olamide Zaccheaus. Tua’s taking most of the first-team snaps right now and he was on fire today. He went 7 of 7 in 11 on 11s today, with completions to Kyle Pitts, Jahan Dotson, Chris Blair, Olamide Zaccheaus, and I may have missed a couple. Right now, in my opinion and to nobody’s surprise, the depth chart currently appears to be Tua Tagovailoa, Michael Penix Jr. (when healthy), Cooper Rush and then Jack Strand. Strand still has upside and I’ve been impressed with how he’s adapted to the speed of the game coming out of such a small program. I wouldn’t hate seeing him land on Atlanta’s practice squad. Ethan Onianwa, the rookie out of The Ohio State University, is getting plenty of run with the 1s. He and Michael Jerrell also stacked up on the right side of the line for a jumbo package. Onianwa is one to keep an eye on. Speaking of Ohio State, DE Zach Harrison was back in 11-on-11s today. And speaking of young players to keep an eye on, Darnay Holmes spent some time in the nickel with the 1s today. FloridaFalconFan asked me today if CJ Henderson was getting any action. Today on the field with the second-team defense, he put such tight coverage on Cooper Rush’s intended receiver (forgot to write the number down) that the play went nowhere. Both Harold Perkins and Kendal Daniels ran with the first team with Deablo out, and Daniels had the green dot today. This is a relief after Perkins left practice for a bit yesterday to be examined by trainers, but clearly he’s OK. After practice, Tua spoke to the media. On what he expects in terms of playing time in the preseason, Tagovailoa said he will do whatever the team asks him to do. Stefanski said during the first week of camp (I think) that he does think it’s important for starters to get some snaps in preseason to prepare for full-speed contact Week 1. He also said he expects the starters to get a bunch of work in next week’s joint practices, so I’m eager to see what that looks like. Tomorrow, the Falcons will practice in the afternoon, and Stefanski will speak before practice, while Penix Jr. will address the media after practice. As always, I’ll have my reporting in the Feed and we’ll have details for you right here on The Falcoholic.

full_text: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Falcons fans and fans across the country. The regular season hasn’t started yet Kevin Stefanski and Ian Cunningham find themselves managing their first crisis. While expectations aren’t particularly high in Atlanta, the idea of a team that hasn’t made the playoffs since 2017 not being competitive in the league’s worst division is indefensible to fans. They will need to work with Jeff Ulbrich to find an ideal solution to try to replace Jalon Walker’s production. The recent signing of Cameron Sample isn’t necessarily that, but he could be a decent rotational piece if he makes the team. Fans will ponder which veteran pass rusher on the market could be signed. No matter who gets added, rotational players on the roster have to be ready for greater roles. Zach Harrison has shown flashes as a versatile defensive lineman. Bralen Trice has stood out in training camp as a player ready to take on an expanded role. Samson Ebukam and Azeez Ojulari are players who had their moments as rotational edge rushers. Those are the likely four pass rushers on the roster who will get the most opportunities, as James Pearce Jr. will likely serve a lengthy suspension. title: Finding the Top 10 Falcons in Bleacher Report’s 1000-player NFL Rankings
summary: Before we start this exercise, close your eyes…well, read this first, and then close your eyes. Who are your top ten players for the Atlanta Falcons right now? Obviously, there’s the trio of Bijan Robinson, Kyle Pitts, and Drake London that should be locks, but who else makes the cut? Jessie Bates is a lock […]
full_text: Before we start this exercise, close your eyes…well, read this first, and then close your eyes. Who are your top ten players for the Atlanta Falcons right now? Obviously, there’s the trio of Bijan Robinson, Kyle Pitts, and Drake London that should be locks, but who else makes the cut? Jessie Bates is a lock as well, but there’s not a lot of room left for some pretty good players that don the red and black right now. Xavier Watts and A.J. Terrell were both recognized as the top 99 defensive players . That’s already six slots looked to be taken up. Who is going to fill those last four as we find the top ten Falcons in Bleacher Report’s 1000-player NFL ranking ? Let us know in the comments if you think Bleacher Report got it right, and if they didn’t, who should be recognized as a top ten Falcon right now. Bijan Robinson, RB, Grade: 94, Rank: 6, Tier: Franchise Cornerstones Bijan Robinson is one of the best running backs in the NFL. He is the engine and best player on the Atlanta Falcons offense. Robinson is a natural, elite ball carrier with a strong impact in the passing game as a receiver. He accounted for 2,298 yards from scrimmage and 11 total touchdowns. Robinson is a game-changing player who elevates the offense. His vision, elusiveness, stop/start ability, and burst make him one of the most difficult offensive weapons to defend in the league. Robinson’s pass protection is an issue. He allowed over 10 pressures and three sacks last season. He prefers to lunge or throw a shoulder at incoming defenders. Robinson’s pass-protection technique must improve. 94 seconds of Bijan Robinson on zone runs against the Saints pic.twitter.com/4BB79CZNN7 — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) November 27, 2023 Jessie Bates, S, Grade: 91, Rank: 25, Tier: All-Pro Ability Jesse Bates sees things before they happen and shows up exactly where he needs to be to make the play. It’s like watching Mysterio fighting Spider-Man, always appearing in places the quarterback doesn’t want him to be and taking the ball away. Bates is one of the prominent ball-hawks in today’s game, and he seamlessly rotates all around the back end, handling a ton of mental responsibilities. He played closer to the line of scrimmage last season than ever before and played fast, took away underneath routes, and helped condense the offense. A continually impressive player continues an impressive career. Jessie Bates picks off Daniel Jones before the half! ATLvsIND on @NFLNetwork Also streaming on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/MRMc6htH15 — NFL (@NFL) November 9, 2025 Drake London, WR, Grade: 85, Rank: 71, Tier: Pro-Bowl Caliber Drake London is one of the league’s better young wide receivers. He has never played with a top-shelf quarterback in the NFL during his career, yet he consistently puts up good numbers. He’s held back by that uncertainty with the Falcons quarterback situation. London is an uber-efficient route-runner with strong footwork and use of hands to fend off bump-and-run coverage. He’s the prototypical X-receiver, but he plays all over the formation, forcing advantageous matchups. London isn’t in the elite tier of No. 1 receivers in the league, but with better quarterback play, he will enter the conversation. Michael Penix Jr. 🚀 to Drake London pic.twitter.com/aL9ArAQMaU — Nick Penticoff (@NickPenticoff) September 28, 2025 Kyle Pitts, TE, Grade: 81, Rank: 112, Tier: High-Quality Starter Kyle Pitts had some truly lofty expectations to live up to coming out of Florida, and 2025 was an offensive explosion for the fifth-year tight end. He set career highs in targets, receptions, and touchdowns while playing over 200 snaps more than any previous year of his career. Pitts showed growth in nuance in route running, using more speed dilation and deception to get into space while still showcasing his top-tier athletic ability after the catch. He’s a true three-level weapon, and the Falcons use him as such to maximize their passing attack. While Pitts isn’t a game-changer as a run blocker and doesn’t show the effort all the time, his power at the point of attack has improved, and on the move, he can be useful. But he’s out there for one reason: to be a match-up problem. Kyle Pitts Sr. 11 REC, 166 YDS, 3 TDs vs TB Tonight. HAVE A NIGHT KYLE PITTS. pic.twitter.com/l2ZAHeFwQx https://t.co/nesfyquOpL — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) December 12, 2025 A.J. Terrell, CB, Grade: 81, Rank: 121, Tier: High-Quality Starter One of the more underrated corners in the NFL, AJ Terrell is a technician on the outside who forced tight-window throws at the fourth-highest rate in the league last season. He mirrors well, attacks the catch point consistently, and is a willing and able run supporter. Bigger route-runners with a good catch radius take advantage of the space he gives them in off coverage, but he closes and uses leverage well. He doesn’t create a ton of turnovers, but still gets his hands on the football a lot. A.J. Terrell Jr. (24) with a clinic "Search" technique in Weak Rotation Cover 3 for the Falcons. The Bills run a Mesh concept with 3 verticals to the front side. For Buffalo, the goal is to get Terrell to either chase the shallow or "hang" with vision, looking for another… pic.twitter.com/Puc1wkRkEA — Cody Alexander (@The_Coach_A) June 25, 2026 Xavier Watts, S, Grade: 81, Rank: 124, Tier: High-Quality Starter Xavier Watts deserved a stronger push for Defensive Rookie of the Year in 2025. He makes up half of the best safety duo in the league with Jessie Bates, allowed Bates to roam closer to the line of scrimmage, and helped unlock the defense and create turnovers. Watts had five interceptions and 11 passes broken up as a rookie, was a plus run defender from depth, and, while there were some lapses, he showed the ability to recover not just physically but also mentally. He didn’t look like a rookie out there; he handled more rotations, living on top of the defense, and the NFL stage like he was meant to be there. Rookie Xavier Watts highlights He really fell to the 96th pick LOL pic.twitter.com/d7I5Z14gSg — NFL Draft Files (@NFL_DF) July 24, 2026 Chris Lindstrom, G, Grade: 76, Rank: 237, Tier: Critical Roster Piece Lindstrom remained one of the league’s most durable and dangerous run-blocking guards in 2025, but Atlanta’s schematic shift over the last two seasons made his pass-protection limitations more visible. With the Falcons using far less play-action and exposing the line to more true dropback reps, Lindstrom’s lighter frame and tardier anchor were stressed more often against high-end power. He remains an elite zone run-blocker, winning with rare quickness, leverage, leg drive and strain to reach landmarks, steer defenders and finish at angles most guards cannot access. The contrast is in pass protection, where his profile carries more variance. Lindstrom relies heavily on jump-sets and first meaningful contact to erase rushers’ runway before they can build force, a strategy that is more forgiving off play-action than in static dropback situations. When he lands first, he can still close space and end reps quickly. When he misses or is forced to absorb power late, the losses can be immediate. In the right structure, Lindstrom’s pass protection can play a tier higher, but his current profile is driven by elite run-game value and capped by the volatility of his true pass sets. Chris Lindstrom was going to work on the frontside of these zone runs on Sunday. Bijan is incredible, but Lindstrom was playing really well too pic.twitter.com/wqxzE0kXsp — JP Acosta (@acosta32_jp) September 29, 2025 Divine Deablo, LB, Grade: 73, Rank: 354, Tier: Reliable Contributor After flaming out in Las Vegas, Deablo signed with Atlanta last offseason and had a career year. One discernible difference in his play was his instincts against the run, as the former Raider was constantly in the right spot to make tackles for short gains with the Falcons. Also, the college safety finally put it together in coverage on the second…

full_text: Jul 29, 2026; Ownings Mills, MD, USA; Baltimore Ravens cornerback Nate Wiggins (2) stretches during practice at the Under Armour Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Mitch Stringer-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect 5:29 p.m. ET: Wiggins sustained “no structural damage” as a result of his injury on Tuesday, per NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport. No structural damage for Wiggins. Good news for Baltimore. https://t.co/K9GzVSbjfc — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) August 11, 2026 Baltimore Ravens cornerback Nate Wiggins was carted off the practice field at training camp on Tuesday after appearing to injure his left leg. Wiggins went down after a 1-on-1 rep against rookie wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane. Both players were sprinting down the left sideline for a deep pass from Lamar Jackson with Wiggins going to the ground after the ball fell incomplete. He looked to be in considerable pain as team trainers rushed over with the cart following shortly after. He could not put much, if any, weight on his left leg as he went inside the Ravens’ facility. Head coach Jesse Minter did not offer any details regarding the nature or severity of the injury after practice, but expressed “optimism” regarding Wiggins and “a lot of confidence” in the rest of the team’s cornerback room. Wiggins, 22, revealed this offseason that he did not feel 100% during his first two NFL seasons. The 2024 first-round pick underwent groin surgery a few months ago and said last week that he was “feeling the best I have ever felt.” This is a breaking story that will be updated with more information.

title: Takeaways from Buffalo Bills first depth chart before first preseason game
summary: The Buffalo Bills host the Carolina Panthers on Saturday, August 15 for the first preseason game inside the new Highmark Stadium, and now that the team is well into its week of preparation, they’ve released the first depth chart of the summer. Remember, this depth chart isn’t necessarily directly from the coaching staff. And there’s […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 12: Joe Andreessen #44 of the Buffalo Bills warms up prior to playing the Denver Broncos during the AFC Wild Card Playoffs at Highmark Stadium on January 12, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills host the Carolina Panthers on Saturday, August 15 for the first preseason game inside the new Highmark Stadium, and now that the team is well into its week of preparation, they’ve released the first depth chart of the summer. Remember, this depth chart isn’t necessarily directly from the coaching staff. And there’s nothing truly official about it. However, it does give some indication of where specific players are in positional battles. Takeaways from Bills first depth chart Alec Anderson with the early nod over Austin Corbett for the starting left guard role. This is mostly as expected, as Anderson took most of the initial reps with the first-team offense at training camp. This is one battle I don’t believe has much chance to change ahead of Week 1 against the Texans. Despite the spectacular summer from Kaleb Elarms-Orr , he’s still listed behind incumbent starters Dorian Williams and Terrel Bernard at inside linebacker. I’d assume with a few plays made this August, and serious conversations will be had about how to get him onto the field, if they haven’t started already. Nice to see 2025 second-round pick T.J. Sanders in a starting defensive line role. While there’s not much hitting in camp, Sanders had a strong summer in Pittsford. If he emerges in Year 2, it’d go a long way in stabilizing the Bills new defensive front. Kyle Allen still ahead of Shane Buechele despite a seemingly close battle for QB2 this summer. This one is likely to be settled on the field in the preseason. Undrafted rookie Kani Walker finds himself as either the CB3 or CB4 — on the boundary — right now, which is a testament to the steady albeit unspectacular camp the longer defensive back had. Jalon Kilgore listed with the third team is surprising, given how frequently he made plays at camp, and how much of the Bills staff raved about his play at St. John Fisher University in a variety of roles. Another surprise — Joe Andreessen ahead of Keonta Jenkins at inside linebacker. It’s not that Jenkins thoroughly outplayed Buffalo Joe at camp, it’s just that Jenkins took more snaps with the second team throughout the Bills time in Rochester. What stands out to you about this first released depth chart?

title: In defense of the O’Cyrus Torrence extension
summary: The mood about Bills Mafia has changed in the last year or so. Buffalo Bills General Manager Brandon Beane has been under a much higher level of scrutiny by fans of the team as the “talent versus coaching” debate began to rage through both social media and water coolers. Bills owner Terry Pegula came down […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FL - NOVEMBER 09: Buffalo Bills guard O'Cyrus Torrence (64) looks on during the game between the Miami Dolphins and the Buffalo Bills on November 9, 2025 at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The mood about Bills Mafia has changed in the last year or so. Buffalo Bills General Manager Brandon Beane has been under a much higher level of scrutiny by fans of the team as the “talent versus coaching” debate began to rage through both social media and water coolers. Bills owner Terry Pegula came down definitively on the side of coaching being the main issue keeping the team from getting to the Super Bowl when he fired former head coach Sean McDermott, and clearly reinforced that opinion during his press conference discussing the dismissal. But not everybody believes it was clearly one and not the other, and that lingering sliver of blame, however large it is in someone’s mind, has led to Beane’s historic approach to contracts to come under fire. This turn showed up again after the Bills announced a four-year, $78.4 million extension with right guard O’Cyrus Torrence. There were questions about how good Torrence is, how proper and ideal resource allocation should look for a limited resource environment, and the Bills’ cap tightness over the last few years along with its most direct cause. One of the benefits to having been both critical and complimentary of Brandon Beane’s maneuvers over the past almost-decade (there’s a Buffalo Rumblings article out there encouraging Beane to not extend former defensive tackle Jordan Phillips that attracted the attention of the lineman himself on social media) is that I don’t really have to worry about people automatically assuming that I will like the Torrence extension because I like everything the team does or that I will hate the Torrence extension because I hate everything the team does. I will admit, however, that I was a little surprised by the general tone (insert salute here) surrounding the guard’s new contract. I’m in favor; let me explain why: I don’t believe that teams should extend “mid” players regardless of circumstance, but I don’t think Torrence is a “mid player” The argument against a team extending an average or replacement-level player is a simple one: the probability of you finding a similar level of player in the draft for a markedly cheaper cap number in both the short and medium term is very high. The current going rate for reasonable #2 blocking tight ends is $5m – $10m in average annual contract value (AAV). Teams are picking up on this market inefficiency as well, pushing tight ends like Ohio State’s Will Kacmarek (who never had more than 11 catches in a college football season) into round two of the 2026 NFL Draft. Kacmarek’s total four-year contract value is $6.849 million. The more expensive a position gets, the more significant the value proposition is of drafting that position. This is where the addage “the greatest value in sports is a star quarterback on a rookie contract” comes from. The same logic applies to skill as it does to position. There’s a significant value proposition delta between paying an average-level player $8m AAV versus $1.4m, and if I’m confident that I can get an average-level player in the draft, I should do that and save that money in a limited resource environment for a star-level player that I am less confident I could replace in the draft. I don’t think O’Cyrus Torrence is a star player. I’m not sure who studies offensive line play would argue he is either. Bleacher Rerport’s Brandon Thorn, an expert in offensive line play across the league, recently released his offensive lineman rankings for the 2026 NFL season and had Torrence with a grade of 70, which qualitatively titles him as a “reliable contributor” and places him in the top 73 offensive linemen in the league and the 11st best right guard. Of the Bills newly-minted lineman, Thorn wrote: Torrence is a durable and massive right guard with huge hands, good play-strength and a firm anchor. His width and stiff punch make him difficult for power-rushers to work through, and his snatch-trap technique gives him a reliable answer to steal leverage in pass protection. As a run-blocker, Torrence is a sturdy presence that bumps down linemen on double-team feeds, collects movement across his face and uses a nifty jump-hook technique to reach frontside shades. Buffalo’s progressively run-heavier structure has helped maximize his strengths while masking middling movement skills and below-average recovery when pulled out of position. Torrence is not a dynamic mover, but his size, anchor, strength and improving craft have settled him into solid starter territory. Nothing in Thorn’s write-up should have anyone who’s watched Torrence extensively confused, and the classification of him as both a “solid starter” and “reliable contributor” completely tracks. I have nothing further to add about qualitative aspect of Torrence’s play that was not outlined above. The Torrence contract is not an overpay relative to the market for players of his valuation Just shy of 18 months ago, the Bills extended another player on the offense I would consider to be both a “solid starter” and “reliable contributor” in wide receiver Khalil Shakir. In present day, that contract ranks Shakir 33rd in the NFL among wide receivers in practical guaranteed money, per Spotrac. The recent contracts of Rashod Bateman, Romeo Doubs, Rashid Shaheed, and Wan’Dale Robinson (Baltimore Ravens, New England Patriots, Seattle Seahawks, and Tennessee Titans, respectively) have affirmed Shakir’s standing in the pecking order of contracts in the same way that the Matthew Bergeron contract with the Atlanta Falcons, the Aaron Banks contract with the Green Bay Packers, and the Robert Hunt contract with the Carolina Panthers have helped properly frame the O’Cyrus Torrence deal. None of these deals was an outlier or even a market-setter; they were simply good deals given to good players. For reference, Bergeron/Banks/Hunt were given 61/62/65 grades from Thorn in his project noted above. I agree that there is an “optimal” resource allocation, but we don’t live in an optimal environment If there’s one thing I love to talk about it, it’s optimization. Tweaking and tuning aspects of a team’s budget/depth chart when examining market inefficiencies and opportunities for added value can be what separates a good GM from a great one. And in a previously-mentioned limited resource environment, everything has opportunity cost. Every dollar of salary cap allocated to player X is one dollar that can’t be allocated to player Y. The cap is flexible, but it’s still finite. And so the phenomenon of the Bills having four of their five offensive line starters signed to meaningful non-rookie contracts begs the question: is this the best usage of the team’s limited cap dollars? In the NFL Draft, one of the items that consistently gets brought of is one of positional value. Whether it’s a top ten pick on a running back, a top five pick on a safety, or a day two selection on a specialist, the question of resource allocation and opportunity cost inevitably comes up. Those conversations have value, whatever the line is that someone draws. Everybody will admit that taking a punter in round one is a bad value proposition and a massive opportunity cost, regardless of how good the punter is. That means there is a line, no matter where it’s drawn for people. At some point, the value proposition of a maneuver becomes bad enough to make us think that the move is a bad one. Why is this situation any different? The draft situation revolves around the idea that there’s another clear choice. If you don’t take Bob Smith (the safety) at No. 6 overall due to your perception of resource allocation and positional value, you still have another player you can take at a higher value position at No. 6…

full_text: On Monday, the Buffalo Bills held their first training camp practice at the team’s facilities since leaving St. John Fisher University late last week. On a day where rain and lightning once again hovered over the practice, the Bills conducted their drills inside the Kaleida Health Performance Center. Today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off with the latest news and observations from camp, including how defensive lineman Ed Oliver was all over the field, consistently disrupting Josh Allen and the Bills offense. Oliver dominates, injuries mount during Monday’s practice session With the Bills back in pads on Monday, Ed Oliver enjoyed a tremendous performance during the 11-on-11 sessions, posting “at least two sacks” while proving “impossible to guard,” according to Matt Parrino of newyorkupstate.com . What else stood out to Bills beat reporters from Day 8 of camp? Injuries are beginning to add up, especially in the secondary, where several starters missed practice, including safety Cole Bishop and cornerback Maxwell Hairston. Running back Ty Johnson, wide receiver Skyler Bell, defensive tackle Zane Durant, and punter Mitch Wishnowsky were among the other Bills to sit out the session. Then, once practice began, starting safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson, who had previously sat out two practices with a strained right calf, left practice early after breaking up a pass in the end zone. With several defensive backs sidelined, Dee Alford and Jordan Hancock showcased their skills while playing with the first-team defense; embattled wide receiver Keon Coleman flashed his skills as a threat in the red zone; and Lloyd Cushenberry fared well filling in for the injured Connor McGovern at center. title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: inside linebacker Terrel Bernard
summary: The Buffalo Bills dealt with a litany of injuries during the 2025 NFL season. The defense, in particular, was ravaged by injury, especially at the end of the season. In the team’s final game, there were too many plays made by players who hadn’t begun the year with the Bills, and ultimately, those plays stuck […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - DECEMBER 21: Terrel Bernard #8 of the Buffalo Bills waits for the snap during the fourth quarter against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on December 21, 2025 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Buffalo Bills dealt with a litany of injuries during the 2025 NFL season. The defense, in particular, was ravaged by injury, especially at the end of the season. In the team’s final game, there were too many plays made by players who hadn’t begun the year with the Bills, and ultimately, those plays stuck out like a sore thumb in what was a close 33-30 loss. Injuries are the norm, not the exception, in the NFL, so it’s something that every team has to prepare for throughout a season. Keeping starters healthy is always of paramount importance, but sometimes, those injuries are just unavoidable. In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss the captain of Buffalo’s defense, a player who has been injured a whole lot over the last two seasons. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Terrel Bernard Number: 8 Position: ILB Height/Weight: 6’1” 224 lbs. Age: 27 (28 on 5/8/2026) Experience/Draft: 5; selected by Buffalo in the third round (No. 89 overall) of the 2022 NFL Draft) College: Baylor Acquired: Third-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Bernard enters the first year of the four-year, $42.13 million extension he signed last March. For this season, his cap hit is $5.352 million. If Buffalo were to release him, they would carry a dead cap charge of $20.012 million this year. 2025 Recap: Bernard had a rough go of it from the start, as a pulled hamstring in training camp limited his ramp-up for the regular season and served as a harbinger of things to come. He played in Buffalo’s first six games, totaling 30 tackles, an interception, a pass breakup, three tackles for loss, and two fumble recoveries; however, he suffered an ankle injury in that Week Six loss to the Atlanta Falcons. While he missed just one game due to that injury, its effects lingered throughout the rest of the season. Bernard suffered an elbow injury in Buffalo’s loss at the Houston Texans in Week 12, which caused him to miss the next three games. He returned before the end of the regular season, but a calf injury suffered in Week Seventeen against the Philadelphia Eagles ended Bernard’s season, as he did not return for either of Buffalo’s postseason games. Despite playing in only 12 games and dealing with injury for many of them, he was fourth on the team in tackles with 65. He had seven tackles for loss, three pass breakups, one interception, two fumble recoveries, and two quarterback hits. Positional outlook: Bernard is one of eight players listed at inside linebacker on the current roster. Joe Andreessen, Dorian Williams, Keonta Jenkins, Jimmy Ciarlo, Theron Gaines, and Otis Reese IV are healthy. Veteran Demetrius Flannigan-Fowles is on injured reserve. Rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr is listed at linebacker, but he plays ILB. 2026 Offseason: Bernard had surgery to address his ankle issues, but he is completely healthy and participating in training camp practices. 2026 Season outlook: This season is a big one for Bernard, who thrived under former head coach Sean McDermott’s system. Injuries were really the only thing holding him back—that is, unless you consider his smaller stature to be part of the reason for said injuries—and when he was healthy, he was a consistent presence around the ball for the Bills on defense. With new defensive boss Jim Leonhard in town, Bernard has some new responsibilities. How will he perform in a new defense? At the most basic level, Bernard is a football player, and a good one at that. This change in system could help him, especially if there is more “attack” and less “read and react” in his role. Bernard didn’t earn his big extension by accident, and he didn’t earn the “C” on his chest by mistake, either. If he’s fully healthy, and that’s a big “if” given his checkered injury history, the Bills’ defense is going to be better because of it. Whether he’s paired with Dorian Williams or Kaleb Elarms-Orr in the middle, or even if someone else steps up and earns time, the Bills and their new defensive boss definitely want Bernard available and at his best. The question for Bernard isn’t whether he’ll make the roster, or even whether he’s going to start or what role he’s going to play. The real question is whether No. 8 can hold up and remain available for all 17 regular season games and beyond.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 33 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - JANUARY 10: Derrick Brown #95 of the Carolina Panthers looks on prior to the NFC Wild Card Playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Bank of America Stadium on January 10, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #33. Derrick Brown Derrick Brown is the second highest ranked current Panther on our list, coming in at No. 33, and for good reason. The 6’5”, 320 pounder out of Auburn was the rare defensive tackle taken in the top ten of the NFL Draft. The Panthers took Brown seventh overall in the 2020 draft. While he started off his rookie year a little slow statistically speaking, he really started to blossom in his second season especially against the run. 2022 saw his explosion into the conversation of “best defensive tackles in the league” as he logged 67 tackles and was graded as the eighth best defensive tackle in the league per PFF. The following season, Brown started to really gain national notoriety due to an historic statistical season. He set a new NFL record for tackles by an interior lineman with 103 stops. He posted a PFF rating of 90.1, placing him in the “elite” category (fourth overall at his position) and earning him a Pro Bowl nod. That offseason, he signed a well-deserved massive four-year, $96 million contract extension, cementing him as a defensive leader and anchor for years to come. Unfortunately for Brown and the rest of the Panthers defense, he only played one game in 2024, tearing his meniscus on ending up on IR the first week of the regular season. He returned to his stellar play in 2025, notching 73 tackles and a career high five sacks. If anyone ever doubted Derrick Brown’s impact on the Panthers, consider this: the Panthers gave up 2,096 rushing yards in 2023 and 2,081 rushing yards in 2025 with Derrick Brown in the lineup. In the 2024 season without Derrick Brown, the team allowed 3,057 rushing yards. That’s over 1,000 rushing yards difference between having Brown and not having him. While the Panthers are known for their elite linebackers since their inception, they haven’t done too bad at defensive tackle either: KK Short, Star Lotulelei, Kris Jenkins, and now Derrick Brown. Off the field, Brown is a vocal leader, unafraid to hold himself and/or teammates accountable for practice and study habits. For his on-field excellence and off-field leadership, he already lands at No. 33. I am excited to see where he finally ends up in Panthers lore as he continues his stellar career.

title: Chicago Bears have their most physical practice yet
summary: After a low-impact walk-through practice at Stevenson High School yesterday, the Chicago Bears were back at Halas Hall for what head coach Ben Johnson called a “big time practice” today. full_text: Aug 5, 2026; Lake Forest, IL, USA; Chicago Bears linebacker T.J. Edwards (53) walks on the field during training camp at Halas Hall. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect After a low-impact walk-through practice at Stevenson High School yesterday, the Chicago Bears were back at Halas Hall for what head coach Ben Johnson called a “big time practice” today. The plan was to simulate the pregame for all the new guys and have plenty of live scrimmage situations, starting with some short-yardage and goal-line packages. According to CHGO’s Adam Jahns , “The first offense had its way in those periods, especially running to the right side behind 58 and 73.” The Bears were among the league’s best last year, running right towards guard Jonah Jackson (73) and tackle Darnell Wright (58), and I expect that to continue in 2026. Jahns also shouted out D’Andre Swift in the short-yardage situations, and he shared that rookie defensive tackle Jordan van den Berg was with the first string during their goal-line/short-yardage packages. The Chicago Tribune’s Brad Biggs also highlighted the first team offense, saying they “ripped off big plays in short yardage – third and 1 – with runs of 29 and 25 yards and an 8-yard completion off a bootleg.” But he also mentioned the other side of the ball, saying the “Defense responded to close things out in end of game scenario.” Biggs shared another defensive play. “Dontae Manning with a big hit on Roschon Johnson to force a fumble that Jon Rhattigan recovered for a safety in backed up period.” WGN’s Eli Ong spotlighted a defensive standout by writing that “Devin Bush made the play of the day so far… He picked off Tyson Bagent on a play where Bagent wanted to go short, and the RB kept running. Bush returned it from just outside the red zone all the way inside the opposite 20.” And one about the third phase from the Bear Report’s Zack Pearson, “Special teams drill was heated as they went 1 on 1 in blocking. Jahdae Walker was a big winner and let everyone know after each rep.” A few other nuggets from the day. Bad weather again forced the Bears to not allow fans to attend. Jedrick Wills Jr. started with the ones at left tackle, with Kiran Amegadjie rotating in towards the end of practice. ( link ) Linebacker T.J. Edwards, who had only been doing drills, got in plenty of work today and “looked good.” ( link ) There were conflicting reports about why Cam Lewis left the field on a cart (injured or just a quick ride), but regardless, Biggs said he returned. ( link ) Corner Tyrique Stevenson was not on for the final team period, but no one knew if it was injury-related. Malik Muhammad, who had been running with the ones at nickelback, kicked outside for Stevenson. Linebacker Tony Fields was shaken up after a big hit and was carted off. title: The Bears should have one goal on Saturday: Stay healthy
summary: The Chicago Bears and their fans should want to see one thing when they face the Cleveland Browns for their first preseason game this Saturday. One thing, and one thing only. I mean, sure, some clean offensive operation and maybe a touchdown pass from Caleb Williams in his lone drive (assuming he plays) would be […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - DECEMBER 14: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears runs with the ball during the second half against the Cleveland Browns on December 14, 2025 at Soldier Field in Chicago Illinois. (Photo by Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Chicago Bears and their fans should want to see one thing when they face the Cleveland Browns for their first preseason game this Saturday. One thing, and one thing only. I mean, sure, some clean offensive operation and maybe a touchdown pass from Caleb Williams in his lone drive (assuming he plays) would be welcome. And it wouldn’t hurt to see some of these interesting defensive rookies, like Dillon Thieneman, Malik Muhammad, and Jordan van den Berg make some splash plays that give us a glimpse of what they’ll contribute to the Bears. But to be honest, I don’t care if we see anything of note on the football field on Saturday. In fact, I don’t care if we see a single starter take a snap. (We will, most likely.) Because the most important thing the Bears have to accomplish between now and the end of Saturday’s tilt with Cleveland has nothing to do with schemes, points scored, or what undrafted rookie boosted their stock. In fact, it shouldn’t worry anyone if the Bears’ starters (at least the ones that play) look rusty and crusty as all hell. Because the most important thing is that they get through this game as healthy as possible. So far, the Bears have had a really hard time keeping key players on the field in training camp, which is far more alarming than any bad play we’ll see in preseason. Newly signed safety Coby Bryant, who was projected to start next to Thieneman, will now reportedly be out for 4-6 months after undergoing knee surgery, with a return for the playoffs likely the only chance we have of seeing him on the field. Luther Burden, arguably the biggest offensive star of camp in the early going, has a groin injury that could hamper him all the way up until Week 1—hopefully not beyond that. Oft-injured cornerback Kyler Gordon still hasn’t suited up after suffering a calf injury in the offseason. Rookie receiver Zavion Thomas, who’s made a few splashes with his speed thus far, is dealing with a day-to-day knee injury. Projected starting left tackle Braxton Jones, who lost his 2025 season due to injury, and starting defensive end Montez Sweat have been nursing ailments since last Thursday, though head coach Ben Johnson listed them as being day-to-day or week-to-week. Injuries are part of football, of course. But that’s… a lot for not even getting to the first preseason game yet. Perhaps that’s something the Bears coaching staff should be monitoring when it comes to their practices. Seeing all those names piling up on the injury report reminds you just how much good luck plays into a successful season like the one Chicago enjoyed in 2025. All things considered, the Bears survived their rash of key players like Gordon, Jones, Jaylon Johnson, Rome Odunze, and Dayo Odeyinbo being out remarkably well. (A few of the worst injuries—the ones to T.J. Edwards and Ozzy Trapilo—happened in the playoffs.) It’s too early to say the Bears are in major trouble after a few injury-plagued weeks of training camp. It’s likely that many of the major players they need, aside from Bryant and maybe Gordon, will be back relatively soon. But it would certainly help a lot if the Bears didn’t add any more big names to the injury report on Saturday, at least not for a long period of time. Because then it might really be time to freak out.
author: Khari Thompson

full_text: Chicago Bears Head Coach Ben Johnson revealed that new free agent acquisition Coby Bryant will be out for 4-6 months after having surgery this past Friday on his knee. The injury occurred on the first day of padded practices when Bryant went up against Cole Kmet and came down awkwardly after getting tangled up with the 6’6”, 257 tight end. Devastating news considering Bears GM Ryan Poles let 2025 starters Kevin Byard and Jaquan Brisker walk in free agency. To make matters worse, Bryant was Chicago’s highest-paid FA addition this summer – inking a 3-year $40 million deal – with Poles choosing to add to the back seven of the defense with Bryant and linebacker Devin Bush instead of making a big splash up front on the defensive line. Good thing Poles landed safety Dillon Thieneman in the first round, so the position isn’t completely devoid of blue-chip talent. Hopefully, the rookie and newcomer Xavier Woods continue to settle in opposite each other, and the front seven can pressure the opposing QB, or else we may be in for some more shootouts this season. Speaking of injuries, has anyone seen Kyler Gordon?

title: Cash, Stash, or Slash: Jaylon Johnson
summary: When we started the Cash, Stash, or Slash exercise, I’ll be honest, I wasn’t really thinking about including Jaylon Johnson. Johnson is only under contract for two years, so he would be an extension candidate after this season, but with the injuries and the change in defense, I felt better to leave Jaylon be and […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - JANUARY 10: Jaylon Johnson #1 of the Chicago Bears lines up before the snap during an NFC Wild Card Playoff game against the Green Bay Packers at Soldier Field on January 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images When we started the Cash, Stash, or Slash exercise, I’ll be honest, I wasn’t really thinking about including Jaylon Johnson. Johnson is only under contract for two years, so he would be an extension candidate after this season, but with the injuries and the change in defense, I felt better to leave Jaylon be and see how this season plays out for him. But when Jaylon Johnson met the media at the beginning of training camp, he feels that this season is a contract year for him and that he needs to show the Chicago Bears who he is as a player in 2026, that 2025 isn’t the player he is, and that he should receive a fresh contract that keeps him in Chicago for a few more years. So if Jaylon Johnson thinks it’s a contract year, who are we to argue? Jaylon Johnson: Stash I don’t see how it’s at all possible to try and make any determination as to what the future holds for Johnson. First of all, you have to be concerned about injuries for Johnson. Let’s not forget that Johnson was a first-round talent that fell to the Bears in round 2 because of injury concerns. And while Johnson did play in all but 3 games in 2023 and 2024 combined, in his other 4 NFL seasons, he’s missed a combined 21 games. A player that has missed a season and a half worth of games in six seasons is something to be concerned about when you are offering up a contract extension to a player who will be 28 in 2027. You also have to look at performance. And I think most of us believe that the drop-off in Johnson’s play last year was 95% related to injuries and that, when he’s healthy, he would be much closer to the player he was in 2023 and 2024 than the player he was in 2025. But if Johnson’s play recovers slightly, but he’s still far from the player he was, his contract is fairly forgiving if the Bears want to get out of it one year early. Johnson is a player who it’s very possible to see all three possible outcomes. You could see the Bears releasing him and going in a new direction next year, you could see the Bears signing him and making him a part of the defense’s future, or you could see the Bears telling Johnson they want him to play out his 2027 season and they can decide what they want to do with him in 2028. Every single one of those is not only possible, but I feel they are all fairly equal in terms of the probability that that’s the outcome that happens. If Johnson misses a huge amount of time again this season, there’s just no way the Bears are going to pay him the $24 million he’s owed in 2027. If Johnson plays well, but isn’t elite and is relatively healthy, it’s very likely that the Bears would be willing to bring him back in 2027 at the $24 million and see how things go in the final year of the deal. If Johnson stays healthy and is lights out again like he was back in 2023, how do you not extend him based on three of the last four seasons being excellent? Johnson is a mystery at this point. First and foremost, Johnson needs to be healthy in Chicago in 2026, and if he manages to do that, positive things will most likely follow.

title: Bears Question of the Day: Do you like the idea of playing most starters in the preseason?
summary: Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johson has yet to announce if his starters will play this Saturday against the Cleveland Browns in their preseason opener. Last year, he did play Caleb Williams and many staters in weeks two and three, but that was year one of the scheme, so we’ll have to wait and see […]
full_text: Aug 22, 2025; Kansas City, Missouri, USA; Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) scrambles during the first half against the Kansas City Chiefs at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jay Biggerstaff-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johson has yet to announce if his starters will play this Saturday against the Cleveland Browns in their preseason opener. Last year, he did play Caleb Williams and many staters in weeks two and three, but that was year one of the scheme, so we’ll have to wait and see what happens this season. Do you like the idea of playing most starters in the preseason? I asked our WCG staff that question, and here’s what we had to say. TJ Starman: I’d say that I am in favor of playing most starters, yes. The question is ultimately about how much you play them, but not playing starters at all seems like a mistake to me, and that’s something we may have seen in Chicago as recently as the Nagy era. Guys like Joe Thuney and Grady Jarrett don’t need to be out there, but giving the rest of your starters some chemistry reps seems like the best practice at this point. Josh Sunderbruch: I think they need limited reps, so a series or two, and I think the majority of playing time should be for players who are on the bubble or in transition on their roster status (undecided between a 2s and 3s, for example). Sam Householder: Like all things training camp and preseason, everyone fears injuries, but you can’t get better at football without playing football. I think reps here outweigh the concerns. Especially when you see offensive line play, and often some entire offensive or defensive units struggle in September. The Bears had a slow start last year, but can’t have that again with a tough division and schedule this year. To the question, though, do I like it? Not really, but I get the necessity of it. Mongo Peanut: Absolutely. Injuries this offseason aside, Ben Johnson’s approach to the preseason should be enough for fans to be confident in starters playing. These reps will help the Bears prepare for lots of real game situations, which were crucial to their success last year. Jeff Berckes: Football is a dangerous sport, and it always feels extra frustrating when a starter sustains an injury during the preseason. However, these practice games are important for getting into a rhythm for the season, and I think the starters should be ramping up to playing through at least a half of football. The rest of the time should help shape the back end of the roster. ECD: I actually do like playing the starters during preseason. If nothing more than to knock off some of the rust and begin to gel with the new pieces added to all phases of the ball. I’m not advocating for them to play more than a half at any time. Yet it’s also never a good idea to enter week one ice-cold from the shelf. Donald Gooch: No. I do not like the idea of playing most starters in the preseason. I understand all the “players need reps” arguments – but they need to get those in practices (particularly joint practices with another team). Preseason games feature vanilla schemes and desperate marginal players trying to make the team. The number one priority in preseason is to exit the preseason with no major injuries to key starters. Sit ‘em. Gary Baugher Jr.: I used to be a big fan of seeing starters in the preseason, for a half in games 2-3 (back when there were 4), but as I’ve aged, I have put overall team health ahead of everything else. I still think it’s important to get at least 2 quarters of action out of your #1’s in preseason, but beyond that, I’m good. Lester A. Wiltfong Jr.: I liked the Bears’ approach last year in letting most starters sit the first game, and playing most of the ones for weeks two and three. That said, if I’m really being honest, I’m not especially passionate one way or the other. Play the starters; don’t play the starters. Ben Johnson will do what he feels is best for the team in that moment. Last week, one of SB Nation’s national Reacts survey questions was “How much should starters play?” and logic won out with 39% saying as much as they need! Do you like the idea of playing most starters in the preseason? Sound off in the comment section!

title: Bengals News: Zac Taylor has been breaking an NFL rule all this time
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals play football against someone other than themselves this week! That’s not the only thing going on though. We’re nearing preseason Week 1, which means the regular season is also just around the corner. There is plenty going on, though. The front office will begin the process of deciding who will make the […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor walks the field during Bengals practice at the Kettering Practice Fields in Cincinnati, Ohio, on Thursday, August 6, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Cincinnati Bengals play football against someone other than themselves this week! That’s not the only thing going on though. We’re nearing preseason Week 1, which means the regular season is also just around the corner. There is plenty going on, though. The front office will begin the process of deciding who will make the final 53-man roster once they get some game tape on the second and third string guys, and a lot more as the greatest professional sports league in the world comes back to us. Here are some other goings on as we approach the 24-hour mark until the Bengals’ preseason opener: Starting this season, the NFL will allow someone other than the head coach to throw a challenge flag. The only issue with that, is the Bengals have been doing it illegally for the last several seasons . “We’ve been breaking the rule for eight years,” Taylor joked to reporters Tuesday morning. “Because I’ve never thrown the challenge flag. Doug [Rosfeld]’s always thrown the challenge flag, and they know that. They ask you that in pregame, ‘who’s got the flag?’ So it’s never been an issue. I didn’t even know it was frowned upon, I guess, and I know that there’s other coaches in the league; I’m not the only one that’s done that.” Tacario “Bobo” Davis, the Bengals’ third-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, has had a solid camp. Geoff Hobson has a nice piece on Davis’ upbringing and where his nickname came from . He’s going against the best wide receiver duo in the NFL in practice, and the Bengals are hoping that’ll transfer to the field. The Bengals will be wearing white jerseys with black pants on Thursday night against the Lions in Preseason Week 1. The starters, or at least most of them, are taking the field to start the 2026 campaign, which includes Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins and Dexter Lawrence. Chase says Joe Burrow looks more aggressive in camp. He likes it. “His demeanor is more aggressive,” Chase said. “His face is more aggressive, the way he talks is more aggressive. He’s got a little mean mug on his face a little bit. I kind of like when he’s like that.” Tahj Brooks has worked on his receiving skills in the offseason. “That’s something I’ve been working on since day one of the offseason and it’s going to show this year,” Brooks said. “Making guys miss in space, being explosive after the catch, and learning all of my routes. It’s a focal point to take another step in this offense.”

full_text: Jan 4, 2025; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase (1), quarterback Joe Burrow (9) and wide receiver Tee Higgins (5) take the field as captains for the coin toss before a game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Sam Greene/USA TODAY Network via Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con Zac Taylor spoke with the media on Tuesday morning ahead of the Cincinnati Bengals ‘ first preseason action this Thursday against the Detroit Lions. Taylor said that his trio of offensive stars will see some action in the game, with Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins. That likely means we will see the entire first-team offense for at least a series or two this week. The Bengals will remain cautious with backup Connor Lew and rotational player Erick All Jr. on Thursday. Both players are coming off of ACL injuries, and they are being slowly worked back into live action. Both players are progressing well from their injuries and should be back in game action sooner rather than later. On the defensive side of the ball, new defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence will also see action during the game. That will be a welcome sight to see Lawrence making life miserable for an opposing team in a Bengals uniform. Dax Hill has been dealing with hamstring tightness throughout camp. The Bengals will continue to be cautious with that situation, so Hill will miss the game on Thursday. The other defensive starter that will miss the game is Bryan Cook. Cook suffered an undisclosed injury during the Friday night practice in the stadium. While the injury is not expected to be serious, the Bengals have kept him out of practice this week and will do the same for Thursday’s game. Beyond those two defensive starters, the Bengals enter the game fairly healthy. Shemar Stewart is still out with his hyperextended knee, but he has been seen at practice recently with just a leg sleeve on now. BJ Hill will also be out as he remains on PUP, though he’s expected to be cleared soon. Who are some players you are most excited to see on Thursday for Cincinnati?
