In the fourth round of the […]
full_text: EUGENE, OR - SEPTEMBER 07: Boise State Broncos tackle Kage Casey (77), Boise State Broncos corner back Markel Reed (8) and Boise State Broncos safety Ty Benefield (0) lead the team toward the field prior to the start of the game during a college football game between the Oregon Ducks and Boise State Broncos on September 7, 2024, at Autzen Stadium in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Brian Murphy/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Building up the offensive line has been a primary endeavor for the Denver Broncos since Head Coach Sean Payton’s arrival in Denver. The franchise has signed multiple high-profile players, extended several in-house players, but have also been diligent in their approach to finding and developing late-round and UDFA players. In the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft, the Broncos added Boise State product Kage Casey to the group. A three-year starter and two-time All-American, Casey locked down their left tackle position. However, the start of his NFL journey will be inside at interior. In the team’s draft presser, Head Coach Sean Payton spoke highly of Casey’s versatility—a primary reason he was picked. When drafted, Casey acknowledged his willingness to play wherever the Broncos need to. He also highlighted his play style and what fans should expect from him as he begins his pro career. “I play quick, aggressive. My football intelligence, my ability to read the field and slow down the game for myself, read pressure, see where a defender is going to be moving post-snap allows me to play fast. I’m an extremely consistent guy. I’m disciplined, and I’m ready to learn wherever I need to be,” stated Casey. Throughout the offseason and training camp, Casey has been getting a lot of work in the interior, specifically left guard. Yesterday after practice, Head Coach Sean Payton gave an update on the rookie’s progression to date. However, he also revealed a new tidbit of information—that Casey will also see reps and playing time at center leading up to the regular season. “He’s got good feet and he’s smart. I think his ideal position is guard, but we’ll give him some center flex. He comes to us having been well coached. You feel that in his play and we felt that on film. We’ve been pretty fortunate with some of those draft picks or free agents on the offensive line,” noted Paton. With fourth-year pro Alex Forsyth in the final deal of his rookie contract and Ben Powers in the last year of his revised deal, having Casey learn the ropes at both positions makes a lot of sense. That sort of cross-training and ability will fortify their offensive trench outlook long-term.
author: Christopher Hart

title: Horse Tracks: Nix, Broncos ready to test progress in preseason opener
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! Just a few short days until the Broncos get to compare their progress toward the 2026 season against guys in a different jersey, and no one is looking forward to it more than Bo Nix. “I’m excited,” the third-year quarterback said after practice yesterday. “I think preseason’s always a great time […]
full_text: Good morning, Broncos Country! Just a few short days until the Broncos get to compare their progress toward the 2026 season against guys in a different jersey, and no one is looking forward to it more than Bo Nix. “I’m excited,” the third-year quarterback said after practice yesterday. “I think preseason’s always a great time to get back out there and get your feet wet a little bit and see defenses in a live situation before the first game.” But even Nix is unsure how much, or if at all, he’ll get his feet wet on Friday. “No idea,” Nix added. It seems likely he’ll at least run a few plays as Davis Webb will be getting live reps calling plays in a game as well. And getting the QB and his OC in sync during a preseason game seems like a good idea now that Webb will take over play-calling duties from the sideline (with a little “mentoring” from Payton along the way). Either way, Payton is de-emphasizing the new role for Webb and focusing on figuring out the team. “I think it’ll feel and look about the same,” Payton said of preparing with Webb. “We’ll go through where coaches are. The big thing is let’s not ever lose track of finding the right 53.” As Payton noted, there’s not much value in trying to judge a player who is confused by his assignment before the ball is even snapped. “As we get into the developmental players or the younger players, making sure we’re giving them defenses, offenses, reps of things they know well so we can evaluate their ability,” Payton said. “The first thing that can stunt that is complication, confusion or they don’t know what to do.” "We've got it to where we can compete on any level at all times. That doesn't make it any easier." QB @BoNix10 believes 'battle-tested' Broncos will be up to the challenge in 2026 » https://t.co/XcuyZAyrBu pic.twitter.com/ucRdYHQfCX — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) August 11, 2026 But for Nix, there is understandably still some excitement about this new “era” with Webb. “I’m really excited. I know he’s going to do a great job,” Nix said. “He does a really good job preparing. He’s going to work harder than anybody else in the building at his craft, and he’s going to do his job to the best of his ability.” And Nix understands there will be a learning curve for both of them in this new dynamic. “It’s definitely not going to be easy for him to do it for the first time, but that’s why he has the 11 on the field, and Coach to help support him,” Nix said. “We’re going to go with the ebbs and flows of the season. We’re going to learn from the bad and continue to grow from the good. After two years of mostly getting feedback from Webb on the sideline after the offense came off the field, now he’ll have Webb’s voice giving directions in the huddle. “I’m excited to have him in my ear,” Nix added. Of course, Webb isn’t the only Broncos coordinator helping prepare Nix. The quarterback pointed out that feedback from defensive coordinator Vance Joseph is also invaluable. And now that he’s getting better at reading defenses, Joseph’s insight is more important. “We’re seeing every defensive structure imaginable,” Nix said of practice reps. “Safeties going everywhere, blitzes from everywhere, fronts from everywhere. That just helps you as a quarterback get your eyes up and slow the game down once you get into a game setting,” Nix said. “For me, it’s been irreplaceable to be able to go against ‘VJ.’” He can walk over afterward and ask Joseph exactly what the defense was trying to accomplish – and he does. “I can ask him questions and sort of figure out the ‘Why’ behind things,” Nix said. “I also think it’s helped me just as a quarterback in our system being able to see things and find different answers within our system.”
author: Laurie Lattimore-Volkmann

title: 4 takeaways from Dan Campbell’s press conference: High praise of Devin White
summary: Dan Campbell held his typical daily press conference ahead of the Detroit Lions’ 11th training camp practice on Tuesday morning. While there was nothing particularly out of the ordinary in Campbell’s press conference, it felt particularly dense with information. And rather than bombard you with several separate stories, I felt the easiest and best way […]
full_text: Aug 3, 2026; Allen Park, MI, USA; Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell addresses the media prior to Detroit Lions training camp. Mandatory Credit: Paul Barnick-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Dan Campbell held his typical daily press conference ahead of the Detroit Lions’ 11th training camp practice on Tuesday morning. While there was nothing particularly out of the ordinary in Campbell’s press conference, it felt particularly dense with information. And rather than bombard you with several separate stories, I felt the easiest and best way to consume the news was to summarize some of the most interesting takeaways. So, that’s what I did. Enjoy. Devin White is starting to look like his All-Pro self Without a doubt, Devin White’s career has taken a drastic left turn. After earning second-team All Pro honors his second ever NFL season, his play has gotten increasingly uneven. The Buccaneers didn’t offer him an extension, he was released by the Eagles without playing a single snap for them, he started just one game for the Texans, and then even last year—when he started 17 games for the Raiders and finished third in the NFL in tackles—the tape revealed some mixed results and White went unsigned in free agency… until the Lions grabbed him last week. Campbell knows White pretty well. When White was at the top of his game with the Buccaneers in 2019-20, Campbell was across the division, having to game plan against him as the Saints assistant head coach and tight ends coach. The Devin White he’s seen a week into Lions camp is closer to that All-Pro Buc than the Raider who struggled. “He looks like a different guy than what we saw in Vegas last year on tape. I mean, he’s moving well, he’s thumping, pretty smart,” Campbell said. “He’s got speed, still has that speed. And what I’m seeing right now, that’s what I remember in Tampa Bay when I was in New Orleans. That was the guy, he was a headache.” The WR room is the most talented he’s seen—and the WR5/6 battle is HOT I asked Campbell which wide receivers were sticking out besides the players at the top of the depth chart. For the most part, he opted not to name names, but rather offer high praise for the entire room. “This is the best receiver room we’ve had since I’ve been here in camp, top to bottom,” Campbell said. “I mean, those guys are gifted. It’s a really good crew, man. And they’re all pretty tough, they’re all a little bit different the way they’re built. And every one of those guys has flashed on one day or another, has done something pretty damn good.” But Campbell eventually let one name slip, and it’s probably not the one you’d expect. “Tay Martin, man, makes plays every day,” Campbell said. “And he’s intriguing on offense, but he makes special teams plays every day. And that’s important to us.” Martin comes to Detroit after a strong season in the UFL with the Columbus Aviators. The 6-foot-1, 184 pound receiver caught 42 passes for 483 yards and two touchdowns. He’s someone to watch during Thursday’s preseason game. Keep an eye on Erick Hunter Undrafted rookie Erick Hunter has been a fan favorite among Detroit’s 2026 UDFA class because of some ridiculously good tape and incredible production (102 tackles, 14 TFLs in 2025) at Morgan State. Many small school players enter the NFL in over their head, but Hunter has started to make plays on a daily basis, and Campbell has certainly noticed. “He’s athletic and he takes notes, he listens, he works his tail off in practice,” Campbell said. “And every day he’s kind of another one of those guys that makes plays every day. And he certainly makes plays every day in special teams. Every day he’s making a block or he’s making a tackle. And you just see growth on defense.” Campbell was quick to point out that he’s still very much learning and “doesn’t know what he doesn’t know yet,” but the effort he’s putting out both in the classroom and the field has stuck out. Nick Whiteside ain’t scared In my opinion, Nick Whiteside’s ascent has been the story of training camp. In a Lions cornerback room desperate for some optimism, Whiteside climbing from the bottom of the depth chart to the first-team reps has been an injection of hope. Campbell has already commented about how Whiteside is making daily plays and is too hard to ignore right now. But what I found interesting about his comments on Tuesday was how it’s been Whiteside’s attitude that has been particularly impressive. “Here’s what I love about Ironsides is it is not too big for him,” Campbell said. “He doesn’t care who’s across from him, he will compete and he’s going to try to use his craft. And he doesn’t go in a shell and he’s defeated before the play is even snapped. “I mean, really, I know this sounds crazy, but some guys, man, all of a sudden, man, Jamo’s across from me or (Amon-Ra) Saint (Brown), and I’m already done, and the fear is already there. He is not that way. This guy, it doesn’t matter who’s there. He’s going to try to use his craft and compete and you love that.”
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Lions training camp notes: Sam LaPorta starting to shake rust
summary: Tuesday was one of the shortest training camp practices I’ve witnessed in the Dan Campbell era. The Detroit Lions only got in about an hour of work before they decided to call it a day. There’s a relatively good reason for that. Last week, the Lions went fully padded four times in a row, and […]
full_text: Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta (87) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, July 24, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Tuesday was one of the shortest training camp practices I’ve witnessed in the Dan Campbell era. The Detroit Lions only got in about an hour of work before they decided to call it a day. There’s a relatively good reason for that. Last week, the Lions went fully padded four times in a row, and on Monday’s practice, they did it again. With only a couple of days until their preseason opener, the goal was to mostly get some work for the starters who will not play on Thursday against the Bengals. But despite the short day, we’ve got plenty to talk about. So let’s get into Tuesday observations. [ You can see the latest injury news from practice here. ] Sam LaPorta comes alive It’s been a relatively slow start to Sam LaPorta’s training camp. Some of that has been by design, as it’s clear he wasn’t getting a full workload in the early days as he continues to feel out his body following back surgery. But he’s also lacked some of the game-changing, play-making ability that was so valuable for this offense for the past three years. However, he looked like his old self on Tuesday, particularly on the first team drill of the day. LaPorta made back-to-back catches right up the seam. The first went for about 25-30 yards, as he made a twisting, acrobatic back-shoulder catch. The second, he scampered in for a 10-yard touchdown and made it look easy. He’s now put together a few good days, and it appears the rust is off. The ups and downs continue for Ennis Rakestraw Ennis Rakestraw has been sliding down the depth chart as of late, regularly working with the second team, while Nick Whiteside has gotten plenty of first-team work. Campbell called Rakestraw’s camp “up and down” on Monday, and it was more of the same on Tuesday, although I will say I’ve seen progress. The progress comes in the form of his one-on-ones with Jameson Williams. Early in camp, he’d been competing hard with him, but Williams had won the majority of his reps against him. But on Tuesday, it was Rakestraw who won two of his three reps against Jamo. On the first, Williams tried to do a ton of dancing at the line of scrimmage, and Rakestraw was with him on every step. The second, Rakestraw had him completely blanketed during a red zone snap. In between, however, Williams got a free release on an in-breaker, forcing Rakestraw to grab at his jersey and draw a flag—and give up the pass. Unfortunately for Rakestraw, the positive plays did not continue once they broke into team drills. He bit on a double move from Malik Cunningham and gave up a 30-yard touchdown on the play, although he was not too far back in coverage. It’s worth noting that during the final drill of practice, Rakestraw got some looks with the ones—with Rock Ya-Sin on the opposite end and rookie Keith Abney in the nickel—but he also appeared to be in with the third-team defense, so there’s a lot of work to do. Josh Dobbs makes a strong impression… but can’t finish Dobbs only appeared briefly in team drills during his second practice with the team, but he made an immediate impression by throwing a 23-yard shot play to Cedrick Wilson up the seam. It was a great catch by Wilson—high-pointing the ball between Joe Bachie and Loren Strickland—but it was also a good ball from Dobbs to put it where only Wilson had a chance at it. Dobbs worked the ball all the way down to the goal line, but on a third down inside the 10-yard line, the Lions pulled him in favor of Luke Altmyer. Why? Well, understandably, Dobbs didn’t know any of the team’s red zone plays yet. “I wanted (in), but (offensive coordinator) Drew (Petzing) said we haven’t even installed red zone, so he didn’t have anything to call,” Dobbs said. “So it’s a little tough once you get to the 6-yard line and you don’t know the red zone plays yet, but I was just like, ‘Just call a fade, and they’ll figure it out.’” Alas, Altmyer came in, checked down to Greg Dortch, and the offense settled for a short field goal. Defense decisively wins situational drill The offense ended practice but was put in a difficult situation: Down 14-24 with 3:41 left, starting on their own 32-yard line with three timeouts left It wasn’t a particularly strong performance from the offense. They not only failed, but they were also probably bailed out a few times. After ignoring what probably would’ve been an Alim McNeill sack (on Seth McLaughlin), they couldn’t ignore an Aidan Hutchinson sack on the next play. It appeared then the offense was going to be in a third-and-very-long, but after Jared Goff overshot Sam LaPorta, the defense was called for an unclear penalty, giving the offense a fresh set of downs. A medium gain from Isaac TeSlaa and a curl to LaPorta put them in field goal range. But Goff misfired again to Brock Wright on third down, and the veteran tight end could not bring in the bobble. Jake Bates drilled the 47-yard field goal to keep hope alive, though. After the second-team defense got a three-and-out stop on the second-team offense on only run plays, the starting offense recaptured the ball with 1:38 left on their own 20-yard line (after a 68-yard Jack Fox punt). On the first play, Goff bobbled a low snap from McLaughlin, and Avonte Maddox came free on a blitz for the sack. Then after two inefficient plays, the Lions faced a fourth-and-long. Goff made a great back shoulder throw to Williams up the left sideline, but Jamo came down out of bounds after the impressive grab. The Lions coaching staff opted to count it anyway—refs clearly called him out of bounds—but it wouldn’t matter. After another Aidan Hutchinson sack—his third of the day—Goff threw a desperation ball well behind LaPorta, and Thomas Harper made an impressive drive on the ball for the practice-ending interception. Miscellaneous Another strong day for Whiteside. During 1-on-1s, he locked down Isaac TeSlaa in the red zone and had an incredible one-handed interception lined up against Lucky Jackson. Amon-Ra St. Brown had a similarly impressive one-handed grab during one-on-ones with Rock Ya-Sin in coverage, but he just missed out on getting both feet down inbounds. Speaking of Ya-Sin, he is clearly the best Lions cornerback right now with D.J. Reed out. He makes every 1-on-1 rep a complete battle. Lucky Jackson got some praise during full-team red zone work. On the first play, he inserted in motion and got his nose dirty in the run game. On the very next play, he faked like he was doing the exact same thing, but leaked out into the flats and was wide open for the 2-yard TD grab.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Detroit Lions injury updates: Several players inching closer to return
summary: It was a welcomed day of relatively good injury news from Allen Park, as the Detroit Lions took the field for their 11th training camp practice off the offseason. The Lions got a starter back at practice, and a few others appear to be en route to returning—possibly very soon. Lions coach Dan Campbell also […]
full_text: Detroit Lions edge Derrick Moore (9) practices a drill during OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Friday, May 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co It was a welcomed day of relatively good injury news from Allen Park, as the Detroit Lions took the field for their 11th training camp practice off the offseason. The Lions got a starter back at practice, and a few others appear to be en route to returning—possibly very soon. Lions coach Dan Campbell also gave some relatively promising news regarding safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch. “His rehab is coming along very well,” Campbell said of Joseph. “So I still see him on the Branch plan, if that makes sense. And Branch is doing well, too. So those guys, we’re talking about on down the road, the season’s already begun, but I like where Kerby is at.” Here’s a look at the rest of the team’s injury situation, based on my own personal observations, as there are no official injury reports in the offseason. Returned to practice: S Avonte Maddox After missing just one day of practice, Maddox was back out there with his teammates. At this point, Maddox is expected to be a starter, so it’s great news his absence did not appear to be serious. He wasn’t in on many team drills with Thomas Harper working in with the starters. Working with trainers, not practicing: RB Sione Vaki (broken nose, poked eye) LB Malcolm Rodriguez (ankle) EDGE Derrick Moore (groin) Great news to see Sione Vaki out there doing work with a trainer and a helmet on. He was sporting a visor to protect his face and his eye was still bloodshot. It’s hard to know when the Lions would be comfortable putting him out there with such a unique injury, but the fact that he’s putting a helmet on is certainly a good sign. Rodriguez did as much action with a trainer as I have seen since his exit with an ankle injury. He could be on the track to returning soon, but it’s still been Devin White filling in with the first-team defense. Moore continues to get in work, and is likely nearing a return. We are on Day 8 of Campbell’s 7-to-10 day estimate for Moore’s absence. Not practicing: RB Isiah Pacheco (knee) RB Jabari Small (undisclosed) OT Giovanni Manu (NFI) OT Devin Cochran (undisclosed) C Cade Mays (wrist) G Juice Scruggs (undisclosed) EDGE Payton Turner (back) DT Aidan Keanaaina (undisclosed) LB Damone Clark (undisclosed) LB Jimmy Rolder (leg) CB Khalil Dorsey (undisclosed) S Kerby Joseph (PUP, knee) S Brian Branch (PUP, Achilles) Small has been favoring his knee for several practices now, so it’s not surprising to see him take a day off. But he can’t afford to take too many days off, as he is locked in with Jacob Saylors for the RB4 battle. “Small’s having a good camp,” Campbell said Monday. “I mean, I feel like those two guys are just jockeying with each other right now. One guy’s a little bit ahead. The next day, the other guy’s a little bit ahead. And I love where they’re at on special teams because that’ll be big for both of those players.” Cochran left practice very early on Monday, so his absence is not unexpected. Miles Frazier continued to get plenty of reps at tackle to help with the shorthanded unit. I didn’t see Dorsey out there, leaving Ennis Rakestraw to pull some double duty with the second and third teams. Injured during practice WR Jameson Williams (wind) There was a scary moment during the final drill of practice when Jameson Williams came down with an out route on the sidelines and stayed down for a minute or two. However, word is he only got the wind knocked out of him, and he was all smiles coming off the field, so there is no concern there.

title: Detroit Lions to don ‘Rivalries’ uniforms vs. divisional foe
summary: The Detroit Lions announced on Tuesday that the highly anticipated “rivalry” uniforms will be worn during the team’s Week 8 matchup against the Minnesota Vikings. As of now, the actual design of these uniforms has not been revealed. But team president Rod Wood gave a brief hint at what they may look like during the […]
full_text: Sep 30, 2024; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions running back Craig Reynolds (13) wears the Lions new helmets and black jerseys for their Monday Night Football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Ford Field. title: Kerby Joseph injury update: Detroit Lions safety’s rehab going ‘very well’
summary: It’s been a while since we’ve seen Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph working alongside medical professionals at training camp. It turns out there’s a reason for that, and, thankfully, it’s not another setback in his knee injury recovery. However, he is currently dealing with a personal issue, according to Dan Campbell. “First of all, he’s […]
full_text: Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph (31) practices during OTAs at Detroit Lions headquarters and training facility in Allen Park on Thursday, May 30, 2024. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co It’s been a while since we’ve seen Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph working alongside medical professionals at training camp. It turns out there’s a reason for that, and, thankfully, it’s not another setback in his knee injury recovery. However, he is currently dealing with a personal issue, according to Dan Campbell. “First of all, he’s dealing with a personal issue right now, but his rehab is coming along very well,” Campbell said on Tuesday morning. Campbell opted to keep the details of that private, but it sounds like Joseph’s rehab has not taken a step back. Similar to his update a few weeks ago, Campbell still sounds like he doesn’t expect Joseph to be ready for Week 1—same as safety Brian Branch, who is recovering from an Achilles injury—but could return to the field shortly thereafter. “I still see him on the (Brian) Branch plan, if that makes sense, and Branch is doing well, too,” Campbell said. “So those guys, we’re talking about on down the road, the season’s already begun. But I like where Kerby is at.” With both players sidelined this training camp, the Lions have put Chuck Clark and Avonte Maddox into the starting lineup for nearly every first-team rep. Clark, a nine-year veteran, has particularly impressed at training camp, while Maddox has shown significant growth since moving to the position full-time last year. “Maddox has grown a ton just in a year at that position for us,” Campbell said last week. “So, he and Chuck back there, there again, it’s early, but man, they work pretty good together, and they communicate, and they’re both pretty savvy guys.” Detroit will have a tough decision to make with Joseph and Branch at roster cutdowns. If they opt to keep them both on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list, they’ll miss the first four games of the season—but they’ll free up roster spots and could return to practice after two thanks to a new NFL rule. If they opt to take them off PUP, they’ll take up a roster spot even though it doesn’t appear they’ll be ready to start the season.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Detroit Lions’ defensive roster bubble: Nick Whiteside, Devin White make statements
summary: The Detroit Lions roster bubble on defense is enormous. As of right now, we’ve got a total of 25 players fighting for a roster spot on the defensive side alone. And with the constant shifting due to injuries, strong play, or early struggles, our weekly predictions on who is in and who is out are […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive back Nick Whiteside (38) warms up before OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, June 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions roster bubble on defense is enormous. As of right now, we’ve got a total of 25 players fighting for a roster spot on the defensive side alone. And with the constant shifting due to injuries, strong play, or early struggles, our weekly predictions on who is in and who is out are fluctuating pretty drastically. This week’s winners, however, were clear: Devin White and Nick Whiteside. Let’s break down every position battle on defense with our Week 3 Bubble Watch picks: View Link Defensive end : Assumed in: Aidan Hutchinson, DJ Wonnum, Derrick Moore Ahmed Hassanein: 11 “IN” votes (up 1) Payton Turner: 0 votes (down 1) Anthony Lucas: 0 votes The staff is now completely aligned, with Ahmed Hassanein continuing his impressive camp, while Payton Turner remains sidelined with an injury. This is getting dangerously close to being settled completely at this point. Defensive tackle: Assumed in: Alim McNeill, Tyleik Williams New to bubble watch: Levi Onwuzurike : 11 votes Tyler Lacy: 11 votes (no change) Skyle Gill-Howard: 10 votes (up 2) Chris Smith: 5 votes (up 1) Mekhi Wingo: 2 votes (down 4) Tyre West: 0 votes (no change) Aidan Keanaaina: 0 votes (no change) This week, I brought down Levi Onwuzurike to the bubble after being an “assumed in.” Onwuzurike has been primarily repping with the second and third teams this training camp—well behind Alim McNeill (and even Mekhi Wingo) at the three-tech, and comfortably behind Tyler Lacy at the big end position. Despite all of that, we all still have him in , but I think his spot on the roster is up for grabs. Elsewhere, Wingo drops a few votes, likely having to do with him missing a few days due to injury. However, he returned to practice on Monday (after votes were submitted), so this may have been a bit of an overreaction. Still, Gill-Howard’s rise is warranted. He’s started to climb the depth chart—regularly getting reps with the first and second team—and has made a fair amount of plays, as well. Linebacker: Assumed in: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez Devin White: 11 votes (up 5) Trevor Nowaske: 10 votes (no change) Damone Clark: 10 votes (no change) Jimmy Rolder: 0 votes (down 3) Troy Reeder: 2 votes (down 2) Erick Hunter: 0 votes (down 1) Joe Bachie: 0 votes (down 1) After a pretty impressive first week of training camp, Devin White has jumped all the way to a unanimous vote. He’s been the clear top replacement for injured Malcolm Rodriguez in the starting lineup, and has consistently been making plays. It hasn’t been perfect—play-action has gotten him several times—but he looks comfortable in a starting role. Meanwhile, it appears our staff is now convinced Rolder will start the season on injured reserve after suffering an injury a couple weeks back. And while Erick Hunter lost his one vote from last week, I will say that in these past few practices, he’s starting to make some noise, and it wouldn’t shock me if he replaced one of the veteran special teamers we currently have in—especially as Damone Clark continues to miss time with an injury. Cornerback: Assumed in: DJ Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Ennis Rakestraw, Keith Abney Nick Whiteside: 11 votes (up 5) Khalil Dorsey: 10 votes (up 2) New to bubble watch: Roger McCreary: 5 votes Let’s start with Whiteside, whose meteoric rise has been one of the biggest surprises of training camp. He started Bubble Watch with just one vote, but after a strong opening week to training camp, he got promoted to starting reps with D.J. Reed sidelined. He’s clearly jumped Ennis Rakestraw on the depth chart, making it tempting to drop the Lions’ 2024 second-round pick onto the roster bubble… but I’m not there yet. I did, however, drop veteran Roger McCreary down to the roster bubble. While McCreary has been getting a fair share of first-team nickel reps, coach Dan Campbell accurately called his camp thus far “up and down.” With only $800,000 in guaranteed salary, it’s fair to wonder if Whiteside’s rise means McCreary’s fall. After all, Detroit has several other options at nickel, including Christian Izien, Avonte Maddox, and Rakestraw. Dorsey continues to dominate on special teams. In my opinion, it’s not even a question that he’s the best special teamer on the roster. Safety Assumed in: Christian Izien, Avonte Maddox (NEW), Chuck Clark (NEW) Thomas Harper: 11 votes (no change) Brian Branch: 3 votes (down 1) Kerby Joseph: 0 votes (down 4) Dan Jackson: 0 votes (down 1) Loren Strickland: 0 votes (no change) First off, we’ve moved Avonte Maddox and Chuck Clark off the bubble and onto the “assumed in” category, because both had taken essentially every starting snap of training camp until Maddox’s absence on Monday. More and more, they not only look safe, but the likely Week 1 starters. The other shifts involve both Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph. Despite some optimism surrounding Branch—including his first on-field work with trainers—most of the staff believes he will start the season on PUP. Now everyone believes Joseph is headed for that fate after he’s been neither seen nor heard from in the past week. After some vigorous training in the first week, it’s been all silent on that front. Personally speaking, I believe the best argument for keeping both on PUP to start the season is a new rule implemented this year . Players who begin the season on PUP are now allowed to return to practice after just two weeks instead of four. They still can’t play in the first four games, but it gives those players an opportunity to ramp up and be ready by Week 5. That seems like a reasonable goal for both Branch and Joseph, and it’s a good way to preserve roster spots early in the season.

title: Discussion: What should the Detroit Lions do at center following Cade Mays’ injury?
summary: Detroit Lions fans were delivered some tough news to swallow on Monday morning when coach Dan Campbell revealed that starting center Cade Mays suffered an injury in training camp that will force him to miss “significant” time. Media reports suggest Mays has a broken bone in his wrist and will miss 8-10 weeks with the […]
full_text: Aug 3, 2026; Allen Park, MI, USA; Detroit Lions offensive lineman Juice Scruggs (70) walks off the field following Detroit Lions training camp. Mandatory Credit: Paul Barnick-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Detroit Lions fans were delivered some tough news to swallow on Monday morning when coach Dan Campbell revealed that starting center Cade Mays suffered an injury in training camp that will force him to miss “significant” time . Media reports suggest Mays has a broken bone in his wrist and will miss 8-10 weeks with the injury. It’s particularly tough news, because the Lions clearly made upgrading the offensive line—and particularly the center position—a priority this offseason. Mays earned a three-year, $25 million contract with Detroit, the most the Lions spent on an external free agent this offseason. So what do the Lions do now? They clearly hold their offensive line to a very high standard, and we all saw what it looked like when that line doesn’t live up to that standard last year. So today’s Question of the Day is: Do the Lions need to add another center after Cade Mays’ injury? My answer: In an ideal world, sure. It would be great to just add another starting center. In reality, that’s going to be almost impossible unless Detroit would be willing to part with valuable draft assets. Just think back to this past offseason. There were several center-needy teams and very few on the free agency market. That’s why Tyler Linderbaum got the ridiculous deal he got, and it’s why the Lions got aggressive with Mays. This time of year, there aren’t likely many (if any) teams that would just be willing to part with their starting center. That’s going to increase the price. The Bears got Garrett Bradbury for a fifth-round pick, but the Patriots already had third-round pick Jared Wilson in place. With free agency and the draft well in the rear-view mirror, teams aren’t likely to have a sufficient backup plan in order to trade their starting center away. There is maybe one exception: the Seattle Seahawks. Last year, the Seahawks had a camp battle for the starting center job between 2023 fifth-round pick Olu Oluwatimi and 2024 undrafted player Jalen Sundell. Oluwatimi suffered an injury in training camp, giving the job to Sundell, but Oluwatimi jumped back into the lineup when Sundell suffered a mid-season injury. Now it appears Sundell has hold of the job again, leaving Oluwatimi—and his 13 career starts—as an option for Detroit. It seems realistic the Lions could possibly pull him from Seattle for a 2027 Day 3 pick, if they deem him a fit. What’s more likely, however, is the team rolls with what they’ve got. For one, while it sucks to lose Mays, he’s only projected to miss just over a month of the season. The Lions may not want to part with draft resources for a five or six-game band aid—particularly when that first leg of the schedule is relatively easy and includes zero divisional games. One player missing five games should not derail the entire season—and if it does, there were far bigger problems. Additionally, the Lions likely want to explore the options they already have. They’ve talked highly of a center they’ve already traded for, Juice Scruggs. The veteran lineman already has eight career starts at center—earning a respectable 64.5 PFF grade over that stretch (19th out of 38 qualifying centers). Seth McLaughlin, who won the Rimington Trophy for best center in college football in 2024, is certainly an intriguing option as well. He hasn’t had a chance to prove himself in the pros while recovering from a torn Achilles suffered in 2024, but he’s already getting first-team reps in Detroit while Scruggs is sidelined. My guess—and preference—is the Lions just roll what they’ve got, build that chemistry the best they can, then give the job back to Mays hopefully out of the team’s Week 6 bye. Do you think the Lions should make a run at a new center? If so, who? Share your thoughts in the comment section.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Training camp shaking up the depth chart
summary: The Packers’ training camp competition is reshuffling their depth chart. Sort of. Public depth charts don’t mean much, but they at least give us a glimpse into how the team is thinking as they careen toward the regular season. And right now it shows a team in flux. Now, the Packers are supposed to be […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers player Brandon Cisse stands on the field during training camp at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin, on August 2, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Packers’ training camp competition is reshuffling their depth chart. Sort of. Public depth charts don’t mean much, but they at least give us a glimpse into how the team is thinking as they careen toward the regular season. And right now it shows a team in flux. Now, the Packers are supposed to be in flux right now. Every team is. That’s the whole point of training camp. You throw the team into controlled chaos for a month or so, play a couple of exhibition games, sort out a couple of injuries, and see what comes out the other side. That’s how you make a football team. The depth chart is little more than a symptom of that process. But it’s still surprising in some ways. Who ends up where and how long they stay there is important, and a publicly released training camp depth chart is a noteworthy data point. Does it mean Karl Brooks will actually start ahead of Javon Hargrave? Does it mean Anthony Belton is safe as the starter at right guard? No, of course not. But it gives us something to compare everything else to, and with news that Brandon Cisse (listed with the second teamers) is getting first team reps, it gives us an opening to ask what’s changed — or if the status quo is worth preserving at all. title: Packers roster 2026: Keisean Nixon, Zaire Franklin, and Chris McClellan are underrated
summary: Matt LaFleur became the Green Bay Packers’ head coach in 2019, and since then, he’s put together quite the historical resume. LaFleur currently ranks 16th all-time in regular-season win percentage in pro football history (.654), which is a pretty nice place to be. Outside of the 2022 season, the franchise has never missed the postseason […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JULY 31: Chris McClellan #55 of the Green Bay Packers rides a bike during the Green Bay Packers training camp at Ray Nitschke Field on July 31, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Matt LaFleur became the Green Bay Packers’ head coach in 2019, and since then, he’s put together quite the historical resume. LaFleur currently ranks 16th all-time in regular-season win percentage in pro football history (.654), which is a pretty nice place to be. Outside of the 2022 season, the franchise has never missed the postseason when he’s been the head coach, and no NFC team has more regular-season wins since 2019 than Green Bay’s 76; only the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills have more overall, and Green Bay is tied with the Baltimore Ravens for third overall. Of course, doing all that stuff in the regular season without a Super Bowl to show for it can get complicated after a while. Ask Sean McDermott and John Harbaugh, whose Bills and Ravens let them walk this offseason in part because the postseason records weren’t making anybody happy. Not that LaFleur should keep his head on a swivel per se, but a 3-6 postseason record says what it says, and Wild Card exits over the last two seasons tend to amplify that story. Last season’s 31-27 loss to the Chicago Bears after holding a 21-3 halftime lead was particularly galling. “We’ve got to look at it,” LaFleur said after that particular disaster. “We’ve got to talk. There’s a lot of pieces. All you’re trying to do in the moment is, when mistakes are made, you’re correcting them. There’s not long discussions on the sideline. It’s just, you correct the mistakes and you try to keep it moving. And I felt like just our team got a little bit disheveled in the second half.” The organization signed LaFleur, general manager Brian Gutekunst, and Executive Vice President/Director of Football Operations Russ Ball to multi-year contract extensions in January, and team President Ed Policy expressed all the faith needed. “While we are all disappointed with the way this season ended, we remain aligned in purpose and have spent considerable time over the past weeks collaborating on a path forward,” Policy said. “I am exceedingly confident we have the right people to achieve our goal. The entire Packers organization looks forward to supporting every effort to bring our community and fans another championship that they very much deserve.” Well, if that’s going to happen in 2026 — if the Packers are to run through the brutally competitive NFC North and bring another title to Titletown — it will require everybody’s best. Not just coaches and executives, and not just the star players, but also the guys whose names you may not know if you’re not an ardent Packers fan. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the new season. Generally, we go with one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent, and one underrated draft pick. We’re bending the rules a bit here, but when you look at this roster overall, it’s easy to get encouraged… to a point. Now, it’s time for the ghosts to go away. Underrated veteran: CB Keisean Nixon Back in 2022, Keisean Nixon was an angry young man . The 2019 undrafted free agent from South Carolina spent his first three NFL seasons with the Oakland/Las Vegas Raiders, and came to Green Bay in 2022 for his first season with the Packers. At that point, Nixon was more of an afterthought as both a cornerback and as a return man, but with his new team, things started to turn around. Not that Nixon was having any of it at first. “I did not wanna come here,” Nixon said last October when recalling his early time in Green Bay. “I hated it here when I first got here and I used to just be kind of miserable, just wasn’t comfortable, just trying to get to know guys, and stuff like that,” and It was Green Bay’s starting quarterback at the time — some dude named Aaron Rodgers — who got under Nixon’s skin in a good way. “Aaron used to always be like, ‘Why you so mad and angry?'” Nixon recalled. “When Kei first came, he carried himself like a No. 1 corner,” Rodgers said last year. “I always loved his confidence, and just everything he was about. He was a little bit angry sometimes, so I’d just always try to find him, give him a big ol’ hug and tell him I loved him. He was one of my favorite guys over the years, for sure. “I’m happy for Kei, the way he’s playing.” Nixon had his breakthrough as a return man, making First-Team All-Pro as a kick returner in both 2022 and 2023. Then, the path opened for his acceleration in development as a cornerback. He jumped from 169 to 633 coverage snaps in 2023, and he’s had at least that many in every season since. In 2025, he made the Pro Bowl as a defender for the first time. It’s a great story, and if Nixon can get a handle on the nuances of the position, he could make it even better. Right now, as is the case with a lot of less experienced cornerbacks, there’s a ton of boom-or-bust in his game. Last season, he allowed 55 catches on 88 targets for 623 yards, 117 yards after the catch, seven touchdowns, one interception, 17 pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 105.4. Nixon also had 11 penalties last season, so yeah… there is some work to be done. But if Nixon can turn some of those deflections into picks, and manage the St. Anger side of his play in a penalty sense, the sky is the limit. Keisean Nixon is quite the box of chocolates; you never know what you're going to get. Could be an awesome PBU. Could be a touchdown that's much more WTF. Would love to see him put it all together in 2026. pic.twitter.com/wmgBxqieLD — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 10, 2026 If Aaron Rodgers can spot it, that’s a pretty good sign. Underrated free agent traded player: LB Zaire Franklin Sometimes, I like to cheat with these things. When I saw that the Packers had traded defensive lineman Colby Wooden to the Indianapolis Colts for veteran linebacker Zaire Franklin in March, that certainly caught my attention. So, he’s not a free agent, but Franklin could do a lot for his new defense, despite the fact that he’s rarely discussed when the league’s most versatile linebackers comes up. The 6’0”, 235-pound Franklin, a seventh-round pick by the Colts in 2018, can do just about everything at a pretty high level. Last season for the Colts, he had three sacks, 19 pressures, 80 solo tackles, 39 stops, seven tackles for loss, and one forced fumble. In coverage, Franklin allowed 58 catches on 75 targets for 610 yards, 337 yards after the catch, two touchdowns, no interceptions, three pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 109.3. He also had 21 missed tackles last season, one of the highest totals for any linebacker in the NFL, but there are mitigating factors here. As far as the coverage stuff, the extent to which the Colts asked Franklin to cover the whole field was a bit much sometimes. Woo, buddy. The Colts asked LB Zaire Franklin to cover a LOT of ground last season. And he did it well for age 29. We'll see what plans the @packers have for him in 2026. pic.twitter.com/8Fwes3i1U9 — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 9, 2026 Regarding the missed tackles… yeah, he can clean that up a bit. Franklin has had more than 20 missed tackles in each of the last four seasons, so it is a thing. But it’s also part of a breakneck style that has served Franklin well more often than not. And again, when you ask a linebacker to play with this much range, there are going to be physical blunders. Not everybody can be Bobby Wagner in his prime. Another reason the Packers moved quickly to acquire Franklin once word got out that he was on the block for salary cap reasons is that the current linebacker group could use some veteran seasoning. Especially Edgerrin Cooper, whose ceiling is still undefined as he heads into his third NFL season. “I just feel like every moment that I’ve had in my career has prepared me for this moment,”…
author: Doug Farrar

title: Texans roster 2026: Kamari Lassiter, Reed Blankenship, Lewis Bond are underrated
summary: The 2025 Houston Texans will go down as one of the most remarkable “What If?” stories in recent NFL history. DeMeco Ryans’ defense, which ranked third in DVOA the year before, bumped it up to second last season, and the Texans were able to make that leap with about as “vanilla” a defense as you’ll […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JANUARY 18: Kamari Lassiter #4 of the Houston Texans looks on during an NFC Divisional Playoff game against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on January 18, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2025 Houston Texans will go down as one of the most remarkable “What If?” stories in recent NFL history. DeMeco Ryans’ defense, which ranked third in DVOA the year before , bumped it up to second last season, and the Texans were able to make that leap with about as “vanilla” a defense as you’ll find in the league these days. That’s a compliment, by the way. It’s not that Ryans and defensive coordinator Matt Burke were calling Matt Eberflus levels of genericism out there — there were some neat stunts and safety switches and whatnot — but these guys were playing at breakneck speed with evil intentions, and the playbook didn’t get in the way. The Seattle Seahawks ranked first in Defensive DVOA, but if you wanted to argue that Houston’s was even better, you wouldn’t hear too much dissent. Problem was, Seattle’s offense ranked 10th in DVOA , which was good enough to get them a Lombardi Trophy with a defense like that, while Houston’s offense ranked 19th. The real problem from last season reared its ugly head in the playoffs, when C.J. Stroud had the worst postseason DYAR since 1977, which is as far back as FTN’s (formerly Football Outsiders’) metrics go at this point. Which is what happens when you complete 41 of 79 postseason passes in two games for 462 yards, two touchdowns, five interceptions (including four picks in Houston’s 28-16 Divisional Round loss to the New England Patriots), and a passer rating of 51.8. (Apologies for the 2015 Brian Hoyer flashbacks, by the way). Stroud’s developmental issues over the last two seasons after his remarkable rookie campaign in 2023 have been distressing, but not unusual. You could ask Vince Young, Robert Griffin III, or Mac Jones about things going south after they looked so good to start. But if the Texans are to find themselves among the class of the NFL overall, they’ll need that offense to click up a bit. They’ll also need great performances from everybody on the roster — the stars like Stroud, of course, but also the guys whose names are not as well-known. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems on the 2026 Texans roster — one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent signing, and one underrated draft pick. Hopefully, they can help take the Texans from “What If?” to “We Did It!” Underrated veteran: CB Kamari Lassiter For that Texans defense to work as well as it does, it has to be about more than just the edge-rushers, or cornerback Derek Stingley Jr. I could have put five or six different Houston defenders in this spot, but the more I watched Kamari Lassiter’s tape last season and into this offseason, he had to be the guy. In 2025, the second-year man from Georgia was targeted a lot, and he was all about making opponents pay for their insolence. Lassiter saw 95 targets last season, the NFL’s seventh-most, and he allowed just 51 catches for 554 yards, 181 yards after the catch, five touchdowns, four interceptions, 17 pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 71.1. Any cornerback who is targeted that often will give up a few, but when Lassiter played in phase last season, he was dominant — especially in press coverage, where he allowed just 19 catches on 42 targets. When Kamari Lassiter is on point, receivers have no shot. Like, none. Derek Stingley Jr. isn't the only eraser in the @HoustonTexans ' secondary. pic.twitter.com/DRWnYlin7S — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 10, 2026 “I mean, he’s been who he is since he stepped out there on the field,” Stingley said in June of his estimable bookend. “He listens to whoever has anything to say to him, whether it’s coaching for him, or just letting him know what to do. But he’s also a leader to the young people that are on the team now. I wouldn’t say it’s competition, obviously, I want to see him make a play just like anybody else and I’m sure it’s the same for him to me, and everybody else. So, [if] he goes out there and has 20 picks this year, I’m like, ‘Come on, let’s do it again, keep on doing it.’ “But yeah, he’s going to keep on making plays just being who he is.” There’s no doubt about that, and if Lassiter cleans up the little things in Year 3, we could easily be talking about him as one of the NFL’s best at his position sooner than later. Underrated free agent: Safety Reed Blankenship The Texans defense also got smarter in free agency with the acquisition of former Philadelphia Eagles safety Reed Blankenship. Houston signed the undrafted Middle Tennessee State alum (Go Blue Raiders) to a three-year, $24.75 million contract with $16.75 million guaranteed, and if you talk with anybody familiar with Vic Fangio’s Eagles defense over the last few years, they’ll tell you that Blankenship was the green dot guy as much as anybody on those teams. Blankenship’s new teammates are already impressed. “He just jumped right in, and he’s just playing,” Stingley said of Blankenship earlier this month. “There were no drop-offs. There were no communication problems. It wasn’t forced. He’s a ball player. He’s been doing it in a different place, but now he’s with us. He’s just out there making plays like we know he can do.” 2025 was a bit of a down year statistically for the veteran — he allowed 32 catches on 45 targets for 379 yards, 92 yards after the catch, four touchdowns, one interception, two pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 116.8 — Blankenship’s highest to date in a season. Given that both Blankenship and Texans safety Calen Bullock played mostly in the deep third for their defenses last season, the plan could be to keep Bullock there, and move Blankenship around more, giving him box and overhang opportunities. Regardless, Blankenship is already very excited about his new defense. “From the outside looking in, especially playing in Philly, I was fortunate enough to be on a few really good defenses,” he said in his introductory press conference. “Sitting back and watching Houston fly around at times, I’m like, ‘Dang, this defense is legit.’ Fast forward to being able to play for [the Houston Texans] now, it’s crazy that a team like that wants me to come in and to perform at a high level. It speaks volumes. I feel like with me coming into this defense, I feel like I can give everybody a sense of calmness. That’s part of my game. I want to be the communicator out there. “I don’t want to step on anybody’s toes at all, but I want everybody just to play free. Play free, have fun and at the end of the day, just go and hit dudes. That’s just part of defense. I’ve always been coached like an old school type coach. I’ve been born and raised to go run and hit dudes for a living. I feel like this is a great fit. I know there’s a bunch of dawgs in the secondary, linebackers, defensive line, everywhere. I’m super, super excited, super stoked for this. I’m just ready to build that relationship between all the levels, for sure.” The 27-year-old Blankenship is more than a coach on the field — he’s still got some good tape — and the obvious hope is that he can return to his 2024 best. As if Houston’s defense needs even MORE intelligent smashmouth out there. Is it fair for the @HoustonTexans to have ANOTHER really smart defensive player who can do all kinds of stuff? Regardless, they now have Reed Blankenship to pair with Calen Bullock at safety. Blankenship was Vic Fangio's green dot guy, and everybody knew it. pic.twitter.com/tLs2UDsQvf — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 10, 2026 Underrated draft pick: WR Lewis Bond And now, back to that uncertain offense. It’s awesome that Tank Dell is back on the field after the gruesome injury stuff , though we’re still uncertain how it will all play out when the games begin. And we all know that Nico Collins is one of…

The plan is then […]

He also said Daniel Jones will not be playing in any preseason game. pic.twitter.com/eDEM6RyUG3 — WISH-TV News (@WISHNews8) August 11, 2026 The plan is then for Leonard to start a week later when the Colts host the Atlanta Falcons in preseason, with Richardson then coming in relief of him in the 2nd half of action. Of course, as noted above, Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones, who’s so far looked very sharp in training camp and has shown no lingering effects of last season’s Achilles tear, will not play in any preseason games. Regarding the Colts QB2 competition behind Jones with Richardson and Leonard as the challengers, neither backup quarterback has clearly separated himself from the other throughout training camp so far. Preseason could be an ideal opportunity for either backup quarterback to make their clear case for the QB2 job. Regarding Richardson, he’s still made the occasional ‘highlight reel’ throw in Colts camp, but it’s just a matter of achieving greater consistency. Of critical importance for Richardson will be showing that some of the fumbled snap issues he’s had in training camp are just an aberration and not a lingering issue of potential vision loss. Colts head coach Shane Steichen can’t accept unnecessary turnovers—and rightfully so, no NFL coach could. For what it’s worth, Leonard, who’s also had an up-and-down camp so far, reportedly had a strong showing running with the 2’s during Tuesday morning’s joint training camp practice with the Patriots just ahead of the two teams’ Week 1 preseason game.

title: Colts GM Chris Ballard clarifies no second PRP injection for WR Alec Pierce’s rehabbing ankle
summary: According to FOX59/CBS4’s Mike Chappell, Indianapolis Colts longtime general manager Chris Ballard clarified on Tuesday in Foxborough to the covering media that starting wide receiver Alec Pierce did not actually receive a 2nd PRP injection in late June—contradicting an earlier circulating report: The plan is still for Pierce to ready for the Colts regular season […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce (14) catches a pass Friday, July 25, 2025, during training camp held at Grand Park in Westfield. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co According to FOX59/CBS4’s Mike Chappell , Indianapolis Colts longtime general manager Chris Ballard clarified on Tuesday in Foxborough to the covering media that starting wide receiver Alec Pierce did not actually receive a 2nd PRP injection in late June— contradicting an earlier circulating report : Per Colts GM Chris Ballard: WR Alec Pierce did not have a second PRP injection. That being said, Ballard did indicate that Pierce’s injury was both to his ankle and heel . It will be interesting to see if Pierce can make it back by the time training camp ends, because the Colts have just four training camp practices left this offseason. Regardless, the Colts need their leading wide receiver back on the field sooner rather than later because the remaining outside receiving corps of Ashton Dulin, Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, and rookie Deion Burks looks a lot less formidable without his playmaking presence in the starting lineup as the team’s undisputed WR1.

title: Thursday could determine the Colts backup quarterback
summary: The starting quarterback for the Indianapolis Colts is known. Daniel Jones is back and appears to be at full strength. Nothing in the preseason is going to change that. Many starters’ roles are safe, but NFL teams are comprised of 53 players. Depth is needed behind those starters, and the preseason is the best opportunity […]
full_text: The starting quarterback for the Indianapolis Colts is known. Daniel Jones is back and appears to be at full strength. Nothing in the preseason is going to change that. Many starters’ roles are safe, but NFL teams are comprised of 53 players. Depth is needed behind those starters, and the preseason is the best opportunity to rise to the top and claim a role on a team. That is exactly why this Thursday could prove pivotal in the race to be the backup quarterback. One quarterback’s stock is high. Coming off an encouraging performance in Week 18 against the Texans, fans were buzzing about Riley Leonard, wishing they had gotten to see more of what he could do. The rookie impressed, but Houston wasn’t exactly putting their best foot forward. What we saw might not translate into real game action. Remember Sam Ehlinger, the preseason king? Who isn’t going to look better against backups? Nevertheless, seeing Leonard put on a show in the first preseason game will give him a definite edge towards the backup role. The other quarterback’s stock couldn’t be lower. A former fourth overall pick who can’t stay healthy and was on the trade block all offseason has plenty to prove. Anthony Richardson is on the comeback trail. That’s a long hard road. He fell from grace and will have to be twice as good as Leonard for consideration. He has to win back the trust of Shane Steichen, his teammates, and the fans. That won’t be easy, but it’s certainly possible. He has to impress on Thursday against the Patriots, or this might be the end. Will he get more reps as the preseason continues? Sure, but it might be too little too late. Is Thursday the end-all-be-all for either quarterback in the race to be Daniel Jones’ backup? Maybe not. You can bet, however, that Shane Steichen is going into this game with an idea of who he prefers. A bad performance from Riley Leonard or a stellar one from Anthony Richardson could create room for doubt. If neither bucks the current trend, look for Leonard to maintain his position in the driver’s seat.
author: Jon Spradley

title: 10 Takeaways From Jaguars First 2026 Depth Chart
summary: With joint practices against the New Orleans Saints finally arriving Thursday and preparations underway for Saturday’s preseason opener, the Jacksonville Jaguars released their first look at the pecking order, releasing the first (unofficial) depth chart of the 2026 season on Tuesday. While the first depth chart of the year should never be treated as a […]
full_text: With joint practices against the New Orleans Saints finally arriving Thursday and preparations underway for Saturday’s preseason opener, the Jacksonville Jaguars released their first look at the pecking order, releasing the first (unofficial) depth chart of the 2026 season on Tuesday. While the first depth chart of the year should never be treated as a final declaration of who will start in Week 1, it does provide an interesting snapshot of where several position battles currently stand. We break down our top takeaways from the first depth chart, including what it tells us about Jacksonville’s offensive line situation and which players may be making a serious push for starting roles. One Consistent Theme #Jaguars unofficial depth chart pic.twitter.com/YFeEufPJvv — Ryan O'Halloran (@ryanohalloran) August 11, 2026 Perhaps the biggest theme identified throughout the initial depth chart release is fairly straightforward: the players who were already in Jacksonville in 2025 generally remain ahead of the newcomers, for now. That doesn’t mean those positions are settled. In fact, some of the most intriguing battles are just beginning. But, it does mean that much of the hoopla surrounding the initial release may not mean as much as has been made about it by the media. That’s simply the blunt truth. Tuten OR Rodriguez One of the more interesting, yet expected, developments comes at running back, where Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez are listed as co-starters to open the offseason. Both players have generated plenty of discussion throughout the offseason, and the Jaguars appear to be keeping the competition open rather than handing the job outright to Tuten, as has been heavily expected throughout the offseason. How the workload eventually gets divided during the preseason, and what happens when the Jaguars face the Saints in joint practices, should provide a much better indication of where this battle may be headed. Mekari Retains Role Patrick Mekari is still listed ahead of Wyatt Milum at right guard, and that has understandably generated some reaction considering how Milum has performed at guard, while Mekari has been load managed with a back issue. Milum has taken a significant number of snaps at guard throughout the offseason and has looked good there. His work at tackle has been more inconsistent, although I’d describe it as generally fine. Some may look at the depth chart and wonder why Mekari remains ahead despite his limited workload. Personally, I think it’s simply too early to draw any major conclusions. The biggest tests of this competition haven’t happened yet. The last time I recall a big Mekari play from this offseason was the play that featured the long Chris Rodriguez run on the first day of padded work. If Milum is ultimately going to win this job, he’ll need to do it by demonstrating consistency in health and performance over the next several weeks. He’s going to get plenty of opportunities to make that case. Harrison at LT Perhaps the most fascinating development along the offensive line is Anton Harrison being listed as the starting left tackle. What initially looked like an experiment has now progressed to the point where it has to be taken seriously. The Jaguars have continued giving Harrison opportunities on the left side, and his placement atop the initial depth chart suggests this isn’t simply a temporary offseason curiosity. What started as an offseason experiment now appears to be a legitimate possibility for Jacksonville. Hunter’s Unique Spot Travis Hunter’s placement is another obvious headline. Hunter is listed as the starting cornerback while also appearing as the backup at wide receiver behind Brian Thomas Jr. While not a surprise, based on how Hunter has been used this offseason, it’s possible confirmation that should BTJ suffer any in-season injuries or knicks, Travis would likely be the receiver to step in as that alternative vertical threat in the offense. Meanwhile, he would continue his role as the starting corner. At least, that’s how I’m interpreting it, deciphering the unusual role Jacksonville is building for Hunter. How much he actually plays at each position during the preseason joint practices will also be something worth closely monitoring. Miller OR Combs At linebacker, Ventrell Miller and Branson Combs are listed with an “OR,” indicating another competition that remains open. Miller enters this offseason with plenty of experience in Jacksonville’s defense, but the team appears willing to give Combs a legitimate opportunity to challenge him. As with Tuten and Rodriguez, similar to the 2025 offseason where Miller opened the offseason as a co-starter with Devin Lloyd, the preseason and joint practices should provide more clarity than an initial depth chart ever could. Dickerson Gets First Crack The defensive line features one of the more intriguing surprises. 30-year old veteran defensive tackle Matt Dickerson is currently ahead of Ruke Orhorhoro as the backup at the 3-technique tackle spot behind Arik Armstead. Dickerson played a healthy 39% of defensive snaps (196) last season for Jacksonville. Following the Jaguars’ offseason trade that sent Maason Smith to Atlanta in exchange for Orhorhoro, it was reasonable to assume that Orhorhoro would have an inside track to that backup role. Apparently, that’s not a given. For now, Dickerson has been given the first opportunity on what could be described as an open runway behind Armstead. That doesn’t mean Orhorhoro has lost the competition. It means he has to take the job. He has, notably, flashed in multiple practices over the past week while rushing the passer. The next several weeks will be important for the third-year defensive lineman as he gets the opportunity to demonstrate why Jacksonville acquired him in the first place. Lewis Over Jarrian At slot corner, Jourdan Lewis remains ahead of Jarrian Jones. That isn’t necessarily surprising, particularly considering Lewis’ experience and his role as a leader. However, the circumstances surrounding this battle make it worth monitoring. Lewis has been limited or out through much of training camp as he continues working his way back from the foot injury that ended his 2025 season. Meanwhile, Jones has performed well and is widely viewed as a legitimate candidate to push Lewis for the starting slot role. For now, Lewis maintains his position on the depth chart. That could change as early as this week. Battle For CB3 Christian Braswell is currently listed as the No. 2 corner behind Montaric Brown. Jabbar Muhammad, meanwhile, is listed as the No. 2 corner behind Travis Hunter, as both players fight for potentially one spot. Those placements also offer a glimpse into how Jacksonville currently views its reasonably untested cornerback depth, particularly considering Hunter’s two-way role. However, Jarrian’s ability to play outside provides significant fluidity in how things could actually play out in case of a true injury. The bigger picture The most important thing to remember about this depth chart is that it’s only a snapshot, not a verdict. A consistent theme throughout Jacksonville’s initial release is that players who were already on the roster in 2025 generally remain ahead of the newer additions entering this week, which makes sense. Returning players have familiarity with the system, terminology, and staff. New additions still have to prove that they can translate their offseason work into consistent performance against NFL competition. In other cases, competing players have to prove they can remain healthy, while providing consistent outcomes to earn a role (IE: Wyatt Milum, Caleb Ransaw, Jalen McLeod, etc). The Jaguars are about to get their first real opportunity to evaluate several of these competitions against another team in joint practices with the Saints. Then comes the preseason opener this weekend. The initial depth chart tells us where Jacksonville stands today. The next three weeks will tell us where…

title: Jaguars Camp Notebook: Coen Confirms Starters To Sit vs Saints
summary: Jacksonville Jaguars training camp is entering its physical stretch, and Tuesday showed it. A 93-degree, burning, Florida afternoon, a pair of skirmishes, and a pre-practice roster move all made for one of the more eventful days of camp so far, with Thursdays joint-practice debut against the New Orleans Saints now squarely in view. Here are […]
full_text: Jacksonville Jaguars training camp is entering its physical stretch, and Tuesday showed it. A 93-degree, burning, Florida afternoon, a pair of skirmishes, and a pre-practice roster move all made for one of the more eventful days of camp so far, with Thursdays joint-practice debut against the New Orleans Saints now squarely in view. Here are our top takeaway from Tuesday’s practice at the Miller Electric Center Practice Fields. Many Starters To Rest Saturday Liam Coen made clear he isn’t expecting to see many starters on the field in Saturday’s preseason opener, once the Jaguars complete joint practices against New Orleans on Thursday. His expectation is that the ones and twos will handle the majority of the snaps, with the veterans held back after getting their primary on-field work on Thursday. Per Coen, The ones we’re planning on getting the majority of the work anyway in the joint, so hopefully we can survive with the ones and twos getting the majority of the joint, and then the younger guys, give them a little bit of a break so that they can play in the game.” Udinski primarily calling plays With the offensive coordinator Grant Udinski confirmed as the primarily play caller for Saturday, Coen confirmed that he would have more flexibility to be involved with defensive updates and conversations, in addition to being in charge of the challenge flag decisions. More importantly, Coen touched on Udinski’s possible challenges in calling plays for a roster with current injury limitations, along with normal preseason playbook limitations, as the team works through a numbers crunch at offensive line this week. “It’s challenging when you’re thin, and you have a limited inventory of plays. It’s not easy. Everybody thinks it’s really easy to come up with your preseason call sheet, and it’s actually a little challenging because you want to make sure that you do enough to do what is going to maybe give the defense a problem. But also, when you don’t have a ton of guys that have maybe repped it a lot, you’ve got to keep it simple. But it’s great exposure for him to work through situational football, get his flow a little bit of how he calls in and how he sees it within the system…” Tempers Flare The Florida heat brought some friction with it. One scrap broke out involving running back DJ Dallas, with a small punch thrown before it was broken up. A second, more heated exchange involved Jabbar Muhammad and Parker Washington, which took four players to separate. With joint practices on the horizon, the timing tracks, as these guys are clearly ready to hit someone that isn’t wearing the same colored jersey. Additions At Linebacker The Jaguars signed linebacker Amari Burney and waived cornerback Keni-H Lovely. Burney, 26, spent two seasons with the Las Vegas Raiders, appearing in 24 games (one start) and posting 27 tackles, five special-teams tackles, three tackles for loss, one sack, and a forced fumble. He was also a teammate of Ventrell Miller’s at Florida. Burney’s addition also comes on the heels of last Thursday’s signing of Jahlani Tavai, and together they provide additional depth to the linebacker room. With Parker Hughes profiling as a small-school developmental piece and Jack Kiser still working back from injury, the math on that group’s path to the final 53 is genuinely interesting to watch play out. OL Experimentation Patrick Mekari is still being limited to minimal teams work, Cole Van Lanen on the PUP, and Walker Little again missing practice after his mock scrimmage injury on Friday is probably not an ideal combination of circumstances. Emmanuel Pregnon returned with limited work after being dressed, though not practicing much in teams on Sunday. The Jaguars again mixed and matched up front, even more than prior days, with recently signed tackle Geron Christian again getting extended run at left tackle against the starting defense. Coach Coen commented on the need for increased repetitions for many of the depth offensive linemen, with joint practices and week one’s expectation that those players may be participating more. “You just get thin. You get thin. You start putting more reps on other guys that may not be truly prepared for the amount of reps that they then have to take, which, as you could see today, thins out a little bit of the groups. Your twos are more so mixed of threes and fours and it just kind of gets a little bit thinned out, unfortunately.” With the offensive line adjustments came would-be sacks from Dennis Gardeck, BJ Green, and Travon Walker in the teams period. The offensive line will need to heal up quickly to be ready by week one, with everyone working well together. "The communication on the back end has been good… It's always fun to see like who's going to be the next @dstriggow23 , @bjgreenII , – who are going to be those next guys?" Coach Coen on what he's liked from the defense. pic.twitter.com/iJm6Z0M3pa — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) August 11, 2026 Run Game Emphasis With the offensive line combinations in flux, the team leaned into more run-game work on Tuesday. Coen singled out Albert Regis and Arik Armstead as both having active days, noting that Regis took a notable step forward compared to his recent acclimation period. In whole, defense seemed to clearly win the day for the Jaguars, with Liam Coen somewhat mentioning same in his post practice availability. Coen confirmed that practice was cut short as a result of the defense’s dominant performance, which could be partially influenced by the offensive line limitations. Play Of The Day The passing game’s headline moment came on a Trevor Lawrence deep shot to Parker Washington down the sideline for a 40-to-45-yard gain, with Washington beating Travis Hunter off the line, stacking him, and finishing with strong hands. One-on-one matchups like that are exactly what camp is for, with Parker winning the rep and pushing the uber-competitive Hunter. Hunter’s Up & Down Day It wasn’t Travis Hunter’s cleanest outing. Beyond the deep ball he surrendered to Washington, he had a shot at a difficult one-handed reception in the seventh period that fell incomplete. It wasn’t clear whether he pulled up to avoid a collision with a nearby defender, but it looked like it cost him the play, only going up for the attempt with one hand. He settled in with a few shorter receptions later in practice to get back on track, however. CB Roster Battle Continues Christian Braswell came up with a strong last-second pass breakup against Brady Boyd, tracking the ball well with his back to the quarterback in an early period. A few reps later, Jabbar Muhammad answered with a PBU of his own covering Michael Wortham. These two both had notable days, something to keep an eye on with each possibly jockeying for one roster spot. Coen, again, praised Muhammad’s offseason progress following practice, as this camp battle continues. “I’d say Jabbar, you go back to the spring, he’s probably one of the most improved players on the team. He’s doing a heck of a job playing obviously corner and nickel. I’m excited. I want to see him get in the game mix. I remember last year in the first preseason game, he showed up on a play just like running it down from the other side of the field and you’re just excited to go see what that could look like. And if he’s truly taken that next step that we’ve seen, ultimately, we do need to see it in a game-like scenario.” What’s Next The Jaguars will hold a walkthrough Wednesday before departing for New Orleans, where they’ll practice with the Saints on Thursday, ahead of Saturday’s preseason Week 1 matchup.
