title: Ranking the Titans’ 5 projected wide receivers from best to worst
summary: The Tennessee Titans‘ passing offense ranked 30th in the league last season, averaging 166.1 yards per game. It was a collective issue on offense, with the wide receivers, offensive line, and play-calling deserving the majority of blame for the lack of success. That’s precisely why Mike Borgonzi made major offseason changes at wide receiver (and […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Nashville, TN, USA; Tennessee Titans wider receiver Carnell Tate (14) talks with the media post practice during day 1 of mini-camp at Vanderbilt Health Football Center. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | Steve Roberts-Imagn Images The Tennessee Titans ‘ passing offense ranked 30th in the league last season, averaging 166.1 yards per game. It was a collective issue on offense, with the wide receivers, offensive line, and play-calling deserving the majority of blame for the lack of success. That’s precisely why Mike Borgonzi made major offseason changes at wide receiver (and across the coaching staff). The Titans drafted Carnell Tate and signed Wan’Dale Robinson. Elsewhere, they’re relying on offensive coordinator Brian Daboll to drastically improve the aerial attack. Also taking Cam Ward’s sophomore growth into consideration, we’ve ranked the Titans’ projected top five wide receivers from best to worst. Carnell Tate The Titans drafted Tate at No. 4 overall to be Ward’s go-to playmaker for years to come. His combination of explosiveness and savvy route running could make him the passing offense’s primary read on most dropbacks in 2026. Tate could be in-line for an Offensive Rookie of the Year season. Wan’Dale Robinson Robinson is an easy projection into the offense because he played four seasons for Brian Daboll with the New York Giants. Expect Robinson to be the Titans’ most targeted receiver as he’s such a reliable and detailed route runner underneath the coverage. He’ll be Ward’s security blanket in the short and intermediate areas. Chimere Dike We’re projecting Chimere Dike to eventually take over as the primary No. 3 receiver. The rookie All-Pro as a special teamer flashed serious upside as a receiver down the stretch of 2025. Dike has legitimate juice as an explosive downfield threat and route runner. Calvin Ridley Calvin Ridley is an unknown commodity for the Titans heading into the 2026 campaign. He’s a former 1,000-yard receiver who is coming off a serious injury at his advancing age. It would be a huge bonus for the Titans if Ridley recaptured his previous effectiveness, but it’s a good thing they’re not totally relying on it happening. Elic Ayomanor Elic Ayomanor must compete for reps as a sophomore. He’s a red-zone threat and good blocker. Those two attributes could get him onto the field with Tate and Robinson in certain personnel packages. Securing reps over Dike and Ridley won’t come easy, but he’s certainly capable.

So I’m just looking forward to spilling that out for my team this year.” Two owners, four head coaches, four offensive coordinators, four wide receivers coaches, an astounding 15 starting quarterbacks, and yet, McLaurin always delivered. He recorded five straight 1,000-yard seasons from 2020 to 2024, and during his second Pro Bowl season (2024), racked up a career-high 13 touchdown catches. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN Brandon Coleman says he wishes he had trained like this in the past Coleman missed time in his rookie training camp because of a shoulder injury. From Weeks 9 to 17 as a rookie, he played every snap but missed 18 in the regular-season finale. “There’s injuries that I’ve had in the past during training camp,” Coleman said, “that fully could have been prevented if I would’ve just sacrificed a little more time in rehab and working on certain things.” To help, Coleman said he has taken more care to use preventative maintenance on his body — from how he stretches to how he eats, to his daily recovery sessions after workouts. He hired a nutritionist. He worked out with Dominic Studzinski, a former Ole Miss strength and conditioning coach who has trained Tunsil for more than a decade. “Just taking care of myself a lot better,” Coleman said. “There are priorities I didn’t do the first couple years that I just have to reflect on and kind of be accountable on. I changed that last year, but then even more this year.” That included spending several weeks training with Tunsil in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, this summer. “I dragged my wife out there to the middle of nowhere,” Coleman said. “What she understood is just really seeing how one of the greatest tackles ever does it. How do I need to live to give myself a chance to be like that guy?” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated The Good and Not So Good From Commanders’ Tenth Training Camp Practice Several veterans received maintenance days, which shifted reps to younger players and roster-battle candidates ahead of Wednesday’s joint session with Miami. On the day: Joshua Josephs continued forcing his way into the conversation, Antonio Williams produced multiple touchdowns, and Washington’s backup tight ends made several plays. Josephs beat Brandon Coleman with a rip move quickly enough that the play might have been a sack in live football. Later in the day, Josephs was able to disrupt things again with another would-be sack, this time on Marcus Mariota. It will be interesting to watch Josephs line up against the Dolphins tackles Wednesday to get a good sense of what we are working with there. His quickness and motor are impressive. Cager grabbed two touchdowns from Mariota, including a seam route on the first play of the two-minute period that left him open for an uncontested score. Yankoff continued to receive a healthy number of targets and added to a camp in which his athleticism and receiving ability have consistently stood out. The two have been forcing the Commanders to decide whether they want a fourth tight end and then who it should be, all at the same time. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Riggo’s Rag Javon Kinlaw set to be unleashed in new-look Commanders defense Kinlaw’s already loving how the plan is unfolding at training camp. He explained the variety to reporters after a recent practice . “I’m getting to play everywhere. The shade, the two wide, the three, the four, the five, the six. I’m playing it all, man. I’m loving how I’m getting to just give guys different looks and be all over the place, man. And I think it’s going to play to my strengths well, man. You know, give a lot of guys fits.” This is an intriguing, multi-faceted role for Kinlaw. One that only shows how much the Commanders still believe in his so far largely untapped talents. The new approach to deploying big No. 99 is also the latest example of how first-year play-caller Jones is willing to find creative ways to get underperforming senior personnel more involved . This isn’t the first time the Commanders have planned to move Kinlaw from the interior to the edge. Jones’ predecessor, Joe Whitt Jr., wanted to do the same , but there’s a little extra nuance to this year’s attempts to unleash the South Carolina product. First, the system Jones is likely to call, the type he learned from Brian Flores with the Minnesota Vikings, is more elaborate. He’ll use moving pieces to disguise coverage and pressure in ways Whitt rarely did. That’s good news for Kinlaw, who could find himself facing more one-on-one matchups against offensive linemen on the lookout for blitzing linebackers and defensive backs. Few individual blockers are going to want to stand up to the 6-foot-5, 319-pound player on the edge. title: Washington Commanders free agency: LB Curtis Jacobs signed
summary: The Commanders have added another linebacker to the mix, and it’s one diehard D.C. football fans should know well. Former DC Defenders linebacker Curtis Jacobs was signed to Washington’s roster, the Commanders announced on Tuesday. There was no corresponding move with this afternoon announcement, as Washington released two players earlier in the day, when the […]
full_text: The Commanders have added another linebacker to the mix, and it’s one diehard D.C. football fans should know well. Former DC Defenders linebacker Curtis Jacobs was signed to Washington’s roster , the Commanders announced on Tuesday. There was no corresponding move with this afternoon announcement, as Washington released two players earlier in the day, when the Byron Cowart signing was made formal. Jacobs joins an athletic position group featuring Sonny Styles, Leo Chenal and Frankie Luvu, plus Jordan Magee, Kain Medrano and Ale Kaho. Jacobs was signed by Kansas City as an undrafted free agent in 2024, but was also a Defenders draft pick that year. Jacobs had a practice-squad stints with a few teams, but never stuck around long. The Glen Burnie, MD, native and Penn State product had 42 tackles, a sack and a fumble recovery in 10 regular-season games with the Defenders. The 24-year-old will be added to the mix as a depth piece and, surely, a special-teams contributor. As a note,the Commanders released guard Sala Aumavae-Laulu and safety Rob McDaniel as part of the transaction to add Cowart on Tuesday morning.

title: How Stefon Diggs will change Washington Commanders offense this season
summary: Fans were banging the drum for additional help at wide receiver all offseason. They received it in the form of Maryland native Stefon Diggs. The team had reportedly been in talks with the free agent for some time and reached a favorable agreement early enough to integrate Diggs in time for the regular season opener. […]
full_text: Fans were banging the drum for additional help at wide receiver all offseason. They received it in the form of Maryland native Stefon Diggs. The team had reportedly been in talks with the free agent for some time and reached a favorable agreement early enough to integrate Diggs in time for the regular season opener. So, how will Diggs change the Commanders offense? Let’s put culture concerns aside and take a look at his fit within new coordinator David Blough’s proposed scheme. Diggs was very efficient in limited snaps last year. He played 55% of the New England Patriots offensive snaps but was first in catch rate and second in success rate in the entire league, while his 75% contested catch rate was the second-highest of his career. His productivity is proven over 11 seasons, which includes four consecutive Pro Bowl appearances and 11,504 receiving yards. Not only does that rank 38th all-time, but it’s also sixth among active players. Diggs has recorded seven 1,000-yard seasons in his career, including a 2020 campaign where he paced the league with 1,535 yards. Additionally, Diggs has the versatility David Blough looks for in his offense with the ability to play X, Z, or the slot role. Patriots offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels described his versatility as a “9 out of 10,” and he used Stefon in an approximately 50/50 mix between in the slot and as an outside receiver. Diggs wins with refined route running, tempo, and elite footwork. While the 32-year-old wide receiver has lost a step in terms of pure speed, he still has the ability to get the better of cornerbacks on the outside. That said, he thrives in the short to intermediate parts of the field and should be expected to run plenty of deep overs, high crossers and dig routes. Diggs is particularly adept at adjusting his routes to capitalize on space versus both man and zone coverage, with David Blough stating , “In just a couple days – he had four catches the other day, at least 2-3 today – the ball finds him because he finds space.” Big fan of the Stefon Diggs tape from last year. He clearly still has the juice and can separate at a high level. Here's a few of my favorites pic.twitter.com/vNC7kxj6Em — Nick Akridge (@nick_akridge) August 6, 2026 Yesterday, I broke down what new Commanders WR Stefon Diggs brings to Washington. Today, I'm looking at how he might fit in David Blough's new offense, with the flexibility to play Z or slot. Full breakdown: https://t.co/NXzV8AAU9r pic.twitter.com/jKm4ez8ZOu — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) August 7, 2026 There is one more statistic that I did not mention before but would like to touch on here. Diggs ranked eighth in total receiving yards on motion plays last year. Keep in mind, he only played half of the Patriots total offensive snaps, so the number shows how effective he can be was when used in motion concepts. Not coincidentally, Blough is expected to incorporate them heavily in his new offense. As Blough stated earlier in the offseason: I want it to be creative, aggressive, and I want whenever the coach on the other side turns the film on, I want them to feel stressed for every time we have the ball in our hands, of shifts, motions, breaking the huddle with urgency, getting us into premier plays.” This is how Diggs will alter Blough’s offense. He won’t change it conceptually but instead improve its effectiveness. Having another true threat opposite Terry McLaurin will allow Blough to stress the defense with motion and formation changes. If the veteran receivers line up on opposite sides, the defense must decide whether to shade safety help toward one boundary or the other. If Terry and Stefon align on the same side, Washington can stress and test communication through stacks and switch releases. Move either wide receiver into the slot; the defense has to reveal whether it will follow with a cornerback, pass the assignment to a nickel defender or change the coverage. Washington can also use orbit or return motion to identify man coverage pre-snap. Forcing those decisions helps provide a clearer picture of the defense for quarterback Jayden Daniels before the snap and reduces the amount McLaurin needs to win in static alignments. Diggs represents that threat, and for those that have been following training camp, you can quickly see how Diggs differs from the players Washington already had in the wide receiver room. Stefon Diggs looks GOOD!! That 18 ain’t bad either 👀 #Commanders #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/skLLjntt66 — Josh Taylor (@JoshTaylorFB) August 7, 2026 Being “multiple” out of heavy personnel only works if the offensive play calling stays balanced out of these looks. The addition of Diggs will also allow the team to be effective with only two wide receivers. Along with Chig Okonkwo at tight end and a dual-threat running back, the defense must choose between a lighter coverage group or a heavier run-stopping option. If they go light, the offense can run the ball. If they go heavy, they can isolate a receiver against a linebacker or safety. Signing Diggs will allow Blough to keep both options credible and force the defense to honor them improving both the passing and rushing attack. Just as importantly, Diggs gives Daniels another receiver he can trust, especially in hot reads and critical situations. Of Diggs’ 85 catches last season , 51 of them resulted in first downs, for a 60% conversion rate. That falls in line with how Stefon has been for most of his career, as he has accounted for 561 first downs during his time in the league. Diggs also knows how to separate and win quickly, which has increased importance following the loss of Laremy Tunsil to a triceps injury.…

title: Bill Croskey-Merritt among Commanders to watch in Dolphins joint practice
summary: The Commanders held several top players out of Tuesday’s training camp practice. That made logical sense.   Washington experienced a long, physical padded practice on Monday, with a late-morning joint practice against the Miami Dolphins on Wednesday. No sense in pushing it between those two important sessions.   The Commanders want to be ready for Wednesday’s […]
full_text: The Commanders held several top players out of Tuesday’s training camp practice . That made logical sense. Washington experienced a long, physical padded practice on Monday, with a late-morning joint practice against the Miami Dolphins on Wednesday. No sense in pushing it between those two important sessions. The Commanders want to be ready for Wednesday’s experience, which offers great benefit. Joint practices ramp up the level of competition, against new players and new schemes, in a more controlled environment without live tackling. Frontline players will get plenty of reps on Wednesday they likely won’t take in Friday night’s preseason opener against the Dolphins at Northwest Stadium. The first of two joint practices – the other occurs on Aug. 26 versus the host Baltimore Ravens – will provide a valuable progress report on Commanders training camp. There are several names to keep an eye/ear out for during this session over the preseason. Let’s discuss a few of them heading into Wednesday. RB Bill Croskey-Merritt You still can’t bring running backs to the ground in joint practices, but this might offer as clear an evaluation picture for Croskey-Merritt, who shouldn’t see many snaps in preseason games. Wednesday offers a great chance for him to show improvement in the passing game , as a receiver and a blocker, after hard work spent in that ares this offseason. He’s got to hold onto the football, though. Every drop is a big deal when ball security has been somewhat of an issue. WR Luke McCaffrey We get it. Depth charts released by the team are unofficial. But I used to work for a team and I know the head coach looks at it and has some say in how it reads. So, Luke McCaffrey being listed as a first-team receiver with Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs ain’t nothin’. By all accounts, McCaffrey has had a strong start to camp with made some big plays and contested catches in traffic. The battle for receiver snaps is fierce with the top veterans and rookie Antonio Williams. McCaffrey must capitalize on big moments like these joint practices and continue to shine. EDGE K’Lavon Chaisson The veteran edge rusher has been highlighted several times this summer as a disruptive presence. Can that continue against another team, especially against mobile Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis? DB Jeremy Reaves Head coach Dan Quinn has made a point to say veteran Jeremy Reaves has “earned the right” to compete for a first-team defensive slot. He’s in the mix at free safety, and the Commanders use a lot of three-safety looks. Reaves must continue his strong camp in this joint practice and continue to prove himself worthy of regular-season snaps. LT Brandon Coleman This one’s obvious. Every practice is an important test for the young player taking over for Laremy Tunsil . While Quinn made it clear Tuesday that Coleman is the Commanders’ starting left tackle, he must continue to inspire confidence in his teammates, especially quarterback Jayden Daniels, that he can get the job done. CB Rasul Douglas Trey Amos has missed most of camp, and is back on the sidelines with an ankle issue. That provides more first-team reps for a savvy cornerback with a penchant for creating turnovers. Douglas signed with Washington in July with an eye on regular playing time, and will continue pushing for the chance to start at on outside cornerback spot. TE Chig Okonkwo Okonkwo’s the type of player who might not see much time (if any) in preseason games. This joint practice should provide some insight into his receiving ability in a competitive environment and his use within the offense. Offensive coordinator David Blough won’t be giving away trade secrets, but watching Okonkwo function in-line and as a receiver will be important as we continue to see how he fits into this scheme. title: Daronte Jones, Commanders are challenging Sonny Styles to push limits
summary: Sonny Styles can do things other NFL linebackers can’t. Elite athleticism, rare physical skills and football smarts allow for that, which is why the sky’s so high for the No. 7 overall draft pick out of Ohio State.   The tough part, it seems, is convincing Styles to maximize those traits at this point in […]
full_text: Sonny Styles can do things other NFL linebackers can’t. Elite athleticism, rare physical skills and football smarts allow for that, which is why the sky’s so high for the No. 7 overall draft pick out of Ohio State. The tough part, it seems, is convincing Styles to maximize those traits at this point in camp. The rookie is naturally trying to do everything right and fulfill his schematic responsibilities perfectly. That’s not a bad thing. It’s not necessarily what Commanders coaches want during these training camp practices. They want Styles to push himself to the edge and attempt big plays others wouldn’t try. Now’s a perfect time to test his limits, with errors not costing the Commanders in games that count. “We’ve challenged him in that way and, you can see at times that he cuts it loose,” defensive coordinator Daronte Jones said after Tuesday’s training camp practice. “You can really see that speed on tape. That’s what most guys who are young and still playing tentative a little bit. That happens, but, alright, let’s go. I’d rather you go full speed and make a mistake than to be too slow and be right. That’s something all young players have to learn, their range of what they can and cannot do.” Head coach Dan Quinn said something similar last week. Styles’ aggressiveness is important for the player to learn his limits. It’s also key for the coaches to see how far they can push him and how much the rookie can do at this super-early point in his career. “I want to push him to make a mistake. Go for it,” Quinn said, per ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler . “Take the shot right here. I want to encourage him. He’s such a respectful, do-it-right [guy]. No, you can make that play and the other guys can’t. So, you have permission to try it. Where are the spaces I can get to? If you can, all right. If not, we know it’s not the right call.” Styles knows the assignment. While he’s not pushing the limits physical contact – there have been times when he appropriately thudded a ball carrier over blowing them up – he’s starting to go for it a bit more. He understands the attacking nature of Jones’ defense and his role within it. “We like playing offense on defense. We like to determine the numbers,” Styles said in a Saturday interview with NFL Network. “We’re playing on our terms. I love that mindset. The way he teaches it, too, is so easy to digest information. … The stuff is just super easy to understand. Sometimes you look at it and it seems complex, but it’s easy for us. He has done a great job with that.” Our full interview with #Commanders LB Sonny Styles, the rookie who walked up the hill to see us instead of getting the cart ride the veterans usually get around here. “I’ve got some fresh legs. I’ll be all right.” pic.twitter.com/ioVNQQIT5S — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) August 8, 2026 Despite being faster than most at this level. Styles is still going through speed-of-the-game adjustments transitioning to NFL football. It may not come with footspeed but instead a decreasing margin for error or hesitance. “When switched to linebacker (from safety, at Ohio State), I started to feel routes a little bit,” Styles said in that NFLN interview. “As I’ve gotten better over time, I’ve started feeling them more and more. Now, the biggest adjustment is that the ball’s coming out so fast and so precise that you have to get there faster. You can drop and the guy’s five yards away, but if No. 5 (Jayden Daniels) is throwing the ball, it’s going to be there now. The timing and the accuracy on throws … you have to get there faster.”

title: Commanders Camp Talk: Practice updates from Dan Quinn and Daronte Jones
summary: The Washington Commanders training camp rolls on for Day 10 in Ashburn, VA. The team was in pads yesterday, but will have a lighter practice on Tuesday. The Commanders are hosting the Miami Dolphins on Wednesday with a later start time, and that session should be loaded with action for fans to watch. Head coach […]
full_text: The Washington Commanders training camp rolls on for Day 10 in Ashburn, VA. The team was in pads yesterday, but will have a lighter practice on Tuesday. The Commanders are hosting the Miami Dolphins on Wednesday with a later start time, and that session should be loaded with action for fans to watch. Head coach Dan Quinn spoke to reporters before the start of Tuesday practice. Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones is scheduled for his first Q&A of training camp after practice, along with players getting interviewed on the field. Nick Allegretti (calf) and Trey Amos (ankle) will both miss the first preseason game vs the Dolphins on Friday night. Quinn said he expects Allegretti to be on the field when the team returns to practice on Sunday, but Amos needs to be reevaluated after landing awkwardly while covering Terry McLaurin shortly after returning to practice. Washington is dealing with a more serious injury that will affect most, or all of the season depending on if Laremy Tunsil can return from a torn triceps. Brandon Coleman is shifting over to left tackle from a position battle at guard. He’s the starter there again, a position he has started 18 games at over his first two years in the NFL. Quinn said Tunsil’s injury isn’t ideal, but the team has confidence in Coleman and he’s put he work in to be able to take over. Quinn praised Stefon Diggs’ high football IQ, and said his addition could shift roles for other players, though he’s also elevating his new teammates. That’s especially true for the younger players. Quinn talked about other veterans like Van Jefferson, who he called “exacting, sits down in the zone, the catch location, so…man is that a good feeling for a QB. OK, this zone, right spot, right location, get the right yards.” Treylon Burks slimmed down this year, and Quinn said he’s been able to go faster and be more athletic with his lighter weight. He brought up big catches on the sidelines and on the field as examples of that. title: Commanders News: Offense still sharp with Brandon Coleman at left tackle
summary: The Daily Slop – August 11, 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room […]
full_text: The Daily Slop – August 11, 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) What can the Commanders expect to get from Brandon Coleman? [I]t’s easy to forget that Coleman actually filled in for Tunsil a few times down the stretch last year and held up relatively well. In the run game, I think Coleman will be absolutely fine. He showed he was a strong run blocker when he started at left tackle in 2024 and even when he struggled at guard last year, he was still good in the run game. The Commanders are expected to become more of an outside zone run team this year and Coleman has the athleticism to play that scheme to a high level. A lot of lineman struggle to make blocks in space because linebackers and defensive backs are more agile than them and can avoid the block, but Coleman uses his momentum and runs over [defensive players], bulldozing [them] to the ground. It shows off incredibly range and athleticism in the run game, which should be a strength for Coleman even as the starting left tackle. But Coleman’s issues as a rookie left tackle weren’t in the run game. His pass protection was inconsistent, often flashing some nice moves but frequently mixed in some poor reps too. Let’s start with the positives first. In 2024, he took on a variety of good pass rushers and had some nice reps against all of them. He was particularly efficient with a hand flash technique that got the better of both Brian Burns and Trey Hendrickson, two of the better pass rushers in the NFL. With star LT Laremy Tunsil injured, the Commanders are likely to turn to Brandon Coleman as his replacement. But what can the Commanders expect to get out of Coleman and how can they help him? I took a closer look: https://t.co/e1cdYdjZnp pic.twitter.com/aoylwFF1TT — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) August 10, 2026 Commanders.com Commanders confident Coleman can move back to tackle after ‘excellent’ offseason Coleman was the Commanders’ original plan for the position. There was some ambiguity among scouts on his role as an NFL player, but general manager Adam Peters and Quinn felt like he could be a quality tackle because of his size (6-foot-4 ½, 313 pounds), nearly 35-inch arms and smooth footwork. Although he missed some time in training camp, he ended up winning the job and received the seventh-best offensive grade among his fellow rookie offensive tackles from Pro Football Focus. The additions of Tunsil at left tackle and Conerly at right during the 2025 offseason forced Coleman to move to guard, where the Commanders felt he could still contribute because of his physicality in the running game. Coleman…did start the last three games at left tackle and allowed just two pressures on 87 pass blocking snaps. The transition back to tackle, Coleman said, is “kinda like riding a bike.” he looked natural working at the position during Monday’s practice. “We know that he’s ready for it,” Quinn said. “He’s put in an excellent offseason.” The transition from tackle to guard and back has not been a difficult one for Coleman. He tried to stay prepared for any possibility, even taking reps at center, because “you never know what happens. “My feet are good,” Coleman said with a smile, “so being able to dance with those guys, I’m able to keep up. And now that I’m getting my hands under control in terms of knowing where to punch, knowing what I wanna do, that stuff just helps out my feet even more.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) Tunsil’s mentoring helped prepare Brandon Coleman to take his place Coleman said moving back to tackle is “like riding a bike” and hasn’t been a difficult transition because of his experience at the position. The more impactful change has come from his work away from the field. He spent much of the offseason in Tuscaloosa, Ala., training alongside Tunsil, who has become a mentor to Coleman and Conerly and invited both down to take part in his offseason training regimen. For several weeks, the three were immersed in Tunsil’s preseason boot camp , which includes on-field work with Tunsil’s personal offensive line coach, Mike Wahle; strength and conditioning work with his longtime strength coach, Dominic Studzinski; nutritional expertise from dietician Jacob Mertens; and customized meals courtesy of Tunsil’s personal chef, Ronald Shaw. For Coleman, the work was about both prepping for the season and learning what it takes to be a top offensive lineman. The Commanders replaced him at left guard last season in part because of nagging injuries that, Coleman believes, could have been prevented with better habits. “There’s priorities that I didn’t do the first couple years that I just had to reflect on and kind of be accountable on,” he said. “I changed that last year, but then even more this year. That’s why I went with Laremy for that month, and dragged my wife out there to Alabama, the middle of nowhere. But she understood. It’s just really seeing how one of the greatest tackles to ever do it does it. Like, how do I need to live to give myself a chance to be like that guy?” Coleman said he’s already incorporated some of Tunsil’s regimen into his own. He now uses Mertens regularly for nutritional guidance. He also hired a local chef to prepare meals, has used the coaching points and techniques Wahle taught him over the summer and started using some of the recovery modalities that helped him in Alabama. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated The Good and Not So Good From Commanders’ Ninth Training Camp Practice Brandon Coleman responded well in his first day replacing Laremy Tunsil, while Jayden Daniels stayed sharp and Washington’s kicking competition took a major step backward It is important to remember that while he is not Tunsil, Washington drafted Coleman to play tackle, and he started there for 12 games during his rookie season before eventually moving inside last year. Coleman’s day was highlighted by holding his own on one rush against Odafe Oweh , carrying him out of the play rather than allowing him to turn the corner. No one is expecting Coleman to miraculously become Tunsil, but the team is desperate for him to be competent enough to secure the spot. Andrew Wylie also received work at left tackle, giving Washington another option behind Coleman, but it’s important to remember that Wylie has only played a handful of snaps at the position in live game action. One name that is not going away on defense is Joshua Josephs, who was able to get his hands on Marcus Mariota for a sack during Monday’s practice. Josephs has repeatedly shown up in padded practices and has me legitimately ready to watch him closely once preseason starts. The proverbial bottom fell out of the kicking competition Monday as Jake Moody went 2-for-6, missing four straight field goals from 44, 49, 51 and 55 yards, while Drew Stevens did not fare much better, going 3-for-6, missing from 39, 51 and 55. Moody has hit a really bad spot now with 11 misses over the last four practices, after starting camp matching Stevens, kick-for-kick . Moody was not alone in having a bad day, as Stevens also posted his worst day of camp, and it was a moment he was not able to capitalize on Moody’s collapse. Moving forward, Stevens still has the advantage based on the larger body of work, but his first truly bad day keeps this from becoming a settled competition before the joint practice and preseason opener. Washington’s offense has now committed six pre-snap penalties over the last two practices, with the latest coming on third down during Monday’s two-minute drill. The reason something like this matters? A third-down penalty during a two-minute situation is exactly the type of procedural mistake that can sabotage an…

title: What have 2026 NFL rookies spent their first paychecks on?
summary: Jeremiyah Love, Drew Allar and Carnell Tate are among the NFL rookies who just got their first pro contracts. How did they spend their new money?
full_text:
For NFL rookies, that first paycheck represents more than just a payday. After years of working toward the league -- which kicks off Thursday with a full slate of Week 1 preseason games  -- many first-year players have used that money on long-awaited purchases and priorities.

 For some rookies, it's a new car. For others, it's a house or an opportunity to take care of their parents. And then there are those who aren't ready to spend a dime.

 Buffalo Bills fourth-round pick Skyler Bell , who said NIL money at UConn helped him buy his first car, is already eyeing his next ride -- "maybe like an AMG or something." New Orleans Saints sixth-round pick Barion Brown has a different approach: "Nah, I'm a sixth-round guy, man. I've got to save every penny I can get!"

 Here's a look at what some of the NFL's top rookies told ESPN's NFL Nation they have done or plan to do with their first professional paycheck.

 

 
 Jump to a category: 
 Savings, investing | Homes, goods 
 Sports equipment | Apparel | Family 
 Travel, vehicles | Electronics | Exotic pets 

 
 

 

 Savings and investing 

 

 Jeremiyah Love , RB, Arizona Cardinals 
 Round 1, No. 3 | Age: 21 

 Love hasn't been shy about how he's going to spend his rookie contract, which is worth a fully guaranteed $53.9 million over four years -- or rather, how he won't be spending his rookie contract. Love said he plans to live off his endorsement money and not spend his NFL paychecks. He has deals with PayPal, New Balance and Celsius. Reports put Love's NIL valuation at Notre Dame at around $600,000, which Love said taught him how to live off what he already makes.

 "I'm not going to touch the money," he said. "I'm probably going to put it all away and live normally like I've been doing now."

 

 

 Arvell Reese , LB/Edge, New York Giants 
 Round 1, No. 5 | Age: 20 

 Reese also won't being spending big, even though his deal includes $47.8 million guaranteed. "I just signed it and then went to the hotel and then just got ready for the practice the next day," Reese said. "I don't really got [anything] to buy right now. I already got everything. I got a car and an apartment. So, I'm good right now."

 

 

 Malachi Lawrence , Edge, Dallas Cowboys 
 Round 1, No. 23 | Age: 23 

 "I got a truck, a TRX, that was my first purchase, but that was with NIL. It wasn't with my bonus," Lawrence said.

 So, what about his NFL money?

 "I haven't spent really any of that yet. I think like 70% of the players after the NFL go bankrupt or something like that, and I want to be in that 30%."

 
 

 Peter Woods , DT, Kansas City Chiefs 
 Round 1, No. 29 | Age: 21 

 "I wouldn't say there is [anything specific I want to buy]," Woods said. "Nah, I'm just kind of letting my money make money right now. I had a pretty blessed college situation [at Clemson]. It's a different landscape [now]. It allows me to kind of be disciplined in that area. I'm not really worried about it, for real."

 
 

 Zachariah Branch , WR, Atlanta Falcons 
 Round 3, No. 79 | Age: 22 

 The Falcons' rookie wide receiver wants to be frugal, the way his parents taught him to be. Branch said he has already spent "a little bit" of his NFL money but on an investment in the stock market. Specifically, S&P 500 companies. "I think I'm all good right now," said Branch, a third-round pick. "I don't think I'm in a position to get to doing certain things that's not smart. I'm trying to create generational wealth. So, whatever comes it may come, but right now I think I'm good on the investments and just food, family."

 

 Eventually, the Georgia product said he wants to get into real estate. His father, Sheva, is a prominent realtor in the family's hometown of Las Vegas. "Trying to get some properties and things like that to expand my real estate portfolio," Branch said.

 

 

 Homes and household goods 

 

 Blake Miller , OT, Detroit Lions 
 Round 1, No. 17 | Age: 22 

 Miller isn't looking to purchase anything crazy but is looking to buy a home. "I'm trying to be smart with it and not be a big, big spender," Miller told ESPN. "But, I guess a place to live would be it." Miller, who was selected by Detroit as the 17th pick, learned the value of being smart with his finances from his parents and by managing his money at Clemson from 2022 to 2025, where he started all 54 games of career.

 "Obviously being in college in the whole NIL era, that helped a little bit because I kind of was there when it was getting going and you get to see the progression of it," Miller said. "Like guys now, you don't just get a big chunk of money deposited in your account. You're still making good money, but it's not as crazy as it is now. So, I feel like that kind of helped me be able to deal with more and more money, and then my parents as well set a good example. They're always there with questions or anything, and they're really helpful."

 

 

 Jadarian Price , RB, Seattle Seahawks 
 Round 1, No. 32 | Age: 22 

 With some of the $8.7 million in signing bonus money he received as the 32nd pick in the draft, Price bought his family a new house in his hometown of Denison, Texas. It was something he has wanted to do since he was young and his biggest goal once he reached the NFL. "Checked that off the list," he said. His family's reaction? "A bunch of smiles," Price said.

 

 

 Treydan Stukes , S, Las Vegas Raiders 
 Round 2, No. 38 | Age: 24 

 "I actually got a house," Stukes said. "I went the real estate route. That was the big purchase, and everything else went into the savings [account]."

 
 

 Jacob Rodriguez , LB, Miami Dolphins 
 Round 2, No. 43 | Age: 23 

 "I went and got a bed," Rodriguez said of his first purchase. "I went and got a mattress. So, you know, in college for a little bit, when I was a walk-on, I slept on the ground in my brother's apartment. And so like, I'd never slept good when I was 13 and on, and so then I moved to the college, like three-inch mattress or whatever. So I never bought a mattress until I was [drafted] because I always said my first purchase is going to be a bed. So, I bought a nice Tempur-Pedic."

 

 

 Brandon Cisse , CB, Green Bay Packers 
 
 Round 2, No. 52 | Age: 21 

 Cisse's first paycheck wasn't his first payday. "I had mostly all my stuff already thankfully because of my NIL deals and stuff like that," he said. "But I was able to purchase a house for my family. At the time I purchased the house, I was having a daughter. Now she's here, so that's why I wanted to buy a house here in Green Bay." His daughter was born on July 17, just before training camp opened.

 
 

 

 Antonio Williams , WR, Washington Commanders 
 Round 3, No. 71 | Age: 22 

 

 The third-round pick from Clemson made one big purchase. "My first big purchase was a home about 10 minutes away from the [Commanders'] facility. I'm not a big spender. I feel that was a good investment. No cars, nothing crazy, man. I didn't want to make any dumb decisions."

 

 Sports equipment 

 

 Caleb Lomu , OT, New England Patriots 
 
 Round 1, No. 28 | Age: 21 

 

 "I'm not really a guy who spends too much money, but one of the first things I got was a new golf set," Lomu said. "I'm big into golf. I love playing some golf. I had to get some longer ones. I kind of outgrew my old set."

 

 Family support 

 

 Jordyn Tyson , WR, New Orleans Saints 
 
 Round 1, No. 8 | Age: 22 

 "I sent my dad some money. I looked at his USAA account. ... I was like, let me give Pops some money. [I didn't tell him]. When he saw me, he just gave me a hug," Tyson said. "For myself, I bought a house. I'd say that was the big thing."

 

 

 Zion Young , Edge, Baltimore Ravens 
 Round 2, No. 45 | Age: 22 

 Young, who is the youngest of 11 siblings, used the money to help his parents. "My parents have [had] a house full of kids my whole life," Young said. "The first thing I wanted to do was put a little money in their pockets and pay for some [house] renovations." Now, Young is supporting his…

title: 2026 Arizona Cardinals training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Cardinals training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The Arizona Cardinals ' camp is at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona, and Cardinals reporter Josh Weinfuss has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Cardinals camp. We will update this file often. How will Arizona's quarterback situation shake out with  Jacoby Brissett  back on a reworked contract? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive into all the updates and check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Thursday.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest on the Cardinals 
 
 Tyler Allgeier 'building' relationship with rookie RB Jeremiyah Love 
 Source: Cardinals' Brissett guaranteed $15.5M in reworked deal 
 Cardinals TE Trey McBride walks back dig at Arizona fanbase 
 Sweat (knee) among four Cards added to PUP list 
 With deal done, Brissett can focus on Cardinals' playbook 
 
 

 Aug. 11 

 The Cardinals' starters will make their preseason debut Thursday night on the road against the Las Vegas Raiders , coach Mike LaFleur said Tuesday. They'll play one drive, for sure, and possibly two at most.

 Quarterback Jacoby Brissett said he's looking forward to getting hit for the first time since January and starting to run the Cardinals' new offense in real time. But the goal in a drive or two is simple, he said.

 "Obviously, new coach, new system, operation hearing him in the headset, going out there in the game and just clean communication and operation in and out of the huddle, I think that's the mindset of this game," Brissett said.

 More observations: 

 
 The Cardinals broke training camp at State Farm Stadium in Glendale on Tuesday. They'll fly to Las Vegas on Wednesday, play the Raiders on Thursday and when they practice again over the weekend, it'll be at their practice facility in Tempe. 
 Second-year defensive lineman Walter Nolen III was wearing a brace on his left elbow and had both his hands wrapped. LaFleur said Nolen's hands were "good." 
 

 

 Aug. 10 
 Despite expressing his desire to keep Michael Wilson in Arizona long-term, Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort didn't seem too sure that he'd be able to get an extension done with the receiver.

 When asked Monday if he expects to get a long-term deal done with Wilson, who had his first 1,000-yard season in 2025, Ossenfort wouldn't commit to the idea.

 "He's a guy that we want around here a long time," Ossenfort said. "There's no question about it. So, I mean, expect, that's a tough word.

 "I mean, I think our interest is in keeping him here and Michael's been a good player for us. He's going to continue to be a good player for us. So, I know coach [Mike] LaFleur feels the same way and we want Michael here for a long time."

 The two sides have already been negotiating, however, a deal has yet to be agreed upon.

 

 More observations: 

 
 Ossenfort didn't want to get into talks about an extension with left tackle  Paris Johnson Jr ., whose fifth-year option the team picked up for next season. "Honestly, just going to keep extension talks between us. Never really talked about that and don't really want to plan on getting into that." 
 Ossenfort said he always thought he'd get a new deal done with quarterback Jacoby Brissett and said that sometimes negotiations take a while. "This one was no different. And so I think that involves communication back and forth. And we had a lot of conversations over the course of those, the spring, throughout the summer up into training camp. So no, there's never a doubt in my mind that it was going to get done." 
 

 

 Aug. 9 

 Cardinals starting quarterback Jacoby Brissett struggled with the deep ball throughout practice Sunday, missing approximately seven deep balls. Some were long. Some were wide. Four were to Marvin Harrison Jr .

 It was an atypical performance from Brissett, who, until Sunday, had been consistent with his deep balls throughout training camp, typically putting them in a place where only his receivers can catch them.

 After practice, Brissett set out to rectify his misses.

 He and Harrison spent about 15 minutes working on deep balls from approximately 30 yards. It looked as though Brissett was working on his deep touch to get his passes where Harrison can make a play.

 
 Rookie quarterback Carson Beck had a strong finish to Sunday's practice. He hit rookie wide receiver  Reggie Virgil  for a touchdown in the back of the end zone and had a quiet celebration to himself afterward. That came after Beck hit wide receiver Bryson Green on a deep ball but then threw an interception. 
 The Cardinals tried a variety of defensive lineups Sunday. At one point, third-year cornerback Elijah Jones , who has played defense in just one game in his career, took first-team snaps. Second-year defensive back Kitan Crawford , who played 12 games on defense last season, also got some first-team reps. 
 Wide receiver Ihmir Smith-Marsette continued his impressive camp with another touchdown Sunday. He continues to make big catches and has been consistently making plays throughout camp. 
 

 

 Aug. 4 
 Thursday night's Hall of Fame game will not just be a run-through for the players, it will also be the first time the Cardinals' coaching staff will have a chance to be together during a game.

 "I think that's another great thing for us to have this game, to just get a little quick dry run-through on how game day operations go, just from time management, all that stuff," offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett said. "I think it's going to be great for all of us and there'll be some ups and downs and you work through those and grow every day."

 Hackett said he'll be in the booth watching the action unfold from above but with new coach Mike LaFleur calling the plays and quarterback coach Matt Schaub handling Carson Beck , Hackett will be able to help whoever needs help. But that'll also be part of this staff's first time together: Figuring out his role in all of it.

 More observations: 

 
 Even though Josh Sweat hasn't practiced this camp and there isn't a set timeline for his return, defensive coordinator Nick Rallis said Tuesday that Sweat is "locked in" with meetings and post-practice tape. 
 

 
 Aug. 3 
 Deep balls were the theme of the day for the Cardinals as Jacoby Brissett ,  Gardner Minshew II  and Carson Beck put on an aerial display.

 Brissett unleashed a bomb to Marvin Harrison Jr ., who, after letting a deep ball earlier in practice go off his fingertips, came down with a diving grab that would have gained more than 50 yards.

 Beck showed off his deep ball, hitting fellow rookie Reggie Virgil on a beautiful pass. On another deep shot, Beck froze two defenders in the second level before finding a receiver who made the catch a step in front of a defender.

 More observations from the day:  

 
 Tight end Trey McBride was banged up briefly after he was hit in the middle of the field. He went down and was slow to get up but later returned to the offensive drills. 
 The tip drill paid off for the defense on two different plays Monday. On one, defensive lineman  Zachary Carter  tipped a pass by Minshew and L.J. Collier came down with it. On another play, defensive lineman  Roy Lopez  batted down a Beck pass. 
 The catch of the day came from Virgil, who made an impressive one-handed catch in mid-air as he was falling to the ground on a pass from Beck along the sideline. 
 

 

 Aug. 2 
 Jacoby Brissett continues to get more and more comfortable with the offense, as was evident Sunday.
 He had seven drives with the first-team offense, totaling 29 snaps, and finished 13-for-16 passing…

title: 2026 Atlanta Falcons training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Falcons training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The Atlanta Falcons ' camp is taking place in Flowery Branch, Georgia, and Falcons reporter Marc Raimondi has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Falcons camp. We will update this file often. How will the QB battle play out between  Michael Penix Jr . and  Tua Tagovailoa for QB1? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Falcons stories 
 
 Sources: Falcons, RB Robinson reach 3-year deal worth up to $75M 
 Falcons sign Matthew Bergeron to four-year, $96M extension 
 Falcons' Jalon Walker tore ACL, out for season 
 Wife of DC Ulbrich dies of cancer 
 
 
 

 Tuesday, Aug. 11 
 Quarterback Tua Tagovailoa has been a full participant in practice for about a week now. And his performances have really turned the corner since late last week.

 Tagovailoa was 7-of-7 passing in 11-on-11 team sessions Tuesday. The tight back issue seems to be in the rearview mirror and Tagovailoa is starting to show comfortability with this new offense under head coach Kevin Stefanski and offensive coordinator Tommy Rees.

 "Oh, he's getting better every day," Falcons quarterbacks coach Alex Van Pelt said Tuesday. "I think he's becoming more comfortable with the system and the play calls and protection adjustments and everything. It's tough always to come into a new system. So, picking that up -- missing the first part of camp set him back just a little bit -- but really the last three or four days he's really come on."

 
 The Falcons defense is dealing with some injuries. Safety Jessie Bates III (back), inside linebacker Divine Deablo , defensive back Natrone Brooks and cornerback Avieon Terrell all missed practice Tuesday. Defensive tackle  Da'Shawn Hand  has been out since last week. 
 The Falcons signed veteran running back Trey Sermon to add depth behind Bijan Robinson and Brian Robinson Jr ., who has gotten some run as a kick returner. Sermon will complete with Tyler Goodson , Nathan Carter and Cash Jones to make the 53-man roster. 
 

 

 Monday, Aug. 10 
 Quarterback Michael Penix Jr . is still not cleared for 11-on-11 sessions, but he has mostly been sharp in practice lately.

 On Monday, Penix was 9-of-11 passing during a 7-on-7 series, including a beautiful completion to tight end  Kyle Pitts Sr . down the right sideline. The throw was right in the bucket and would have gone for a big gain. Penix did get picked off by cornerback Clark Phillips III on his final throw.

 Tua Tagovailoa was 4-of-6 in 11s and working more on pushing the ball down the field.

 Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski said he has not yet made a decision on whether Tagovailoa will play in the team's first preseason game Friday against the Denver Broncos . As for Penix, he can't play in any game until he is cleared for 11s in practice, Stefanski said.

 More observations: 

 
 The Falcons signed defensive end Cameron Sample , who was waived last week by the San Francisco 49ers . Sample will provide depth off the edge after second-year standout Jalon Walker went down with a torn ACL last week. 
 Right tackle Jawaan Taylor was activated from the reserve/physically unable to perform list. He is likely to be the team's starting right tackle. The Falcons have been rotating Michael Jerrell , Brandon Walton and rookie seventh-rounder Ethan Onianwa in that spot. 
 

 

 Saturday, Aug. 8 
 Quarterback Tua Tagovailoa had his best practice of camp, though it did not last long. The practice, that is.

 Lightning halted the Falcons' open practice at Lanier High School in Sugar Hill, Georgia, early on Saturday night. There was still more than 30 minutes left when things were called on the field of a packed stadium.

 Tagovailoa was 6-of-8 passing in 11-on-11 drills, including his best two passes of training camp: a 30-yarder with touch to wide receiver Jahan Dotson and a play-action rollout lob to wide receiver Drake London .

 Tagovailoa returned to full practices earlier this week after dealing with a tight back to start camp.

 
 

 
 
 Friday, Aug. 7 
 Quarterback Tua Tagovailoa hit running back Bijan Robinson on a wheel route that would have gone for a 90-yard touchdown or so during an 11-on-11 session Friday. The series was situational. The Falcons offense was backed up against the opposite goal line and Tagovailoa floated it nicely to Robinson, who had complete daylight.

 It was just another play in another practice this summer here in Flowery Branch, Georgia. But it also felt like more than that, something symbolic. Like a sigh of relief.

 For the first time this training camp, Tagovailoa and Robinson were both full participants in practice. Tagovailoa has been dealing with a tight back and Robinson was a hold-in before signing a three-year contract extension Wednesday that is worth up to $75 million. Robinson got his first carries in 11s Friday.

 More observations: 

 
 Quarterback Michael Penix Jr . is still not cleared for 11s, but has looked sharper lately in 7-on-7 work. On Friday, he was 6-of-9 in the red zone, helped out by a diving catch from wide receiver Keelan Marion . 
 Matt Ryan, the team's president of football and former franchise quarterback, threw to wide receivers Drake London and Jahan Dotson separated from everyone else during a drill Friday. 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 5 

 Michael Penix Jr . explained his current situation in the clearest way possible Wednesday.

 "If I can't be on the field," Penix said, "how am I going to be the starter?"

 Penix has been on the field. He has done individual drills and 7-on-7 sessions. But what the Falcons third-year quarterback means is that he has yet to be cleared for 11-on-11 work. And until he does, there cannot be any kind of quarterback competition.

 That is not necessarily news. The Falcons coaching staff made that clear in the spring. But back then there was some expectation Penix would be fully ready for training camp. That has not been the case and Penix said it could be another several weeks before he's good to go.

 Tua Tagovailoa (tight back) took another step toward a full return Wednesday with more work in 11s. He went 5-of-7 passing. At this juncture, it's fair to say Tagovailoa will be the team's Week 1 starter unless something major changes.

 More observations: 

 
 Edge rusher Jalon Walker was officially confirmed as out for the season with a torn ACL after getting injured Tuesday at practice. It's a major blow for a pass rush that was depending him on to make a major impact. He had 5.5 sacks as a rookie last season. 
 Running back Bijan Robinson officially put pen to paper on his three-year extension, which is worth up to $75 million. He is still limited in practice and has not done any 11s as the team ramps him up. 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 4 
 Falcons running back Bijan Robinson returned to practice after a five-day hold-in Tuesday. Robinson got a three-year extension worth up to $75 million and is now the highest-paid running back in the NFL.

 Head coach Kevin Stefanski referred to Robinson's hold-in as "very amicable." Robinson had been at every practice on the hip of running backs coach Michael Pitre prior to actually coming back.

 "He wants to be out there practicing," Falcons running back Brian Robinson Jr . said. "You know he wants to be competing. So, I used to just tell him, 'Yo, take your time, handle your business. Whenever your time comes, it's going to come. I know you want to be out there with us, but we going to hold it down until you come…

title: Tracking 2026 NFL hold-ins: Vea and Tuipulotu
summary: Here is the latest on the Bucs' Vita Vea and the Chargers' Tuli Tuipulotu and where they stand with their deals.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL preseason kicked off with the Pro Football Hall of Game on Thursday , with three weeks of action to follow, but there are two players who are waiting for their contract situations to sort out.

 The start of NFL training camps brought these negotiations to a head. Players can hold out and stay away from camp until their financial situations are addressed, or they can hold in, where they report to camp to avoid fines but skip practice while waiting for a new contract. We're tracking the important hold-ins across the league, with updates from our NFL Nation writers on each situation.

 The list of stars not practicing has come down to one after Atlanta Falcons running back Bijan Robinson signed a  new historic deal  last Tuesday, with  Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs  surpassing him with a  new contract  two days later. Chargers outside linebacker Tuli Tuipulotu is also practicing, and said on Tuesday that he'll play this season regardless of whether he gets a deal.  

 Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea  is now the last one standing. 

 Which player will be next in resolving his contract dispute? Are any of these four willing to miss games once the season begins? Let's examine each situation.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Gibbs | Robinson | Vea | Tuipulotu 

 
 

 

 Vita Vea , DT, Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
 Status: Holding in, requesting a trade 

 Aug. 7:  Vea still is not practicing because of a back injury and his contract dispute. He also wasn't on the practice field either. However, as of right now, Bowles expects him to travel with the team Monday to joint practices at the New York Jets .

 "Right now, yes, everybody's going," Bowles said.

 Aug. 6: The Buccaneers have "no plans" to trade Vea, according to general manager Jason Licht when asked Thursday about Vea's hold-in. Collin Roberts, Vea's agent, told the Tampa Bay Times this week that he "doesn't see it ending in anything but a trade."

 "We love Vita," Licht added. "We've been engaged with his agent recently. I don't know how it's gonna end, but we've been engaged and that's at least some progress." Vea has been present at the Bucs' facility, taking part in classroom instruction and observing practice from the sideline. He has also been seen helping coach teammates up during positional drills, but he isn't physically participating.

 Aug. 2 update: The star defensive tackle remains sidelined with a back injury, as well as his contract hold-in. Coach Todd Bowles said there is "nothing new" to report on his injury, and he is unsure if Vea will make the trip to the  New York Jets  for a pair of joint practices starting Aug. 11.

 July 31 update: Vea, who stayed indoors to receive treatment Thursday, was back out on the practice field Friday with teammates but was still sidelined with a back injury sustained during the team's conditioning test. Bowles said he does not have a timetable yet for Vea's back.

 July 30 update: While Vea was on the sidelines during Wednesday's first training camp practice and was standing alongside teammates during positional drills, he was not on the practice field Thursday. Bowles said Vea tweaked his back in the team's conditioning test Tuesday and he was getting treatment. Vea did, however, participate in an interview on the "Up & Adams Show," but he did not discuss his contract. Vea is set to earn $17 million this season, but none of it is guaranteed, along with a per-game roster bonus that is capped at $1 million total. Bowles said they are preparing for the season as if Vea will play. 

 -- Jenna Laine, Bucs reporter 

 

 
 

 Tuli Tuipulotu , OLB, Los Angeles Chargers 
 

 Status: Seeking a new contract, but planning to play.

 Aug. 11 update: Tuipolotu said he'd play this season regardless of whether he gets a new deal. "I'll let my agents and the guys upstairs handle that. Let the business handle business. I'm a football player. That's all I do. That's all I know."

 Aug. 6 update:  Tuipulotu participated in team drills during Wednesday's padded practice, his second day in a row after not participating in team drills for the first six days of training camp.

 Tuipulotu looked like himself, bursting by the line of scrimmage to shut down running back Omarion Hampton on one of his first snaps and generating pressure throughout practice.

 Coach Jim Harbaugh originally said that Tuipulotu's absence was being "handled internally," then later said it was a "ramp up." Neither Tuipulotu, his representatives or the Chargers have acknowledged a contract-related absence, but his return to the field signals that whatever matter was being handled internally is resolved.

 Aug. 5 update:  Tuipulotu, who has been a limited participant in practice this training camp amid ongoing contract negotiations, was a full participant in Wednesday's practice. The caveat is that the practice was a walkthrough, so Tuipulotu and the other Chargers players were going at half speed. He still has yet to participate in a non-walkthrough practice 11-on-11 period, but his participation could be a sign that things could be headed toward a resolution.

 Aug. 4 update:  Coach Jim Harbaugh said Tuesday that Tuipulotu's absence from team drills remains part of "his ramp up." Harbaugh stopped short, however, of explaining any further, saying, "I don't know for sure where it's at. If I knew for sure, then I would say for sure."

 After noticing a reporter's facial expression, Harbaugh went on to explain he doesn't know exactly what's happening with Tuipulotu because he is not a medical professional.

 "Am I in somebody's body? A doctor? he said. "A lot of things that hang on my wall, but a medical degree is not one of them."

 Tuipulotu participated in one 7-on-7 rep but did not take part in the remainder of team drills on Tuesday, marking his sixth straight practice with limited participation as his contract situation remains unresolved.

 Aug. 3 update: Tuipulotu again did not participate in team drills, continuing his limited participation as his contract situation remains unresolved. The Chargers, Tuipulotu, and his representation remain mum about Tuipulotu's absence from practice, though it appears to be contract-related. Tuipulotu remains in good spirits and engaged throughout practice. His routine has been the same each day: he participates in individual drills, jokes with teammates, works with a trainer briefly, then watches practice with the team.

 Aug. 1 update:  Coach Jim Harbaugh declined to say whether outside linebacker Tuli Tuipulotu's absence from team drills at practice is contract-related, saying only the situation is being "handled internally" and repeatedly describing Tuipulotu as "ramping up."

 July 31 update:  Tuipulotu continued not to practice amid ongoing contract negotiations Friday. He went through individual drills, worked off to the side with a trainer and watched practice.

 July 30 update: The Chargers outside linebacker did not practice Thursday for the second straight day amid ongoing contract negotiations, but he did more on-field work with teammates than on the opening day of camp. Tuipulotu wore a helmet and jersey Thursday and went through individual drills with the team before working off to the side with a trainer. On Wednesday, he was in a T-shirt and shorts and worked off to the side with a trainer.

 -- Kris Rhim, Chargers reporter 

 

 
 

 Bijan Robinson , RB, Atlanta Falcons 
 

 Status: Signed a new deal 

 Aug. 4 update:  The two-time Pro Bowler and the Falcons reached agreement on a three-year extension worth up to $75 million that now will make him the highest-paid running back in NFL history, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

title: 2026 Baltimore Ravens training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Ravens training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Baltimore Ravens ' camp is taking place at Under Armour Performance Center in Baltimore, and Ravens reporter Jamison Hensley has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Ravens camp. We will update this file often. Can new coach Jesse Minter get  Lamar Jackson  and the Ravens to the Super Bowl? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Ravens camp 
 
 Zay Flowers, Ravens agree to four-year, $140M extension 
 Derrick Henry, entering 11th year, not thinking about retirement 
 Ravens waive rookie Diego Pavia to make room for Ethan Pocic 
 Ravens' Madubuike (neck) practices for 1st time in 10 months 
 
 
 Tuesday, Aug. 11 
 Pro Bowl wide receiver Zay Flowers surprisingly returned to practice after suffering a quad contusion on Saturday. He missed one practice.

 Flowers ran before Tuesday's practice and participated in positional drills. He looked fast and smooth cutting around the cones before heading early into the team facility.

 "That was all part of the plan as he's working back just through the soreness of the quad," Ravens coach Jesse Minter said. "I expect him to be Zay here any day."

 In other encouraging injury news, starting nose tackle Travis Jones was activated off the Physically Unable to Perform list and practiced for the first time this summer. He worked in positional drills after missing the first two weeks of training camp with a pectoral injury.

 "He's been chomping at the bit," Minter said. "He'll be a guy that in the first few days we'll probably have to hold him back, which is sometimes a good thing. But, 'Trav' looks amazing striking the sled. He's been putting in a ton of work off the field, in the weight room [and in] conditioning. I expect big, big things from 'Trav'."

 Other observations: 

 
 Ravens QB Lamar Jackson and other "established players" won't play in Saturday's preseason opener against the Philadelphia Eagles , Minter said. Jackson hasn't played in the preseason since 2021. 
 Ravens kicker Tyler Loop had another perfect day, making all seven of his kicks. Loop is now 33 of 35 (94.2%) in training camp and has made all eight of his tries beyond 50 yards. 
 Minter said he hasn't decided how the Ravens will handle challenges. The NFL will allow head coaches to designate a member of their sideline staff to throw the red flag. "That's certainly something to think about -- it could be helpful in certain situations, potentially," Minter said. "But, we'll figure that out as we get closer to the game. I may try it a couple different ways, even in the preseason, and see what gives us the best opportunity as a team." 
 

 
 Sunday, Aug. 9 
 Putting on full pads for the fourth time in training camp, the Ravens had one of their most physical practices of the summer. It was also their sloppiest.

 Baltimore's first, second and third offenses totaled eight false starts during the two-hour practice. The Ravens' starting offense jumped offside twice during a red-zone drill.

 Ravens coach Jesse Minter indicated the offense was trying to mix up the quarterback cadence on Sunday to keep the defense on its heels.

 "I think it's a great message of just the focus and the details that's required for that to become a real weapon and not something that puts you behind the chains like it did a few times today," Minter said.

 Other observations:  

 
 Just like he's done all camp, rookie wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane had a couple more big plays, including working back to make a 15-yard grab in front of cornerback Marlon Humphrey . But Lane's most impressive play Sunday was his block on the perimeter that helped running back Derrick Henry gain some extra yards. 
 Minter reiterated that wide receiver Zay Flowers won't miss much time after leaving Saturday's practice with a quad contusion. "I feel good that he'll be back out there being Zay pretty soon," Minter said. 
 Safety Jaylinn Hawkins has made it difficult for wide receivers to go over the middle. On Saturday, Hawkins' collision with Flowers caused him to leave practice with a quad contusion. A day later, Hawkins crashed into Rashod Bateman to force an incompletion. Asked if there is a lesson for Hawkins to learn, Minter said, "I really don't want to put that on him. When you're a safety and you're breaking on the ball, there's just a little bit of an awareness of not trying to have the body-on-body collisions. We certainly want Jaylinn to play with the mindset that he plays with. So we'll continue to just be really, really careful about that." 
 Starting nose tackle Travis Jones "will be starting to work back in real, real soon," Minter said. Jones is on the Physically Unable to Perform list with a pectoral injury. Defensive end Calais Campbell participated in team drills for the first time in camp. Both Jones and Campbell should be ready for the Sept. 13 season opener. 
 Kicker Tyler Loop was 8-of-8 on field goal attempts, including three from beyond from 50 yards. Loop, whose missed 44-yard kick ended the Ravens' season, has been starting to hit a groove in camp. 
 
 

 Saturday, Aug. 8 

 On a day when  Zay Flowers ' injury scare headlined practice, wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane continues to record one of the most impressive training camps by a Ravens rookie with more highlight-making receptions.

 Lane caught a deep touchdown pass from Lamar Jackson on a go route in a one-on-one drill against top cornerback Nate Wiggins and then made a one-handed catch on a back-shoulder throw by Tyler Huntley 25 yards down the field. After Lane's latest one-handed grab, running back Derrick Henry leapt in the air to give a shoulder bump to the impressive third-round pick.

 "There is consistency of making really contested, nice catches -- being a really friendly target for the quarterback," coach Jesse Minter said. "He's certainly starting to see a vision of maybe what he can become in the offense."

 Lane's strong camp has solidified a spot in Baltimore's three-wide formation, along with Flowers and Rashod Bateman .

 

 Other observations:  

 
 Running back Justice Hill called first-year playcaller Declan Doyle "the most detail-oriented" offensive coordinator that he's been with. In Hill's previous seven seasons, he's had two offensive coordinators: Greg Roman, who directed the NFL's highest-scoring offense in 2019, and Todd Monken, who guided Baltimore to the No. 1 offensive ranking in 2024. 
 The Ravens' defense got its hands on a lot of passes. T.J. Tampa , Malaki Starks and Amani Oruwariye all recorded pass breakups. Tampa is having an impressive camp and provides quality depth at cornerback behind Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey . 
 The best route of the day came from rookie tight end Josh Cuevas , who faked outside before running to the middle to shake free of safety Keondre Jackson for the easy catch. The Ravens are hoping for one of their rookie draft picks -- Cuevas and Matt Hibner -- to step up and provide another pass-catching target at tight end behind Mark Andrews . 
 The Ravens signed inside linebacker Jamon Johnson , a local product who attended St. Frances High School in Baltimore. He played in two games last season, making 10 tackles. The Ravens waived undrafted rookie cornerback Matthew McDoom to make room for Johnson on the 90-man roster. 
 

 

 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 The Ravens' third practice of the week in full pads was also their chippiest.

 The first dust-up of camp came when outside linebacker…
