title: 2026 New York Giants training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Giants training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The New York Giants' camp is taking place at The Greenbrier in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, and Giants reporter Jordan Raanan has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Giants camp. We will update this file often. How will the Giants handle increased expectations and a new coach? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive into all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Thursday.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Giants camp 
 
 Cam Skattebo admits doing 'dumb things,' will save backflips for TDs 
 Nabers 'looked good' in 1st practice since knee injury 
 Giants have spoken with Skattebo after Fanatics Fest flip 
 2026 New York Giants training camp preview 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 11 
 It was another rough afternoon for the Giants' offense. The unit sputtered and failed to hit any downfield throws during a practice without full pads.

 During one red zone drill, quarterback Jaxson Dart threw touchdown passes to Theo Johnson and Malachi Fields on two of the first three plays. He followed with five straight incompletions, including an interception at the goal line by Arvell Reese .

 These are the learning curves with a new offense.

 "[Tuesday] was an average practice, maybe below average," offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said. "It wasn't good enough. [Dart] knows that, we know that. We'll put it on tape, but we also talk about success through struggles and ... there's going to be some struggles as we go through this now in training camp and during the season. But how do we react?"

 The season starts in just over a month. The Giants are combining the offenses of Nagy, quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan and senior offensive assistant Greg Roman. They're putting as much as possible on tape and plan to pare it down to accommodate the talent.

 The clock is ticking.

 Other observations: 

 
 Reese's interception included a circus catch. He dropped into coverage, sprinted to the flat and put an arm in the air. The ball hit off the back of Reese's hand, and he tipped it to himself for the interception at the goal line. It was the latest highlight for the No. 5 pick. "He's been impressive," defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson said. 
 CB Paulson Adebo and WR Jalin Hyatt missed practice. That left three of the Giants' top cornerbacks (Adebo,  Greg Newsome II  and Dru Phillips ) on the sideline. Big opportunity for rookie Colton Hood and Deonte Banks . 
 Outside linebacker Abdul Carter (hand) returned to practice after sitting out Monday. Rookie guard Francis Mauigoa  participated only in individual drills after getting banged up Monday. 
 Second-year tight end  Thomas Fidone II  is catching everything these days. He had another highlight-reel diving catch deep down the middle of the field from Jameis Winston . He later added two more catches during live drills, including a touchdown in the red zone. It's going to be hard for the Giants to leave Fidone off the roster. 
 
 

 Aug. 10 
 The Giants' biggest problem last season was their run defense. It was close to historically bad while allowing 5.3 yards per carry.

 It's hard to succeed that way. New coach John Harbaugh is well aware. He and defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson have made it a priority to stop the run this season.

 So far, so good. Veteran nose tackle  DJ Reader  has been a force in the middle throughout training camp. First-round pick Arvell Reese 's physical approach has been a major asset. That was again the case in live drills during Monday's practice, which was the latest reminder that the Giants appear to have made serious gains on this front.

 "It's just technique and mentality," outside linebacker Brian Burns said. "We just really put an emphasis on being in our gap but also having ... a mean mentality when it comes to the run. We've got some goals that we want to reach this year."

 More observations: 

 
 OLB Abdul Carter missed practice because of a hand injury. Harbaugh did not think it was serious. 
 CB  Greg Newsome II  (knee), CB Dru Phillips (knee), WR  JuJu Smith-Schuster  (knee), C John Michael Schmitz Jr. (concussion) and G/C Lucas Patrick (knee) also missed practice. OLB Chauncey Golston left practice because of a neck/head injury. 
 Giants kickers made all 13 of their field goal and extra point attempts. Ben Sauls was 7-of-7, and  Dominic Zvada was 6-of-6. Both have had nice camps. 
 

 

 
 Aug. 8 

 The Giants finished their 12 days in West Virginia with another physical practice filled with goal-line and run-game work. It was a typical John Harbaugh workout. No easy days.

 Harbaugh thinks it's going to make a difference for a team that won seven games combined the past two seasons.

 "Well, I think we got a lot better. That's probably what we got out of it. We improved tremendously," Harbaugh said. "We're much further along than we were when we started. I think we can look back and say that we've come a long way."

 The trip helped with team building and camaraderie.

 "I would give it an A, A-plus for that. It's been really everything," Harbaugh said. "We've been able to focus on the task at hand. There's really no distractions out here. It's a beautiful setting. It's a beautiful resort. Everything has been excellent. And the guys have been able to lock in on the football. The fields have held up extremely well. I mean, every little thing has been good. It's not lavish by any stretch in terms of the facility, but it's everything we could want. Maybe that's even better."

 

 Other observations: 

 
 RB Cam Skattebo returned to practice after stretching out his leg the previous day. He participated in all 10 practices in West Virginia as he returns from a fractured ankle last year. 
 Defensive lineman Darius Alexander had a strong practice with multiple sacks in live drills. It concluded a nice camp for the second-year player whom the Giants are counting on to make a leap. 
 

 

 Aug. 7 
 Wide receiver Malik Nabers looked the best he has this summer during individual drills Friday. He continues to get better -- making sharper cuts, jumping and landing on the affected leg and running crisper routes as he rebounds from a knee injury .

 

 Coach John Harbaugh said he noticed this was the best version of Nabers, who is getting to the final stages of recovery. The next step is for Nabers to "work his way back into practice more and more."

 The expectation seems to be that Nabers will return to live team drills in the next couple of weeks. That would have him trending to be ready for Week 1 against the Cowboys.

 "[Return to play coordinator Allison Boudreau] is working with him, and she's been working on situations where you're off-balance, landing off-balance and unpredictable type situations that you're going to get rather than just doing normal rehab and then getting out there and all of a sudden being surprised by the awkwardness of football," Harbaugh said. "Try to create that as much as you can in a controlled setting."

 More observations: 

 
 The offense had perhaps its best day of camp. On its final drive, the unit went the length of the field with tight end Theo Johnson and running back Dante Miller each making multiple receptions. The series concluded with a 2-yard touchdown from quarterback  Jaxson Dart to wide receiver  Darius Slayton . Dart finished 16-of-19 passing on the day. 
 Malachi Fields on the offense: "It just keeps building over time. We've had almost two weeks now, just getting together, so I think we'll just keep jelling, keep clicking, and we'll…

title: 2026 New York Jets training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Jets training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  New York Jets  camp is taking place at the Atlantic Health Training Facility in Florham Park, New Jersey, and Jets reporter Rich Cimini has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Jets camp. We will update this file often. Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football, and which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Thursday.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Jets camp 
 
 Jets CB Stiggers taken to hospital after collapsing at practice 
 No. 2 pick Bailey living up to hype, bringing 'juice' to Jets 
 Rookie TE Kenyon Sadiq to miss time after hernia setback 
 Jets' Smith rues being 'distraction' after dispute with girlfriend 
 2026 Jets training camp preview 
 

 
 Tuesday, Aug. 11 
 Quarterback Geno Smith and the rest of the starters will play Friday night against the Buccaneers in the preseason opener, coach Aaron Glenn announced Tuesday.

 They can use the work.

 The first-team offense struggled in Tuesday's joint practice with the Bucs, as Smith was intercepted twice (one returned for a touchdown). The offense, learning new coordinator Frank Reich's system, is trending downward after an encouraging start to camp.

 The Jets were out of sync and allowed the Bucs to control the line of scrimmage, with running back  Breece Hall saying, "They beat us up a little today." And, no, he wasn't alluding to the four fights that marred practice.

 There was a spark in a red zone period late in practice, with Smith throwing touchdowns to tight end  Mason Taylor and wide receiver  Garrett Wilson (on a deflection). But it's clear the starting unit -- hardly devoid of talent -- has a way to go. Smith finished 10-for-16 in 11 on 11 periods.

 Glenn said the starters will play about 25 to 30 snaps in the preseason, though he's not sure how that will be divided over the three games. The Jets are installing new offensive and defensive systems. That's one of the reasons why Glenn wants to play his starters.

 Another reason: While many coaches prefer to be cautious, concerned about injuries, Glenn believes the best way to prep for the regular season is to actually play in the preseason.

 "Everybody's playing," he said.

 This isn't a new philosophy. A year ago, starting QB Justin Fields played 28 snaps in the preseason.

 

 More observations: 

 
 If you had to pick a "winner" in the joint practice, it would be the Bucs, who brought more energy and physicality at the outset. The two teams will do it again Wednesday. 
 WR Isaiah Williams , one of the stars of camp, has played his way into a bigger role. Before camp, he was viewed as a return specialist and No. 4 receiver, but that isn't the case anymore. Williams, who made three receptions in the joint practice, could leapfrog first-round pick Omar Cooper Jr ., who has experienced "little pitfalls," receivers coach Shawn Jefferson said. "That's part of being a rookie." 
 Wilson made one of the best plays of the day, catching the tipped pass in the red zone and evading what seemed like half of Tampa Bay's defense to find the end zone. 
 Rookie David Bailey had another impressive day as a pass rusher, making at least one sack and multiple QB pressures. He still needs work against the run, though. 
 Dane Belton , who had a pass breakup, may have the best ball production of any safety in camp. Glenn called him a "ball magnet." He's definitely pushing Andre Cisco for the starting job opposite Minkah Fitzpatrick . 
 Remember last year, when we made a big deal out of "live" tackling in training camp because it's uncommon in the NFL? Well, there won't be live tackling this summer. Glenn said he now prefers "thud" -- when defenders wrap up ball carriers but don't bring them to the ground. Glenn said "thud" promotes better technique and reduces injury. 
 
 

 Saturday, Aug. 8 
 The Jets ended the first phase of training camp with a controlled instrasquad scrimmage.

 There was a scary moment near the end, when prized rookie edge rusher David Bailey walked off gingerly, favoring his left ankle.

 Afterward, coach Aaron Glenn confirmed it was an ankle injury, adding that Bailey likely will be listed as day-to-day. He was able to jog back to the sideline after being examined in the medical tent.

 Bailey, drafted No. 2 overall, continued his strong camp, recording one sack and at least two pressures, unofficially. He probably should've had another sack, but the officials let the play continue.

 This was one of those good news-bad news days. Glenn's new-look defense looked terrific, while the offense struggled, especially in the red zone.

 There were plenty of self-inflicted mistakes. QB Geno Smith started hot, leading a 65-yard touchdown drive and completing his first five passes, but the starting offense unraveled after that. There were five penalties and two sacks.

 Penalties were a bugaboo last season. Glenn noted that most of the penalties came toward the end of the scrimmage, adding, "It's the part that we get tired. And once you get fatigued, mentally things start to get jumbled. So we have to do a better job of that."

 Smith finished 12-of-20 for 157 yards, leading only one touchdown drive in nine series, six of which began in plus territory.

 

 More observations:

 
 The offensive highlight was rookie Cade Klubnik 's 66-yard pass to WR Isaiah Williams in a hurry-up period. Moments later, the former Clemson star threw an 11-yard TD pass to TE Jelani Woods . Klubnik finished 10-of-14 for 154 yards, two TDs and one interception. He's battling journeyman Bailey Zappe for the No. 2 job. Because of his experience, Zappe shows more command than Klubnik, but the battle is far from over. The preseason games will tell a lot. 
 Glenn wouldn't reveal his QB plans for the preseason, but it certainly sounds like Smith will see action. "My mentality is that everybody's playing," Glenn said. You can expect to see a lot of Klubnik and Zappe. 
 Williams has been one of the most productive players in camp; he's a lock for the WR4 job. Whenever his name is mentioned, Glenn lights up. He caught five balls in the scrimmage, including a 36-yard TD from Smith. 
 Some of the defensive standouts: S Dane Belton (interception), NB Jordan Clark (two pass breakups), DT Darrell Jackson Jr (sack), S Minkah Fitzpatrick (QB pressure). 
 injury update: Rookie S V.J. Payne, a seventh-round pick, will be sidelined three to four weeks with a bone bruise. 
 The Jets have no practice Sunday and Monday, then host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers for two days of joint practices before opening the preseason Friday against the Bucs. 
 

 

 Friday, Aug. 7 

 Geno Smith has a big fan in offensive coordinator Frank Reich, who gushed about his starting quarterback after a sweltering practice.

 "He's a leader of the offense and, make no mistake about it, in every way, shape and form," Reich said. "To me, what has come crystal clear ... the attribute that sticks out to me is his laser focus. This man is laser focused like people don't understand. He comes to work. He comes to work, and he is locked in. And I feel like the whole offense plays off of that. That's a big deal."

 Smith is having a solid camp. He delivered another strong practice (8-for-12 in team drills), hooking up five times with WR Garrett Wilson . August optimism is nice; the bottom line is how the player performs in September and beyond.

 Reich praised Smith's upper-body throwing mechanics, calling them "pure."

 "There's only a couple guys in the league that I would say are pure. Geno's one of them," said Reich,…

 Eagles coach Nick Sirianni adjusting to offseason changes 
 
 
 Tuesday, Aug. 11 
 Quarterback Jalen Hurts and receiver Elijah Moore connected for another big play on Tuesday.

 Hurts uncorked a deep shot for Moore, who sped past safety  Andre' Sam  and hauled in the pass for a touchdown. Moore celebrated by punting the ball well over the practice field gate.

 Hurts has been without DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon the past six practices because of hamstring injuries but is finding a lot of value in building chemistry with some of the other receivers.

 Moore is one of the primary players capitalizing on that opportunity, generating a number of highlight plays alongside QB1.

 Other observations: 

 
 Cornerback Quinyon Mitchell sat out of team drills after pulling up during a one-on-one rep against Hollywood Brown . Mitchell went to the sideline and had his right leg stretched out by a trainer. Mac McWilliams took over for him with the first team. 
 Reserve corner Jakorian Bennett has had a good number of pass breakups this summer. He had another one on a Hurts attempt for Moore down the right seam on Tuesday. 
 Cooper DeJean came up with an interception on a reckless downfield throw from Andy Dalton . Later, DeJean blitzed Hurts and registered the "sack." 
 Edge rusher Jalyx Hunt has been one of the more impressive players on the field during camp. He came clean on one rush and chased Hurts to the other side of the field, eventually forcing him out of bounds. 
 
 

 Monday, Aug. 10 
 Eagles cornerback Quinyon Mitchell came up with his second interception of camp -- perhaps foreshadowing a breakout year for him in the takeaway department. Mitchell sniffed out a Jalen Hurts pass intended for Hollywood Brown over the middle and came up with the pick on the first play of a simulated two-minute drive.

 
"Just his patience, his confidence," CB Riq Woolen said on what stands out about Mitchell. "He's been in this defense ... so he has a good understanding of how he can play certain techniques and certain coverages. Being able to watch him make plays, it inspires me to make plays."

 
Mitchell, a first-team All Pro in 2025, has yet to record a regular-season interception in his two years in the league but is tied for the most career playoff interceptions (four) among active players. It feels like a matter of time before he starts posting INTs more regularly.

 Other observations: 

 
 Receivers Makai Lemon and DeVonta Smith both missed their fifth straight practice with hamstring injuries. 
 Interior lineman Willie Lampkin continues to make a push for a roster spot. Listed at 5-foot-11, 290 pounds, he doesn't have the same size as most of his counterparts but is shining despite being asked to flip-flop from center to guard midpractice. Nick Sirianni said when the coaches review these sessions, they find themselves saying, "Willie did it again." 
 Emotions flared on the ninth day of camp. Guard Tyler Steen and DT Ty Robinson appeared to be at the center of an O-line vs. D-line scrum that took a little time to defuse. 
 
 
 Saturday, Aug. 8 

 Eagles running back Saquon Barkley made his presence felt. He got animated after a short touchdown run, chirping at Cooper DeJean before giving Quinyon Mitchell a playful shove.

 The offense switched from goal line to backed up work a short time later. Barkley used a nifty jump cut to speed to daylight on one play and followed that up by shaking defensive tackle Jordan Davis on his next carry.

 Barkley believes this new system can open up some things for him that he hasn't been able to fully showcase to this point in his career.

 "That's the plan," said offensive coordinator Sean Mannion . "Saquon, he's a tremendous player, and I think everything we do offensively ultimately is about how do we put all of our players in the best position to succeed and obviously Saquon is a focal point of our offense, that goes without saying."

 Other observations:  

 
 Linebacker Zack Baun intercepted Jalen Hurts on a throw over the middle. Hurts completed a pass to Elijah Moore on the previous play, and when he tried to go back to the well on a similar concept, Baun was there to jump the route. Baun nearly came up with another pick earlier in practice, but the ball somehow made it past him and into the hands of Moore along the sideline. 
 Hurts' connection with tight end Dallas Goedert is heating up. Hurts escaped pressure by rolling to his right and threw one to the corner of the end zone for Goedert, who pulled it in with Jihaad Campbell in coverage. 
 Center Cam Jurgens left practice early with a trainer for the second straight day. Saturday's exit was at the end of the session, and Jurgens appeared to be moving fine. 
 Receivers Makai Lemon and DeVonta Smith were sidelined for the fourth straight day with hamstring injuries. 
 

 

 
 
 Friday, Aug. 7 
 Right tackle Lane Johnson returned following a four-practice absence for personal reasons. Johnson was originally scheduled to speak after Friday's practice but will likely now talk Saturday, the team said. He was a limited participant as he reacclimates to the grind.

 
"He has a calming presence," defensive tackle Jordan Davis  said of Johnson. "One day, I'm not going to be able to say that I have him in the locker room. It's just very good to have him out here. Everybody knows he's a baller, man. He's a f---ing baller. Lane, man, he's a cornerstone."

 
Rookie Markel Bell continued to get first-team reps at right tackle during team drills. Center Cam Jurgens spent time in the medical tent before heading indoors. Jake Majors took over at center in his absence.

 Other observations:  

 
 The defensive line made life tough for the short-handed offensive front. Jalen Carter ripped past Majors with a swim move to shut down a would-be passing play for Jalen Hurts . He later rose up to deflect a throw. Davis blew up a play in the backfield earlier in the session. 
 Second-year receiver Darius Cooper is making a push for a roster spot. He has enjoyed a strong camp, and that continued Friday with a number of catches, including one from Hurts over the middle with Quinyon Mitchell in coverage. 
 Tanner McKee had perhaps his best day of the summer. He hit Cooper on consecutive attempts before tossing one into the right corner of the end zone for the 6-foot-6 Johnny Wilson , who rose to snag the pass with corner Jonathan Jones nearby. McKee and Andy Dalton continue to split second-team reps. 
 Receivers DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon missed their third straight practice with hamstring injuries. 
 New Sixer Jaylen Brown visited training camp. He chopped it up with coach Nick Sirianni, Hurts and Smith, among others, and got a nice ovation from the fans as he walked by.

title: Eagles have bought into new offensive system
summary: In some ways, the perennial title contenders are starting from scratch on one side of the ball.
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA -- The offensive overhaul is well underway for the Eagles.

 It only takes a few moments of observing training camp practice to notice the stark contrast between how things look under new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion versus what we've seen from Nick Sirianni and his host of playcallers over the previous five seasons.

 Jalen Hurts is under center way more. There is motion on almost every play. They are leaning heavily into play-action. And they've implemented a wide-zone blocking scheme, departing from the more vertical attack orchestrated by former offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland.

 All of this construction is being overseen by an architect in 34-year-old Mannion who was playing in the league as recently as 2023 and has all of two seasons of coaching experience under his belt.

 In some ways, the perennial title contenders are starting from scratch on one side of the ball. That has been apparent at times, with pre-snap penalties and a lack of synchronicity leading to some tough sledding against Vic Fangio's dominant defense. But there have also been enough flashes in which the play design is well-executed and giant patches of daylight open up for the skill players to stir the imagination about what's possible if/when this system clicks in for one of the NFL's most talent-rich offenses.

 "Right now, it's like a Day 1 install almost, a Phase 1 install," offensive tackle Jordan Mailata said during the first week of camp. "But it's been promising to say the least."

 

 One thing that stands out is the resounding buy-in voiced by the players, which has risen above the level of lip service. Count Hurts among those who have struck a positive tone about the direction of the offense.

 No one is being asked to tweak their approach more than QB1. Consider these stats from 2025:

 
 The Eagles were 27 th in under center snaps (23.7%) 
 Hurts' under-center dropback rate of 8.2% ranked 32 nd among qualified QBs (minimum 250 dropbacks), per NFL Next Gen Stats 
 Philadelphia ranked 29 th in motion rate (48.6%) 
 
 Hurts is accustomed to operating out of the shotgun and having a static picture pre-snap as he analyzes the defense. He will be working out of that comfort zone to a large degree. Mannion coached for the Green Bay Packers the past two years and is installing a system influenced by Sean McVay (Rams) and Kyle Shanahan (49ers). A quick look at their tendencies from a year ago helps forecast what's to come this season for Philly.

 
 Under center snaps: Rams 1 st (60.1%), 49ers 6 th (47%), Packers 12 th (38.1%) 
 Motion: Packers 18 th (59.3%). Rams 6 th (67.9%) 49ers 3 rd (69.9%) 
 
 Our reporting suggests Hurts has shown some reluctance to these elements in the past but he has embraced the new scheme by all accounts early on.

 "I like to think of the term calibrating. This is the time where we're kind of putting it together and finding out who we are," Hurts said. "I think it's been very good to be able to compete against the defense who has a built-and-set identity for who they are, and then obviously us on this end we've got a lot of new pieces, an entirely new approach and MO, philosophy to our offense. Being able to put that together and make it our own, I'm excited about where we are."

 A primary focus has been on Hurts' footwork. Mannion has spoken of installing a scheme based on rhythm in which the timing of one route is married to another and all the different elements of a concept work together.

 The process then begins of teaching a quarterback to "really understand that and listen to his feet."

 "That's something that we talk about. If your footwork is sound and your rhythm's good, it's just going to feel like the ball wants to come out, right? Then if it's not, then you move on," Mannion said.

 We have seen plenty of Hurts ripping it in rhythm this summer -- often to the middle of the field, which goes against another tendency of his throughout his career.

 "I love everything about [Hurts] right now," Mailata said. "He's all-in on this system, the way he's commanding the huddle, the way he's getting that ball out, the way he's throwing it, the way he's just embraced it, man. He's all-in and it's refreshing to see -- refreshing to come back in and we're all into this. We have to because it's all new to us, it's not just J, it's all new to us. We always say it starts with the QB and he's taken that off and leading by example  and we're all following. It's fun."

 Mannion has also dialed up a healthy number of designed runs for Hurts, often to good results. Hurts said it's too early to know how such plays will mesh with the new offense, but given how effective those plays have been and how spry Hurts looks this summer, it would be no surprise if there is an uptick in carries compared to last season, when he rushed the fewest times in his career (105) since becoming a full-time starter.

 The offensive linemen have been perhaps the biggest advocates of the scheme change, which is a little surprising at first glance because of the success they had under the old system led by Stoutland, arguably the best offensive line coach of his era.

 

 If there's a sense of relief, it comes largely from having less on their plate. As standout right tackle Lane Johnson noted, he and Mailata have been asked to play on an island for most of their careers. But in the new offense, they'll receive more guard help on the inside in pass protection.

 Left guard Landon Dickerson was one of multiple linemen to note that there's less diagnostic work being done at the line of scrimmage. Previously, their assignments were in part dictated by the defense's alignment and post-snap actions, whereas now they're able to "to make a call, stick with it, and run the play."

 "I think from the standpoint of not going up there and playing chess," center Cam Jurgens said of the system's benefits. "We can kind of play a little faster. This scheme kind of presses the defense. You're able to play fast and not overthink things."

 In the wide-zone design, the linemen are moving more horizontally to stretch the defense and are meeting the defensive front "across the line instead of at the line," as Mailata put it. The offensive linemen mirror their run-blocking looks on play-action passes. Couple that with the pre-snap motion and some misdirection post-snap, and it complicates things for their opponent -- a welcome departure for some after things got a bit too stagnant on offense last season in particular.

 

 "What I like about this is that everything looks very complex to the defense," Johnson said. "To the offense, it's pretty simplified."

 Saquon Barkley acknowledged this will probably be the most under center and outside zone he has done in his career. But he has been doing his due diligence to get ready, including consulting with former Ram great Todd Gurley , who thrived in a similar system. Barkley said the benefits of under center is that backs can see more clearly and can get downhill faster.

 "I feel like I have a chance to be really good in this system too," he said. "I've seen it from afar but now that I'm actually studying it and working it and trying to put myself in the system, I feel like it's going to open up some things that I may not have been able to show in my career so I'm excited for that part of it."

 The running game in camp (a tough thing to judge to begin with, given the lack of tackling) has been hit or miss this summer. We've seen times when linebackers and defensive linemen have quickly dissected a toss and shot into the backfield to stop a play. And we've also seen huge holes open up, which Barkley and Tank Bigsby have exploited for monster gains.

 The same can be said for the passing game. The offense has been repping some plays for the first time and it shows, leading to a penalty or a wrong route run or a misfire. The absence of Johnson (personal) and DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon (hamstring injuries) hasn't helped…

title: 2026 Pittsburgh Steelers training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Steelers training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Pittsburgh Steelers ' camp is taking place in Latrobe, Pennsylvania, and Steelers reporter Brooke Pryor has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Steelers camp. We will update this file often. How will coach Mike McCarthy shape this roster and the offense in his first year in Pittsburgh? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Steelers camp 
 
 'Tempered': Inside Mike McCarthy's new vision for Steelers 
 Steelers' Broderick Jones cleared after eight months (neck) 
 Rodgers: 'Zero debate' 2026 will be last season 
 Jalen Ramsey, Joey Porter Jr. placed on PUP list 
 Steelers revamp wide receiver unit 
 Rodgers reunites with family ahead of final NFL season 
 
 
 

 Tuesday, Aug. 11 
 Entering his 22nd year in the NFL, quarterback Aaron Rodgers  doesn't see a real advantage to playing in preseason games.

 "It's preseason," he said after Tuesday's practice. "It's not real football. So if I do, great. If not, great.

 "... Preseason's a lot different. Teams don't run anything anymore. They just really don't. ... I think preseason football is good to see guys with the pads on, under the lights, how they react to the nerves, but it's not real regular-season football."

 Instead, Rodgers said he's anxious to see how younger quarterbacks Will Howard and Drew Allar react to being in game-like environments for the first time.

 Coach Mike McCarthy said he'll make a decision about the quarterback rotation for Thursday in meetings on Tuesday night, but he envisions using three groups on offense. The first will play one or two series, McCarthy said, while the second will finish out the first half and the third will play the second half.

 Rodgers said if he doesn't play, he views his role as providing comic relief from the sideline.

 "I like to be on the headset and calm everybody down," Rodgers said. "Usually the first game, it's a little hectic on the headset. So I like to be the voice of reason, occasional dad joke or one-liner. Just keep everybody settled in a little bit."

 It wasn't always that way, though.

 "It was my Super Bowl, for sure," Rodgers said of playing in the preseason 20 years ago.

 "I was so locked in and dialed in, and then you get out there and you run on a field and the nerves start flooding you and you start trying to slow your breathing down just to remember what the play was that you just heard in your helmet and not have to ask him again on the sideline and say it with conviction in the huddle, and then break the huddle and try and remember what the hell's going on to play and who's got what.

 "It's a great experience the first time just to be out there and to be live."

 More observations: 

 
 The Steelers moved practice indoors for the second day in a row as inclement weather hit Latrobe during their practice window. This time, the storms came through earlier than the day before, and the Steelers opted to hold the entire practice indoors. Though it was scheduled to go from 11 to 1:20 p.m., practice ended up lasting about an hour and a half. 
 McCarthy said Tuesday's padded practice was a critical one ahead of Thursday's preseason game. "We have a full slate," McCarthy said. "We wanted to have a competitive two drills today and two minutes. ... This practice is important. And frankly, you usually don't have that big of a practice as closer to the game. I get it. But it is preseason. So we'll see how we come out of today." 
 First-round pick Max Iheanachor won't play Thursday night, and McCarthy said Iheanachor is "working his way back" from last week's upper body injury. Iheanachor did individual drills on Monday. "We use the individual drills to see what he can do," McCarthy said. "... There's a strength component that we're trying to get over and there's some things we wanted to see him do in his pads and a helmet on. And he's making progress." 
 With WRs Michael Pittman Jr . and DK Metcalf out of practice for a second day in a row, rookie wide receiver Germie Bernard said he worked with the first team offense again. Rodgers said Bernard has a "really bright future," but acknowledged the wide receiver still has a lot of learning to do. "Germie just needs to learn the offense inside and out," Rodgers said. "And when he does that, he has a lot of great physical traits. He can get his feet in the ground quickly. He's very sudden. He's got natural hands. He's a great kid." 
 

 

 Monday, Aug. 10 
 The Steelers went through Mike McCarthy's planned "Franco Moment" on Monday and then navigated another of the intense drills as inclement weather forced the team to move inside midway through practice.

 "We've been doing it really with the Franco Moments," quarterback Will Howard said. "Kind of just, hey, sudden change, two-minute, whether it's backed up like it was today or if something happens, and sometimes you're going to have to go into the locker room for a couple minutes and then come back out. And just dealing with different changes, different sudden adversities that obviously aren't ideal.

 "I think obviously the rain is one thing, but just kind of dealing with that change of scenery and change of pace, I think we did a really good job of it."

 The Steelers were able to practice outside for about an hour. They went through a series of individual periods before an inside run team period. Then, just before the storm hit, the "Monday Night Football" jingle played over the sound system to signal the Franco Moment. The coaches set the table for the situational period: The offense was backed up at its 1-yard line with a fresh set of downs. The offense could win by picking up a first down. The defense could win by getting a stop.

 The offense sputtered as the fans started to evacuate the field. Rookie wide receiver Germie Bernard  committed a false start on first down. On the second play, Aaron Rodgers hit Brandon Smith for a quick pop pass and a 6-yard gain. Then, RB  Rico Dowdle ran up the middle for a 3-yard gain. Jaylen Warren got the ball on third-and-short, but the defense stuffed him to force a punt and get the win.

 Though the Steelers had to move to Saint Vincent College's indoor facility after the period, Howard said they were still able to accomplish everything they had scheduled.

 "Having that indoor is a big advantage for us this year compared to last year," Howard said. "We were kind of just up in the gym doing more of a walk-through, but we're still kind of half speed in the indoor just because we don't have a ton of space, but we have more space and it's way more real.

 "You can kind of still see those looks and see those reps. It was really smooth, and I thought they handled it really well."

 More observations: 

 
 McCarthy said before practice that rookie first-round pick Max Iheanachor wouldn't practice Monday as he continues to recover from an undisclosed injury sustained in last Thursday's practice. But Iheanachor was in a jersey, pads and helmet when practice started Monday and even went through some individual reps. He didn't participate in the team periods open to viewing. Still, it marked the first action for Iheanachor since he left practice early Thursday after a neck and shoulder examination by team medical personnel. 
 Neither DK Metcalf nor Michael Pittman Jr . was spotted at practice. McCarthy said Pittman got banged up during the Saturday night practice, but the coach didn't disclose any issue with Metcalf.…

title: 2026 Seattle Seahawks training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Seahawks training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Seattle Seahawks ' camp is taking place in Renton, Washington, and Seahawks reporter Brady Henderson has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Seahawks camp. We will update this file often. What is new with the defending Super Bowl champions? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp previews for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Seahawks camp 
 
 WR Tory Horton healthy after cracking tibia last season 
 Seattle Pro Bowl DL Williams confirms deal talks 
 Seattle's Nick Emmanwori has ankle surgery, expected to play W1 
 Who are the Khoslas? Meet the family set to buy the Seahawks 
 
 

 Tuesday, Aug. 11 

 Good news came on the injury front on Tuesday via safety Nick Emmanwori passing his physical, a significant step in his return from July ankle surgery.

 Then came bad news, with the team announcing that second-year fullback Robbie Ouzts will go on injured reserve, ending his season because of the neck issue that kept him out of the NFC Championship Game and Super Bowl.

 It's no small thing given new coordinator Brian Fleury's stated desire to run a good chunk of his offense with two backs on the field at the same time. Fleury came from the San Francisco 49ers , who ran an NFL-high 491 plays last season out of two-back formations, according to ESPN Research. Since 2022, coach Kyle Shanahan's offense leads the league in snaps with two backs.

 "I like using two backs because it can change the formation strength after the snap as opposed to the whole defense being able to identify it before the snap," Fleury said last week. "It creates some fit problems. It's becoming less and less common across the league, so it's more difficult to prepare for. Those are the elements I like about it. I'm more of an old-school traditionalist because of my upbringing in football and so I'm always going to want to play with two backs at some point. I like the guys we have in that role right now."

 At that point, it wasn't known yet that Ouzts would have to miss the season. Brady Russell , a converted tight end, is the Seahawks' next man up at fullback. They also signed Brock Lampe last week.

 General manager John Schneider has a long history of late-summer additions, so the Seahawks could potentially find their replacement for Ouzts via a trade or waiver claim. Or, as Fleury said, they could find creative ways to get a second back on the field.

 "It doesn't have to be a traditional fullback," Fleury said last week. "We've found ways to use receivers in lead blocking roles, other tight ends, even other running backs. We'll find a way to get it done."

 More observations: 

 
 Rookie RB Jadarian Price missed his fourth straight practice. Coach Mike Macdonald has described his issue as lower-body soreness and said Seattle's first-round pick should be back in a matter of days. 
 Tuesday's practice again got contentious. During an 11-on-11 period, S Ty Okada hit WR Tory Horton on a screen pass. Horton took exception, pushing Okada. G Christian Haynes came to Horton's defense and ended up going to the ground with Okada. There were no flare-ups after that, and Okada was laughing about the altercation with fellow defensive backs on the sideline moments later. 
 Okada came down with an interception when CB Josh Jobe deflected a QB  Sam Darnold pass to WR Cooper Kupp near the goal line. 
 

 

 

 Monday, Aug. 10 
 The Seahawks might have more NFL-caliber safeties than they'll be able to keep, and the players who are vying for roster spots have been making plays.

 AJ Finley and Rodney Thomas II both had interceptions during Seattle's annual practice at Lumen Field on Saturday. D'Anthony Bell got in on the action Monday as the team returned to work following an off day.

 In an 11-on-11 period, No. 3 quarterback Jalen Milroe was trying to hit tight end Elijah Arroyo on an out route when Bell jumped in front of the throw and intercepted it in stride for what might have been a pick-six in an actual game.

 "It was great to see him make a play today," coach Mike Macdonald said. "He's doing a good job. There's a lot of competition for the job that he's trying to earn himself, so it's a process. One day at a time, but D-Bell is doing a good job."

 Ty Okada still looks like the heavy favorite to replace free agent departure Coby Bryant in the starting lineup opposite Julian Love . Rookie Bud Clark is a lock to make the team after Seattle drafted him No. 64. The Seahawks were optimistic immediately after Nick Emmanwori had ankle surgery in July that he'd be back in time for Week 1, so it would take an unforeseen issue with his recovery to keep him off the 53-player roster to begin the season.

 Working in Bell's favor is the fact that he has been the primary backup to Emmanwori as the third safety in big nickel packages. He's also a strong special teams player. Bell blocked a punt last season and played the fourth-most special teams snaps of any Seahawk despite appearing in only 14 games.

 That helps explain why they gave him a Super Bowl ring even though he missed their playoff run. The Seahawks waived Bell in Week 18 in the hopes of moving him onto their practice squad, but the Carolina Panthers claimed him. Seattle re-signed Bell in March to a one-year, $1.485 million deal that includes $225,000 guaranteed.

 "It's going to come down to special teams, how we package our personnel groups, things like that," Macdonald said. "But he made a great play today. That was awesome."

 More observations: 

 
 LB Patrick O'Connell , another player vying for a roster spot, made perhaps the play of the day -- a leaping interception of a floating pass into the end zone from Drew Lock . He then punted the football in celebration. You might see that one on HBO's "Hard Knocks." 
 WR Jake Bobo returned to practice, and CB Julian Neal , LB Jamie Sheriff and DL Mike Morris all went through early warmups before working on the side for the rest of practice. 
 RB Jadarian Price remained out for a third straight practice. Macdonald said Saturday that he's dealing with "lower-body soreness" and should return in a matter of days. 
 

 

 Saturday, Aug. 8 
 The Seahawks have been without rookie running back Jadarian Price the past two days as their first-round draft pick deals with a minor leg injury. His absence has given free agent addition  Emanuel Wilson a chance to join George Holani with the No. 1 offense and show what he can bring to Seattle's potentially crowded backfield.

 Which appears to be more than just a rugged, between-the-tackles runner.

 "I'm bringing something different," Wilson said. "A lot of people think I don't got speed, but I've got a lot of speed on my end, and really just bringing a lot of power."

 Case in point was one play from the Seahawks' annual practice at Lumen Field, an off-tackle run in which Wilson stuck his foot in the ground, turned upfield and showed some burst for a gain of roughly 15 yards.

 No one will confuse him for  Kenneth Walker III  -- the explosive runner and Super Bowl LX MVP who signed with the Kansas City Chiefs in free agency -- but Wilson moves well for a back of his size.

 A "heavy runner" and a "230-pound guy with great feet" was how general manager John Schneider described Wilson after Seattle signed him in March to a one-year, $1.595 million contract. Undrafted in 2023 out of Division II Fort Valley State in Georgia, Wilson spent his first three seasons as a backup with the Green Bay Packers .

 Exactly…

title: 2026 San Francisco 49ers training camp: Latest intel, updates

The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The San Francisco 49ers camp is taking place in Santa Clara, California, and 49ers reporter Nick Wagoner has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at 49ers camp. We will update this file often. What does  Mike Evans  look like as a top receiver on the 49ers? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Camp previews for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from 49ers' camp 
 
 Kyle Shanahan nears full strength, plans to coach preseason opener 
 What's next for 49ers receivers Aiyuk, Deebo and Pearsall? 
 Deebo Samuel on reunion with 49ers: 'Just matter of time' 
 WR Ricky Pearsall to have season-ending knee surgery 
 VP Paraag Marathe exits to focus on soccer clubs 
 49ers GM Lynch focused on 'players that are here,' not WR Aiyuk 
 
 
 Tuesday, Aug. 11 
 More than two weeks into camp, the 49ers offense was looking forward to seeing how it would fare against another team Tuesday. The answer? Quite well.

 After a slow start for the unit, QB Brock Purdy continued his strong camp by carving through the Titans secondary for much of the joint practice session, particularly in the latter half of the session. I had Purdy at 21-of-27 on the day, including multiple touchdown passes and no interceptions.

 

 His best throws came in a move in which he dropped a perfect ball between three defenders to rookie WR De'Zhaun Stribling that would have gone for a long touchdown. And then, he had another layered throw over linebacker Cody Barton for a big gain to TE Jake Tonges .

 Even Purdy's toughest critic had to give it up for him after the practice.

 "Brock's a really good player, so I expect him to have good plays," coach Kyle Shanahan said. "I notice all the bad plays ... I didn't notice many bad plays today so I think he had a hell of a day."

 More observations: 

 
 There were a handful of fights early in the practice that looked like they might have ended the day early. San Francisco's defense seemed to be doing most of the early agitating. But both sides settled in and got some good work. 
 Stribling showed that his early flashes aren't limited to producing against his teammates. Regardless of which unit he was working against, he repeatedly made big plays. 
 Veteran WR Demarcus Robinson also had another big day, catching a couple of touchdowns from Purdy and continuing to make the case to be a valuable backup at multiple spots. 
 Speaking of receivers, Mike Evans was back from his quad injury, though he didn't do much beyond individual drills. 
 DE Nick Bosa is still not practicing with soreness and what Shanahan described as tendinitis. Shanahan said the tendinitis is normal for a player coming off a torn ACL; he has no concern about Bosa's long-term status. The hope is to have him at full strength for Week 1. 
 RB Christian McCaffrey watched the practice in street clothes and, like Bosa, Shanahan indicated there's no worry about the tightness McCaffrey is battling. Shanahan said he'd be more concerned if McCaffrey tried to play through it and risked making it worse. 
 Shanahan is out of the cast on his left hand and has traded it in for a black brace. He was out there for the whole session. 
 Warriors GM Mike Dunleavy Jr. was at practice and spent some time chatting with Niners GM John Lynch before the session. 
 Didn't catch who it was, but one of the officials was on the wrong end of a collision and had to be helped off the field. 
 
 
 Monday, Aug. 10 
 The Niners had only one new addition to their "did not practice" report Monday, but it was a big one: running back Christian McCaffrey .

 McCaffrey did not practice because of what the team called "tightness" after participating in every other practice during this training camp. After the session, offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak indicated McCaffrey isn't dealing with anything serious and the team is trying to be smart with him.

 "[He's] a little sore, but he's doing fine," Kubiak said. "Just kind of managing him as we go."

 Kubiak said the team will continue to keep an eye on McCaffrey's workload as it tries to get him to full speed against the Rams in Australia.

 "In terms of his rep load, we're right on track where we want to be," Kubiak said. "And he's a veteran player, so you got to monitor him and get him ready for the first week."

 More observations: 

 
 Legendary Niners receiver Jerry Rice made a cameo appearance at practice, emerging early in team drills and watching from the sideline. 
 Coach Kyle Shanahan continues to work his way back and was on the field for essentially the whole practice. 
 Rookie offensive lineman Carver Willis returned from a concussion. He was back in the mix at left guard with the second-team offense. 
 Tight end George Kittle was doing the most strenuous workout the media has seen him do in this camp on the side as he continues to come back from a ruptured Achilles. Kittle was running routes and catching passes during individual drills. 
 Most of the other injured Niners also continue to work on the side, with RB Kaelon Black and DL Keion White doing some conditioning as they come back from adductor injuries. 
 QB Brock Purdy provided the biggest plays of the day, hitting WR De'Zhaun Stribling for a huge gain on a deep corner route and later connecting with WR Demarcus Robinson on another deep ball. 
 
 
 Saturday, Aug. 8 
 While Kyle Shanahan returned to media duty and is edging close to 100% recovered from his July 14 car accident, 49ers DE Nick Bosa remained absent from practice.

 Bosa, who is recovering from the torn right ACL he suffered in Week 3 last year, has missed the past three open sessions because of what the team is calling general soreness. Before that, Bosa had been working solely in individual drills as part of his recovery. Bosa's absence has raised questions about a potential setback, though it's also worth noting the Niners are always cautious with Bosa in training camp anyway.

 Shanahan said after practice that he expects Bosa to be fine.

 "He was doing great, and then he got sore just going through some of the individuals," Shanahan said. "You wish that didn't happen. But no, there's no concern to where something's happened that is a big setback or anything. But we'll wait until that soreness goes away and evaluating why the soreness has happened. But I still feel pretty good about that."

 More observations:  

 
 The only new addition to the non-practice list was LB Luke Gifford . It's unclear what he's dealing with, though he did some work on the side during the session. 
 CB Upton Stout had a nice day, laying out for a beautiful pass breakup on a throw for Demarcus Robinson in the red zone then picking off a pass intended for Robinson from QB Brock Purdy and returning it for a touchdown. 
 CB Deommodore Lenoir also got an interception against Purdy on a short throw from Robinson that he might have scored on as well. After two strong days for the offense, the defense bounced back. 
 DB Nate Hobbs also had a pair of pass breakups in team sessions, his first flashes in team drills during this camp. 
 LB Dre Greenlaw was back involved in some team periods after missing a couple of days with soreness of his own. 
 The coaching staff was all wearing shirts honoring Roger Craig, the legendary Niners running back who was enshrined into the Pro Football Hall of Fame on Saturday.

 The 49ers offense struggled in Monday's practice, but that session seems to have led the unit to lock in over the…

title: How the 49ers' defense looks different under Raheem Morris
summary: San Francisco's new defensive coordinator is overhauling the 49ers' scheme, and players are loving it.
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- Since his arrival via trade in 2020, San Francisco 49ers left tackle Trent Williams has grown accustomed to stepping on the practice field and looking across the line of scrimmage at a defense that, despite cycling through six coordinators in 10 years, has looked largely the same.

 Coordinators Robert Saleh, DeMeco Ryans, Steve Wilks, Nick Sorensen and Saleh again introduced wrinkles throughout their tenures. But for the most part, the team has run a base 4-3 defense paired with ever-changing zone coverage principles. Until this year.

 Roughly halfway through their first training camp with Raheem Morris in charge of the defense , Williams still isn't sure what to expect from down to down.

 "Everything's different," Williams said. "... Obviously, we're not brand new to it. We played it a lot when [Raheem] was in L.A., played last year in Atlanta. It's actually one of the defenses that a lot of people tend to throw in their repertoire."

 In the locker room, Morris has been a breath of fresh air. That's not because the players lack love and respect for Saleh, who now coaches the Titans and is back in the Bay Area for joint practices and the preseason opener , but because Morris empowers them to play free and challenges them to expand their games.

 To the surprise of no one who watched a Morris defense when he was the defensive coordinator for the Rams (2021-23) or served as the head coach in Atlanta (2024-25), most of the defensive changes aim to create a confusing pre-snap picture for the opposition. And he does so through the use of five-man fronts, which Williams, linebacker Fred Warner , and quarterback Brock Purdy have all pointed out.

 Morris' Atlanta teams played the third-most five-man fronts in the NFL over the past two seasons, while the Niners have only "dibbled and dabbled a little bit" with it, according to Morris.

 

 But the real curveball in the scheme isn't so much the use of five-man front as to what he asks that fifth man to do. At a recent news conference, veteran linebacker Dre Greenlaw made passing mention of a position Morris calls the "fever backer."

 Asked to describe the responsibilities of the "fever backer," Morris joked he has been "making up a lot of terms" before explaining the position can do just about anything. That includes playing off the edge as a pass rusher, dropping into more of a coverage role or being a traditional stack linebacker.

 The goal, not unlike coach Kyle Shanahan's offense, is to utilize personnel groupings that make everything look the same before quickly transforming into something else. Through the first two weeks of camp, three young 49ers -- second-year linebacker Nick Martin and rookies Jaden Dugger and Romello Height -- have emerged as the top candidates for the job. Each has done one of those jobs well over their career, but they're trying to add other tools to their belt throughout camp.

 It's why Dugger spent some time at a recent practice with the defensive line, working to hone his pass-rush moves. And it's why observers have seen Height take reps dropping into coverage. Martin has also occasionally lined up as the fifth defender on the line of scrimmage during team periods in this camp.

 

 Linebacker coach K.J. Wright said the winner of that competition, which he says is still wide open, won't claim the job just based on physical attributes. They'll have to prove they can handle the workload that accompanies so many responsibilities. Hence the position's name.

 "The way I interpret it, it's a sick position," Wright said. "You're off the ball, you're on the ball, you get a fever, you're sick. It's like you can do so many things. It's a football sicko."

 The other unique title Morris brings is the "star" position. The "star" maintains a role as an every-down nickel back, but they also need the skills to defend in the slot, help in the box in run support and occasionally deploy as a pass rusher.

 Though many have played it in the NCAA and NFL over the years, Jalen Ramsey made it most famous during his time with the Rams. He played at the "star" under Morris in Los Angeles for two seasons, including the Rams' Super Bowl LVI win .

 It's one of the most important positions in Morris' schemes because it gives him the most freedom to change up looks. Second-year cornerback Upton Stout  is expected to inherit the role for the 49ers.

 Much like the "fever backer," the "star" has to handle a significant amount of information, something that should come easily to Stout. Cornerbacks coach Ray Brown and defensive pass game coordinator Jerry Gray said Stout normally fires questions at them at all hours of the night. That was even the case while Stout trained in Houston over the summer, as Gray would get text messages out of the blue from Stout about what he saw on tape or ways he could better train for the new job.

 "He really wants to be good. And he knows that that position requires a lot," Gray said.

 Another common refrain from Morris' players in camp has come from the team's starting defensive backs. Cornerbacks Deommodore Lenoir and Renardo Green and safety Ji'Ayir Brown have all made at least some reference to Morris' scheme allowing them to play faster and freer.

 Brown said this is his "favorite camp" and that he "can't remember the last time I had this much fun" playing football. Green said it's "easier to play faster" and that Morris' defense requires "a lot less thinking." Lenoir said Morris "broke the defense down" and "made it as simple as possible to where we are able to just read and react."

 "He wants football players," Brown said. "Previous schemes we've been in haven't wanted that. Raheem wants you to play football. He wants instinctive players. He wants guys who can just get out there and play ball and read the quarterback. The scheme fits all of us."

 Naturally, those comments could lead one to believe that the defensive backs disliked Saleh's 2025 scheme because it asked them to do too much. Though there might be truth in that, explanations exist for it.

 

 Without defensive end Nick Bosa ( torn right ACL ) and lacking any meaningful pass rush -- the Niners finished last leaguewide in sacks (20) and 31st in pressures (157) -- Saleh had to adjust his overall game plan. Instead of allowing the pass rush to dictate opportunities, he had to rely on other positions to disguise coverages.

 Matters became even more difficult in Week 6, when Warner suffered a season-ending right ankle fracture and dislocation . The trickle-down effect of losing Warner's voice and communication skills forced the secondary to diagnose more information both pre- and post-snap.

 The result was a middling defense that finished 13th in scoring (21.8 points per game), 25th in defensive efficiency (43.69), 24th in defensive expected points added (minus-62.22) and 24th in yards per play (5.6).

 "When Fred is out there, everybody listens to what he says," Wright said. "They do what he says. He makes the checks. He directs everyone. When other linebackers play, you hear more voices and people start to overtalk. When 5-4 is out there, do as [he] says and life will be good."

 With Warner back in the mix and Greenlaw re-signed , the communication between the front and back of the defense should vastly improve. However, any steps forward from the entire unit will depend on how well everyone adapts to changing roles and the development of many young defenders.

 Regardless of Morris' changes, Warner is doing everything he can to ensure at least one aspect of the 49ers' defense doesn't change.

 "The thing that will always remain true is just the style of play," Warner said. "That's always got to come first and show through in the biggest way. ... We're not happy with anything that we've done or accomplished. It's always about seeing where we can get better every single day."

title: 2026 Tennessee Titans training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Titans training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The Tennessee Titans ' camp is taking place at the Vanderbilt Health Football Center, and Titans reporter Turron Davenport has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Titans camp. We will update this file often. We are looking at who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football, and which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Titans news: 

 
 Extension makes Peter Skoronski NFL's top-paid guard 
 Titans DT Jeffery Simmons throws punch, sent to side field 
 Will Levis: There aren't 32 QBs better than me 
 Titans WRs join Cam Ward in Miami to build chemistry 
 

 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 11 

 The Titans won't admit it, but Tuesday was a wake-up call, especially for the offense after a spicy joint practice with the 49ers. San Francisco's pass rush was consistently harassing Titans quarterback Cam Ward despite the absence of premier pass rusher Nick Bosa due to knee tendinitis.

 One of the pressures led to Ward climbing the pocket and rushing a throw across the middle that was picked off by 49ers safety  Ji'Ayir Brown . The passing game struggled overall with Ward completing mostly short passes. His longest pass was an 18-yard strike to Carnell Tate on an in-breaking route.

 "If they're going to drop all the way back, we'll check it down, and they've got to come tackle Tyjae Spears and Tony Pollard in space," Ward said. "I don't have to throw the ball 20 yards. I can throw it five yards and let Tyjae and Tony do the rest."

 Both Ward and Mitchell Trubisky made multiple deep passing attempts to Elic Ayomanor , but all four of the passes fell incomplete.

 
 Starting with the first rep of team period, there were multiple skirmishes after plays. Tate took a big hit from Renardo Green along the sideline causing some extracurricular activity. Then Austin Deculus got kicked out minutes into the team period for throwing a punch at a 49ers defensive lineman. Dan Moore Jr . was kicked out after he swung on Osa Odighizuwa after a near sack of Ward. 
 The center and right guard competition took another turn with Fernando Carmona getting early reps again. He was flagged for a false start when Ward tried to use a hard count. Carmona got to protect Ward for back-to-back practices this week. Jackson Slater got reps at center instead of right guard, snapping the ball to Will Levis . Andre James played right guard instead of center. "There's a lot of moving parts," Saleh said after practice. "That right guard's got to get solidified." 
 Saleh said he plans to play everyone in the preseason opener against the 49ers on Thursday. He didn't want to commit to a snap number but said it will be a couple of series for the starters. Ward liked the idea and said he's looking forward to getting into a rhythm in an actual game. 
 

 

 Sunday, Aug. 9 

 Carnell Tate continues to impress in his first NFL training camp.

 One of his standout traits is how effectively Tate is running the full route tree.

 Tate was on the receiving end of three touchdown passes from Cam Ward . The rookie wideout caught a deep pass for a score on a go route with Alontae Taylor being the closest defender. Tate made an impressive catch over Cor'Dale Flott in the corner of the end zone on another play, and he caught a quick out-breaking route for his third score.

 "Tate has an innate ability to attack the ball," Titans receivers coach Greg Lewis said after practice. "He can make contested catches. He has long speed and is really smooth. The guy can also uncover."

 More observations: 

 
 - Joshua Williams was once again in the yellow "non-contact" jersey. Williams had the jersey on in the scrimmage on Friday as well. Titans coach Robert Saleh said Williams is dealing with a pectoral injury that cost him some time during minicamp. Williams was still working in team periods. 
 The center position is still a competition, but it seems like veteran Austin Schlottmann will win the job. Left guard Peter Skoronski said Schlottmann has helped accelerate the learning process for him because of the previous time with Titans offensive coordinator when they were with the Giants. Pat Coogan continues to get early reps but has struggled at times with off-target snaps to Mitchell Trubisky during team periods. 
 Right guard is another position battle to watch. Cordell Volson and Jackson Slater have been the primary competitors, with both getting opportunities to protect Ward during team periods. Rookie Fernando Carmona also got some early reps for the first time on Sunday. 
 

 

 Thursday, Aug. 6 

 The Titans returned to the field after not practicing Wednesday. The pace was noticeably slower to start, but it livened up during team period.

 The offensive line continues to shuffle, especially along the interior, where Cordell Volson and Jackson Slater are the top contenders for right guard while Austin Schlottmann , Pat Coogan and Andre James are battling for the starting center spot.

 All five players have gotten first-team reps in different tandems. Schlottmann has enjoyed going against Jeffery Simmons during team period because "he's one of the best, if not the best interior defenders in the league." Coach Robert Saleh said they're not close to deciding who will start at this point but expects to be closer to a decision leading into the third preseason game.

 Other observations: 

 
 WR  Elic Ayomanor continues to have a solid camp. He caught a deep pass from Cam Ward on a go route in red zone team period to even the score with Alontae Taylor who broke up a pass on the same route earlier in practice. Ward went to Ayomanor again, but the pass fell incomplete. Ayomanor collided with S  Kevin Winston Jr . as they went up for the pass in what Saleh described as a "bang, bang" play. Ayomanor got up favoring his left shoulder after being down for a bit. He went inside for further evaluation. 
 Left tackle  Dan Moore Jr . returned to practice after leaving team period and walking into the building on his own with a trainer Tuesday. Moore took part in team period and got into a small pushing match with linebacker Cody Barton after one of the plays. 
 JC Latham came out during team period towards the end of practice after taking three reps. Reserve tackle Austin Deculus came on in Latham's place and stayed in when the next group of linemen came in. Latham returned for the final team period and had a couple nice blocks on run plays. 
 The Titans will host a Blue/White scrimmage at Nissan Stadium on Friday night. "We'll play move the ball," Saleh said after practice. "We'll play special teams and it'll flow like a game where you'll see first offense against first defense. We have a full scoring system to make it competitive and as game-like as possible. We'll try to get to like 90 plays." 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 4 

 The middle linebacker competition is heating up. James Williams Sr . has strung three consecutive standout days.

 Williams said he's lost about 20 pounds this offseason. The converted safety looked like a defensive back on a jumping one-handed interception of a Mitchell Trubisky pass during team period. Williams got a pass breakup later in practice when Trubisky went to tight end  Kylen Granson  on an out-breaking route.

title: Titans WR Ayomanor standing out above all in training camp
summary: After an inconsistent rookie season, the Tennessee receiver had a laser-focused offseason.
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. --  Tennessee Titans quarterback Mitchell Trubisky dropped back and saw Elic Ayomanor streaking down the field just past cornerback Micah Robinson on the first padded practice of training camp last week.

 Trubisky, whom the Titans signed in the offseason to compete for the backup job behind Cam Ward , launched the pass over 40 yards down the field, and Ayomanor ran underneath it and made the catch in the end zone. He threw the football in the air while letting out a roar.

 That play perfectly encapsulates Ayomanor's approach to his second year. He and Chimere Dike each had four receiving touchdowns as rookies, tied for the team lead. But the Titans brought in reinforcements at the receiver position this offseason -- signing  Wan'Dale Robinson  in free agency to a four-year, $78 million contract and selecting Carnell Tate fourth overall in April's draft.

 

 Ayomanor didn't get bitter. Instead, he chose to get better after posting 41 catches for 515 yards in his first season. Ayomanor's goal during the offseason was to improve his body language and play with a more aggressive mindset.

 "Body language even subconsciously has a lot to do with how you attack each rep," Ayomanor told ESPN. "Starting there has a huge impact on the way you attack each rep, how downhill you are, how aggressive you are in your routes, how aggressive you are in your catching. It all starts with the mindset and the body language. They have a relationship that is very tightly woven together. They're like one and the same almost."

 Ayomanor trained with a receiver training coach in Drew Lieberman in Atlanta. Fellow Titan receivers  K.J. Osborn  and Robinson worked out with Ayomanor as well. Ayomanor said their work days consisted of a little over two hours of route running.

 "The aggressiveness, that's just the way that he approaches playing receiver and the way he makes us approach it," Ayomanor said of Lieberman. "It's a byproduct of just the day in and day out of the sessions and how they go and where you're forced to go and who you're forced to become in order to make it through those training sessions."

 The training sessions and extra work has resulted in Ayomanor making strides in body composition. He still weighs around 206 pounds, but his body fat is now at 6.5%, down from 11% at the end of last season. The improved physique and aggressive approach have helped Ayomanor stand out in what has become a crowded receiver room with the additions of Robinson and Tate along with the return of veteran Calvin Ridley . Veterans Bryce Oliver and Osborn are in the mix as well.

 But it's Ayomanor who has stood out the most so far in training camp. The way he attacks the football has allowed him to make a series of contested catches during training camp. It almost cost Ayomanor last week when he went up for a pass and collided with safety Kevin Winston Jr . in the end zone.

 Ayomanor was down for a moment, then favored his left shoulder as he went inside with a trainer. He returned for the scrimmage Friday and was a full participant in Sunday's practice.

 

 "I love his body language," Trubisky told ESPN. "I think he's super motivated and is going super hard. He brings that juice and energy for our offense. He's just a mismatch problem for a lot of DBs. His speed and strength, his ability to separate at the top and then his downfield ability to get open, he's really impressed me so far.

 "I'm looking for [Ayomanor], and he's getting open. He's making a lot of plays with his offense."

 Ayomanor has managed to turn heads on almost every practice so far in camp, whether it be a back shoulder catch where he goes up and snatches the ball out of the air over a cornerback or making a tough catch in the middle of the field on a dig route.

 "To me, Elic is a star," Ridley said. "The kid's a stud. He's going to continue to get better."

 Ayomanor, standing at 6-foot-2, already checked the box as far as what a receiver is supposed to look like. This year's version of him is even more impressive. There's a higher degree of explosiveness to his routes.

 Ayomanor noted how he wants to run routes with "more forward lean" when asked about offseason improvements during minicamp. That forward lean is something Ayomanor worked to instill into his game while training with Robinson over the summer. He pointed to how Robinson has "good posture often" when he's on the football field.

 "There's really not a phase of the game where you shouldn't be at a forward lean," Ayomanor said during minicamp. "Maybe if you're running like a 40-yard route or you're down the field trying to track the ball, but it's really about having your nose forward, your body forward, staying low in and out of routes especially."

 New Titans coach Robert Saleh praised Ayomanor for working relentlessly during the offseason to set himself up for a successful season. Saleh believes the hard work and preparation is why Ayomanor's confidence is standing out on the football field.

 "When you prepare at his level, both mentally and physically, you feel confident and your body language is going to project that," Saleh said. "He's got great confidence just because he knows he's prepared as well as he can, and he knows he's putting himself in the best position he can be."

 

 Although Ayomanor has gotten off to a good start in camp, the bigger-picture obstacle is for him to be more consistent. Ayomanor flashed at times last season but only caught 13 of the 31 targets that went his way over the final six games. Saleh challenged Ayomanor when asked where he can show growth this season.

 "Everyone can do it once," Saleh said. "The great ones can do it multiple times over time."

 It's safe to say Ayomanor accepts the challenge. He recognizes consistency as an area for improvement and focuses on finding a way to make a difference every time he sets foot on the field.

 Having played at Stanford, Ayomanor is looking forward to returning to the Bay Area when the Titans have a joint practice with the San Francisco 49ers , where Saleh came over from in the offseason after formerly being their defensive coordinator, followed by the preseason opener at Levi's Stadium on Thursday.

 "I'm excited to go back there and put in some work," Ayomanor said. "Obviously, coach Saleh came from San Francisco, so we need to go send a message."
